taking-notes/speaker-attribution.title: Speaker labels
taking-notes/speaker-attribution.description: How speech is attributed to each speaker, what can and cannot be identified, and how to think about telling participants.
taking-notes/speaker-attribution.html:
Speaker labels show the name of the participant who said something above each passage of the transcript. By default speech is only split into “me” and “them”, but with speaker labels set up, the display name from the meeting tool is attached as the name. This helps when reading back the record of a meeting with many participants, or checking whose task something was agreed to be. This article covers how it works, which meeting tools are supported, the limits of identification, and how the recorded names are handled.

Prerequisites

Speaker labels are a desktop app (macOS / Windows) feature and work only while transcription is running. Names are never added retrospectively to a transcript recorded before you set it up. The setup required differs by meeting tool.

#How speaker labels work

Speaker labels read the participant names shown on the meeting tool's screen, along with the indicator showing who is currently speaking, and match them against each section of the transcript. There is no processing that infers who someone is from voiceprints or audio characteristics. What the meeting tool displays therefore determines the result directly.

How that reading is done differs by meeting tool: Google Meet uses a browser extension, Zoom uses macOS accessibility permissions. In neither case do speaker labels record any new audio or video. Audio capture for transcription happens within the scope described in How transcription works.

#Supported meeting tools and how to set them up

Meeting tool Supported OS What you need Setup steps
Google Meet (Chrome or a Chromium-based browser) macOS / Windows the {{PRODUCT}} browser extension Using speaker labels in Google Meet
Zoom (the Zoom Workplace desktop app) macOS only macOS accessibility permission Using speaker labels in Zoom
Microsoft Teams, Zoom in a browser (web client) — not supported at this time the transcript shows “me” and “them”

To deploy across company machines, Setting up speaker labels across your organisation (for admins) covers distributing the browser extension in bulk and pre-granting permissions through MDM.

#What to do during the meeting

Once set up, nothing special is needed during the meeting. Join as usual and start transcription, and participant names appear in the transcript panel.

You do still have to start transcription separately from speaker labels. {{PRODUCT}} transcribes only when you open a note from a notification or an event, or create a new note. Setting up speaker labels does not by itself cause recording to start as you join a meeting. The conditions for starting are covered in How transcription works.

#What can and cannot be identified

Situation How speaker labels behave
Each participant joins individually from their own machine The name shown in the meeting tool is used as-is.
Several people join from one machine in a meeting room Several people speaking through the same machine cannot be told apart individually.
Audio other than the meeting is playing on the computer It may appear in the transcript, but no speaker name is attached.
Several people speak at once Some speech may not be attributed to the right speaker.
A participant uses a display name that is not their real name That display name becomes the speaker name.

Where speaker labels are unavailable or not set up, the transcript is split into “me” and “them”. This corresponds to the distinction between audio from your microphone and system audio (what your computer is playing). Even then, notes are often produced by inferring who spoke from the flow of the conversation and how people address each other; if a name is wrong you can rewrite it directly in the note or tell chat to correct it.

Correcting a wrong name

Where a speaker name is wrong you can edit that part of the note directly. If the same error runs through the whole transcript, telling chat to “replace the speaker name X with Y” fixes them all at once. On recognition accuracy for technical terms and company names, see also Customising transcription.

#Speaker labels and personal information

Speaker names may constitute personal information

The name recorded as a speaker label is the participant's display name in the meeting tool. Where a real name is used as the display name, the speaker name left in the transcript may constitute personal information linked to what was said. Under the Act on the Protection of Personal Information, where personal information is acquired through recording or transcription, the purpose of use must be promptly notified to the individual or made public, unless it has been published in advance. There is no general provision in Japanese law requiring everyone's consent for a participant to record a meeting, but given that the record also captures who said what, telling people at the start of the meeting what the recording is for and how long it is kept makes problems less likely later. The reasoning and sample wording are covered in How far you can rely on AI meeting notes (a guide for teams).

Letting participants know that {{PRODUCT}} is in use is the job of the features described in About telling people you are recording, not of speaker labels. If you want a notice shown during the meeting, set that up instead.

#Turning speaker labels off

If you do not want speaker labels, remove the setting used to read them. In Google Meet, delete or disable the browser extension; in Zoom, switch off the macOS accessibility permission. The transcript then goes back to showing “me” and “them”. For how to exclude particular departments across an organisation, see Setting up speaker labels across your organisation (for admins).

#If something is not working

Q. I set it up but no speaker names appear

A. First check the meeting was held in a supported meeting tool: Google Meet requires a supported browser, Zoom requires the macOS desktop app. Then check that the relevant row under Settings > Preferences > Speaker labels is set to enabled. Detailed steps are in Using speaker labels in Google Meet and Using speaker labels in Zoom.

Q. Can I add names to a past transcript?

A. No. Speaker labels work only while recording, so they do not apply to transcripts created before you set them up. For past notes, add the speaker names in the note yourself or ask chat to tidy it up.

Q. Only some passages have names

A. This happens where the meeting tool was not clearly indicating who was speaking at that moment, or where several people were speaking from a shared machine in a meeting room. Passages containing audio from outside the meeting also get no name.

#Related articles

How transcription worksWhen and what audio is captured→Customising transcriptionRegistering terminology and display settings→About telling people you are recordingThe notice shown when recording starts, and how to tell people→Transcription problemsWhat to do when audio is not captured→

taking-notes/speaker-attribution-for-ent.title: Setting up speaker labels across your organisation (for admins)
taking-notes/speaker-attribution-for-ent.description: How to roll out speaker labels on the Enterprise plan, the permissions needed, and what to tell people at deployment.
taking-notes/speaker-attribution-for-ent.html:
Speaker labels can be made available without each member of staff setting them up individually. These are the steps for IT. They cover distributing the browser extension in bulk, pre-granting macOS accessibility permission, and the internal announcement that goes with the rollout. To set this up for your own account only, see the per-tool steps in Speaker labels.

Enterprise plan

What you need

Distributing for Google Meet requires administrator rights in the Google Admin console; pre-granting for Zoom (macOS) requires administrative rights in the MDM the Macs are enrolled in. The browser extension and accessibility permission you distribute are also used by the transparency features, so if you have already rolled those out, the distribution work in this article may be unnecessary.

#The rollout at a glance

What you need to distribute depends on the combination of meeting tool and operating system.

Meeting tool macOS Windows What to distribute
Google Meet supported supported the {{PRODUCT}} browser extension (distributed from the Google Admin console)
Zoom supported not supported macOS accessibility permission (pre-granted through MDM)

Once distribution is complete, ask each member of staff to open Settings > Preferences > Speaker labels in the desktop app and confirm that the row for the meeting tool they use shows enabled. Wording for that request is under “What to ask staff to do afterwards”.

#Decisions to make before you start

For a company-wide rollout in a Japanese IT department, the announcement and the support arrangements usually take more time than the distribution work itself. We recommend settling at least these four points before you begin.

  1. Scope: distribute to everyone, or only to particular departments or sites? If limiting it, decide whether to divide by organisational unit or by Google group.
  2. Timing and channel of the announcement: how many working days before the rollout, and through which channel (company-wide email, intranet, a general chat channel)?
  3. Support contact: will the IT help desk take first-line enquiries, or will you point people at {{PRODUCT}} support? If you set up an internal contact, share “Likely questions and answers” with them in advance.
  4. Consistency with internal rules on meeting records: enabling speaker labels means who said what is kept on record. If you have internal rules on meeting records, check this does not contradict them.

The name recorded as a speaker label is the participant's display name in the meeting tool. Where a real name is used, that name may constitute personal information linked to what was said; the point, and what the Act on the Protection of Personal Information requires in that case, are set out under “Speaker labels and personal information” in Speaker labels. Notifying staff of the purpose of use, the notice given at the start of meetings with external attendees, and draft wording for internal rules are covered in How far you can rely on AI meeting notes (a guide for teams), so read that before drafting your announcement.

#Google Meet: distributing the browser extension

Speaker labels in Google Meet work through the {{PRODUCT}} browser extension. The extension has to be installed in the browser profile each member of staff uses for Google Meet.

You can distribute it automatically to the whole organisation from the Google Admin console, or narrow the audience using organisational units (OUs) or Google groups.

#Adding the extension

  1. 1

    Sign in to the Google Admin console

    Google Admin console with an administrator account.

  2. 2

    Open the apps and extensions settings

    Devices > Chrome > Apps & extensions > Users & browsers.

  3. 3

    Add from the Chrome Web Store

    Choose the + (plus) button at the bottom right, then Add from Chrome Web Store.

  4. 4

    Search by extension ID

    Choose Search by ID at the top right and paste the {{PRODUCT}} extension ID.

  5. 5

    Add the extension

    Select to add the extension.

  6. 6

    Set the installation policy

    Force install, or Force install + pin to browser toolbar. Pinning it to the toolbar makes it easier for staff to see that the extension is present.

About the extension ID

Before publishing, replace this with a link to the {{PRODUCT}} extension's page on the Chrome Web Store and the real extension ID. No values are given in this article.

#Narrowing who receives it

By default the setting applies to the whole organisation. To distribute only to particular departments, sites or teams, use one of the following.

Option 1: narrow by organisational unit (OU)

Organisational units group users by department, site and so on, so that different policies can be applied to each.

  1. In the Google Admin console, open Directory > Organisational units.
  2. If there is no organisational unit for the group in question yet, create one.
  3. Move the relevant users into that organisational unit.
  4. Devices > Chrome > Apps & extensions > Users & browsers.
  5. In the left sidebar, select the organisational unit rather than the top-level organisation.
  6. Add and configure the {{PRODUCT}} extension against that organisational unit. It will be installed only for users in it.
Option 2: narrow by Google group

Where restructuring organisational units is not practical, you can target distribution using a Google group. This suits teams that span several organisational units, such as a cross-site project.

  1. In the Google Admin console, open Directory > Groups.
  2. Create a new group containing the users you want to distribute to, or use an existing one.
  3. Devices > Chrome > Apps & extensions > Users & browsers.
  4. In the left sidebar, search for and select the group.
  5. Add and configure the {{PRODUCT}} extension against that group. It will be installed only for its members.
The two options can be combined

You might, for example, force install for an organisational unit representing a particular site while allowing installation for a Google group representing a cross-site project team. For a phased rollout, the safe approach is to target only the IT department's organisational unit first, confirm the behaviour, and widen from there.

Browser support limits

The extension works in Google Chrome and supported Chromium-based browsers (Microsoft Edge, Arc, Brave). Force install from the Google Admin console applies to Google Chrome. Staff using another supported browser have to install it from the Chrome Web Store themselves. If browsers other than Chrome are in use internally, check what people actually use before you start.

The setup steps for each member of staff after distribution are in Using speaker labels in Google Meet.

#Zoom: pre-granting accessibility permission

Speaker labels in Zoom use the Zoom Workplace desktop app together with macOS accessibility permission. No browser extension is involved. Support differs by operating system.

Users can grant the permission themselves, but on a managed Mac you can pre-grant it through MDM so that no permission prompt is shown to the user. The steps are under “Pre-granting through MDM” below.

Speaker labels in Zoom do not support Windows at this time. In Zoom meetings held by staff on Windows, the transcript shows “me” and “them”. Google Meet speaker labels do work on Windows through the browser extension described above, so in Windows-centric departments you will only need the Google Meet distribution.

What the permission covers — that {{PRODUCT}} uses it to read the participant names and speaking indicator shown on Zoom's screen, and not to record the screen or audio or to access the camera or microphone — is explained under “About the accessibility permission” in Using speaker labels in Zoom. This comes up often when explaining the rollout internally, so a sentence about it in your announcement will reduce enquiries.

#Pre-granting through MDM

Accessibility permission can be pre-granted on managed devices by distributing a PPPC (Privacy Preferences Policy Control) configuration profile. The profile identifies the {{PRODUCT}} app by its signing details (team ID and bundle ID) and grants it access to the accessibility service.

Below is an example .mobileconfig you can use as-is or adapt to your environment.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
    <key>PayloadContent</key>
    <array>
        <dict>
            <key>PayloadDescription</key>
            <string>Grants the macOS accessibility permission used to read speaker information from Zoom for speaker labels.</string>
            <key>PayloadDisplayName</key>
            <string>Privacy Preferences Policy Control</string>
            <key>PayloadIdentifier</key>
            <string>〔reverse-domain identifier〕.allow-accessibility.pppc</string>
            <key>PayloadOrganization</key>
            <string>{{COMPANY}}</string>
            <key>PayloadType</key>
            <string>com.apple.TCC.configuration-profile-policy</string>
            <key>PayloadUUID</key>
            <string>〔generated UUID〕</string>
            <key>PayloadVersion</key>
            <integer>1</integer>
            <key>Services</key>
            <dict>
                <key>Accessibility</key>
                <array>
                    <dict>
                        <key>Allowed</key>
                        <integer>1</integer>
                        <key>CodeRequirement</key>
                        <string>identifier "〔bundle ID〕" and anchor apple generic and certificate 1[field.1.2.840.113635.100.6.2.6] /* exists */ and certificate leaf[field.1.2.840.113635.100.6.1.13] /* exists */ and certificate leaf[subject.OU] = 〔team ID〕</string>
                        <key>Comment</key>
                        <string></string>
                        <key>Identifier</key>
                        <string>〔bundle ID〕</string>
                        <key>IdentifierType</key>
                        <string>bundleID</string>
                        <key>StaticCode</key>
                        <integer>0</integer>
                    </dict>
                </array>
            </dict>
        </dict>
    </array>
    <key>PayloadDescription</key>
    <string>Grants the macOS accessibility permission used to read speaker information from Zoom for speaker labels.</string>
    <key>PayloadDisplayName</key>
    <string>Allow accessibility permission (speaker labels)</string>
    <key>PayloadIdentifier</key>
    <string>〔reverse-domain identifier〕.allow-accessibility</string>
    <key>PayloadOrganization</key>
    <string>{{COMPANY}}</string>
    <key>PayloadScope</key>
    <string>System</string>
    <key>PayloadType</key>
    <string>Configuration</string>
    <key>PayloadUUID</key>
    <string>〔generated UUID〕</string>
    <key>PayloadVersion</key>
    <integer>1</integer>
</dict>
</plist>
Values to fill in at 〔　〕

〔bundle ID〕 and 〔team ID〕 take the signing details of the {{PRODUCT}} desktop app (the app's bundle identifier and the team identifier on the signing certificate). If these two values do not match the actual signature, the profile will distribute but the permission will not be granted. You can obtain the values from {{SUPPORT_EMAIL}}.〔generated UUID〕 takes a different generated UUID in each of the two places, and 〔reverse-domain identifier〕 takes your own domain reversed (for example jp.example.it).

Distribute PPPC profiles through MDM

A PPPC profile has to be distributed from the MDM the device is enrolled in (Jamf, Microsoft Intune, Kandji, Mosyle, Cisco Meraki and so on). If the profile is installed manually it appears under System Settings > General > Device Management but the permission is not granted. Depending on your macOS version, that screen may be called “Profiles” in System Preferences.

The setup steps for each member of staff after distribution are in Using speaker labels in Zoom.

#What to ask staff to do afterwards

Once you have distributed the extension or the accessibility permission, ask staff to check the following.

  1. Open the desktop app (and confirm it has updated to the latest version).
  2. Settings > Preferences > Speaker labels.
  3. Confirm the row for the meeting tool they use shows enabled. - Google Meet: connects automatically once the extension is installed in the browser profile. - Zoom: even with accessibility permission pre-granted through MDM, choosing Set up on the Zoom row may still be required the first time.

If a row will not connect, point people to the troubleshooting in Using speaker labels in Google Meet and Using speaker labels in Zoom.

What to check on the distribution side
  • In the Google Admin console, the extension is assigned as force install to the target organisational unit or group
  • In the MDM console, the PPPC configuration profile shows as distributed to the target Macs
  • On a test machine, the relevant row under Settings > Preferences > Speaker labels shows enabled, and participant names appear in the transcript of a test meeting

#Sample internal announcements

A company-wide notice to send a few working days before the rollout, and a short chat post for the day itself. Fill in 〔date〕 with the rollout date, 〔help desk contact〕 with your internal support contact, 〔meeting recording and transcription policy〕 with the name of the relevant internal policy, and 〔intranet URL〕 with the URL of your guidance page.

#Company-wide email (three working days before rollout)

Subject: [Notice] Speaker names in meeting notes will be enabled from 〔date〕 (IT Department)

To all staff

Hello, this is the IT Department.

From 〔date〕, we are enabling “speaker labels” company-wide in the meeting notes tool 〔{{PRODUCT}}〕, which show the name of the person speaking in the transcript. We will also distribute the browser extension and device permission required, automatically, from our side.

■ What changes In meeting transcripts, passages that until now showed only “me” and “them” will show the display name from the meeting tool. This makes it easier to see who said what when reading minutes later.

■ What we ask you to do From 〔date〕, open “Settings > Preferences > Speaker labels” in the app and check that the row for the meeting tool you use shows “enabled”. If nothing changes, update the app to the latest version and check again.

■ What we are distributing - If you use Google Meet: the browser extension (installed into Chrome automatically) - If you use Zoom on a Mac: accessibility permission (configured automatically through device management) * This permission is used to read the participant names shown on Zoom's screen. It is not used to record the screen or audio, or to access the camera or microphone.

■ About how records are handled Please follow 〔meeting recording and transcription policy〕 on the extent to which meetings may be recorded and transcribed. In meetings with external attendees, please continue to say at the start that the meeting is being recorded.

If you have any questions, please contact 〔help desk contact〕.

IT Department

#Chat post (on the day)

“Speaker labels” are now enabled in meeting notes, so the name of the person speaking appears in transcripts. Please check under “Settings > Preferences > Speaker labels” that the meeting tool you use shows “enabled”. If it does not display correctly, contact 〔help desk contact〕. Full details are at 〔intranet URL〕.

#Likely questions and answers

Suggested answers for a help desk taking first-line enquiries.

Enquiry Key points of the answer
“An extension appeared without my doing anything — what is it?” Explain that IT distributed it so that speaker names appear in meeting notes, and that it does not capture meeting audio or video.
“What is the accessibility permission used for?” Explain that it is used solely to read the participant names and speaking indicator shown on Zoom's screen, and not for screen recording, audio recording, the camera or the microphone.
“I use a browser other than Chrome” Explain that force install applies only to Chrome, and that Edge, Arc and Brave require manual installation.
“Names do not appear in Zoom on Windows” Explain that Windows is not supported at this time. Google Meet does work on Windows.
“I want to add names to past minutes” Explain that speaker labels work only while recording, so they do not apply to past transcripts.
“I do not want my name recorded” Decide the response based on your internal policy on meeting records. Disabling the permission or extension on an individual's machine stops speaker labels working, but agree in advance how you want to handle this in practice.
“Someone outside the company asked about the recording” Point to the sample wording for a notice at the start of a meeting and the explanation of what is retained.How far you can rely on AI meeting notes (a guide for teams) is worth making available from your intranet too, so people can check quickly.

#Frequently asked questions

Q. Does the browser extension access meeting content?

A. For speaker labels, what the extension reads is the participant names and speaking indicator in Google Meet. It does not access meeting audio, video or transcripts. If your workspace also uses the Google Meet transparency features, the same extension is used to send the automatic notice to meeting chat.

Q. Is separate distribution needed for the transparency features?

A. The browser extension and macOS accessibility permission are common to speaker labels and the transparency features. If you have distributed them for speaker labels, the prerequisites for the transparency features are already met. The transparency features do, however, have their own workspace-side settings, and in Google Meet a setting for pinning the notice in meeting chat. For details see Making recording notices a rule in your organisation (for admins).

Q. Can I stop particular departments from using speaker labels?

A. For Google Meet, you can create a scope that receives nothing by narrowing extension distribution by organisational unit or Google group. For Zoom, limit the scope of the profile granting accessibility permission on the MDM side. In either case, transcripts for staff outside the scope show “me” and “them”.

They cover distributing the browser extension in bulk, pre-granting macOS accessibility permission, and the internal announcement that goes with the rollout. To set this up for your own account only, see the per-tool steps in Speaker labels . Enterprise plan What you need Distributing for Google Meet requires administrator rights in the Google Admin console; pre-granting for Zoom (macOS) requires administrative rights in the MDM the Macs are enrolled in. The browser extension and accessibility permission you distribute are also used by the transparency features , so if you have already rolled those out, the distribution work in this article may be unnecessary. # The rollout at a glance What you need to distribute depends on the combination of meeting tool and operating system. Meeting tool macOS Windows What to distribute Google Meet supported supported the {{PRODUCT}} browser extension (distributed from the Google Admin console) Zoom supported not supported macOS accessibility permission (pre-granted through MDM) Once distribution is complete, ask each member of staff to open Settings > Preferences > Speaker labels in the desktop app and confirm that the row for the meeting tool they use shows enabled . Wording for that request is under “What to ask staff to do afterwards”. # Decisions to make before you start For a company-wide rollout in a Japanese IT department, the announcement and the support arrangements usually take more time than the distribution work itself. We recommend settling at least these four points before you begin. Scope : distribute to everyone, or only to particular departments or sites? If limiting it, decide whether to divide by organisational unit or by Google group. Timing and channel of the announcement : how many working days before the rollout, and through which channel (company-wide email, intranet, a general chat channel)? Support contact : will the IT help desk take first-line enquiries, or will you point people at {{PRODUCT}} support? If you set up an internal contact, share “Likely questions and answers” with them in advance. Consistency with internal rules on meeting records : enabling speaker labels means who said what is kept on record. If you have internal rules on meeting records, check this does not contradict them. The name recorded as a speaker label is the participant's display name in the meeting tool. Where a real name is used, that name may constitute personal information linked to what was said; the point, and what the Act on the Protection of Personal Information requires in that case, are set out under “Speaker labels and personal information” in Speaker labels . Notifying staff of the purpose of use, the notice given at the start of meetings with external attendees, and draft wording for internal rules are covered in How far you can rely on AI meeting notes (a guide for teams) , so read that before drafting your announcement. # Google Meet: distributing the browser extension Speaker labels in Google Meet work through the {{PRODUCT}} browser extension. The extension has to be installed in the browser profile each member of staff uses for Google Meet. You can distribute it automatically to the whole organisation from the Google Admin console, or narrow the audience using organisational units (OUs) or Google groups. # Adding the extension 1 Sign in to the Google Admin console Google Admin console with an administrator account. 2 Open the apps and extensions settings Devices > Chrome > Apps & extensions > Users & browsers . 3 Add from the Chrome Web Store Choose the + (plus) button at the bottom right, then Add from Chrome Web Store . 4 Search by extension ID Choose Search by ID at the top right and paste the {{PRODUCT}} extension ID. 5 Add the extension Select to add the extension. 6 Set the installation policy Force install , or Force install + pin to browser toolbar . Pinning it to the toolbar makes it easier for staff to see that the extension is present. About the extension ID Before publishing, replace this with a link to the {{PRODUCT}} extension's page on the Chrome Web Store and the real extension ID. No values are given in this article. Figure Screenshot: the “Apps & extensions” screen in the Google Admin console Showing the “Add from Chrome Web Store” button and the search-by-ID field. # Narrowing who receives it By default the setting applies to the whole organisation. To distribute only to particular departments, sites or teams, use one of the following. Option 1: narrow by organisational unit (OU) Organisational units group users by department, site and so on, so that different policies can be applied to each. In the Google Admin console, open Directory > Organisational units . If there is no organisational unit for the group in question yet, create one. Move the relevant users into that organisational unit. Devices > Chrome > Apps & extensions > Users & browsers . In the left sidebar, select the organisational unit rather than the top-level organisation. Add and configure the {{PRODUCT}} extension against that organisational unit. It will be installed only for users in it. Option 2: narrow by Google group Where restructuring organisational units is not practical, you can target distribution using a Google group. This suits teams that span several organisational units, such as a cross-site project. In the Google Admin console, open Directory > Groups . Create a new group containing the users you want to distribute to, or use an existing one. Devices > Chrome > Apps & extensions > Users & browsers . In the left sidebar, search for and select the group . Add and configure the {{PRODUCT}} extension against that group. It will be installed only for its members. The two options can be combined You might, for example, force install for an organisational unit representing a particular site while allowing installation for a Google group representing a cross-site project team. taking-notes/speaker-attribution-google-.html:
With speaker labels enabled for Google Meet, each passage of the transcript is tagged with the display name from Google Meet. Setting this up requires the browser extension. This article covers installation, checking it works, and what to do when it does not. How it works and the limits of identification are covered in Speaker labels.

Supported environments

Speaker labels for Google Meet are available in the desktop app on macOS and Windows. The {{PRODUCT}} browser extension (free) is required.

#What you need first

  • the macOS or Windows desktop app (updated to the latest version)
  • a Google Meet meeting opened in a supported browser — Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Arc, Brave, or another Chrome- or Chromium-based browser
  • the {{PRODUCT}} browser extension, installed in the browser profile you use for Google Meet

Identification happens through the browser extension. While {{PRODUCT}} is transcribing a Google Meet meeting, the extension reads the participant names and speaking indicator shown on Google Meet's screen and matches them against each section of the transcript. There is no processing that infers who someone is from voiceprints or audio characteristics, and the extension records no audio or video.

#Setup steps

  1. 1

    Open the desktop app

    Check it has updated to the latest version. If the display does not refresh, press Cmd+R on macOS or Ctrl+R on Windows to reload manually.

  2. 2

    Open the speaker labels setting

    Settings > Preferences and choose Speaker labels under “Features”.

  3. 3

    Open the extension page

    Google Meet row, choose Install browser extension. The {{PRODUCT}} extension's page on the Chrome Web Store opens in your browser.

  4. 4

    Add it to the profile you use for Google Meet

    Extensions are installed per browser profile. If the browser asks you to choose or switch profile, select the profile you use for Google Meet before installing.

  5. 5

    Check the connection

    Go back to {{PRODUCT}}. Once the extension is detected, the Google Meet row changes to enabled. Speaker labels work from the moment it connects; there is no separate on/off switch.

Checking setup worked
  • Settings > Preferences > Speaker labels shows the Google Meet row as enabled
  • the extension is present in the browser profile you open Google Meet with
  • participant display names appear in the transcript of a meeting recorded after setup
About where the extension is published

Before publishing, replace this with a link to the {{PRODUCT}} extension's page on the Chrome Web Store and the real extension ID.

#Using it in a meeting

Start a Google Meet meeting in a supported browser and begin transcribing in {{PRODUCT}} as usual. Where Google Meet can identify who is speaking, that participant's display name appears above their speech in the transcript. Your own speech is tagged with the display name you use in Google Meet.

Because speaker labels work only while transcription is running, names are never added retrospectively to a transcript recorded before setup. What can be identified, and how to think about telling participants, are covered in Speaker labels.

#If something is not working

Q. I cannot find “Speaker labels” in settings

A. “Speaker labels” is under “Features” in Settings > Preferences. If it is not shown there, check the following in order.

  1. Check that {{PRODUCT}} has updated to the latest version.
  2. Press Cmd+R on macOS or Ctrl+R on Windows to reload the screen.
  3. Open Settings > Preferences again.
Q. I installed the extension but it still says “not connected”

A. Check the following in order.

  1. Check the desktop app is running. The extension is only detected while the app is running.
  2. Check which browser profile you installed the extension in. Extensions are installed per profile.
  3. Switch to that profile and open a Google Meet page.
  4. Settings > Preferences > Speaker labels and wait for the status to change to enabled.
  5. If it still shows as not connected, quit {{PRODUCT}} and the browser, then open them again and retry.

If you use a browser managed by your company, extension installation may be restricted by your administrator. In that case, ask IT to distribute it using the steps in Setting up speaker labels across your organisation (for admins).

Q. Transcription works but no speaker names appear

A. Check the following.

  • The meeting was held in Google Meet, opened in a supported browser. Speaker labels do not work in other meeting tools or unsupported browsers.
  • Settings > Preferences > Speaker labels shows the Google Meet row as enabled.
  • That transcript was recorded after you set speaker labels up.

Some passages may have no speaker name — for example where several people are speaking from a shared machine in a meeting room. The situations are listed under “What can and cannot be identified” in Speaker labels.

Q. The speaker name shown is wrong

A. Speaker labels use the participant name Google Meet displays, as-is. If a participant has set a display name that is not their real name, that display name becomes the speaker name. Correct a wrong name by editing the note directly, or tell chat to replace it.

taking-notes/speaker-attribution-zoom.html:
With speaker labels enabled for Zoom, each passage of the transcript is tagged with the display name from Zoom. Setting this up requires macOS accessibility permission. This article covers granting the permission, checking it works, and what to do when it does not. How it works and the limits of identification are covered in Speaker labels.

What you need

Three things: the macOS desktop app (updated to the latest version), a meeting you have joined in the Zoom Workplace desktop app, and macOS accessibility permission granted to {{PRODUCT}}. No browser extension is required.

#Supported environments

This covers meetings joined in the Zoom Workplace desktop app. With accessibility permission granted to {{PRODUCT}}, it reads the participant names and speaking indicator shown on Zoom's screen and matches them against each section of the transcript. There is no processing that infers who someone is from voiceprints or audio characteristics. If you use a Mac managed by your company, IT can pre-grant the permission through MDM. The steps are in Setting up speaker labels across your organisation (for admins).

Speaker labels in Zoom do not support Windows at this time. Transcribing a Zoom meeting on Windows gives you “me” and “them”. To show speaker names on Windows, you can use speaker labels via the browser extension in Google Meet meetings. The steps are in Using speaker labels in Google Meet.

Zoom in a browser (the web client) is not supported on any operating system. And because speaker labels work only while transcription is running, names are never added retrospectively to a transcript recorded before setup.

#Setup steps (macOS)

The app guides you through granting the permission.

  1. 1

    Open the desktop app

    Check it has updated to the latest version. If the display does not refresh, press Cmd+R to reload manually.

  2. 2

    Open the speaker labels setting

    Settings > Preferences and choose Speaker labels under “Features”.

  3. 3

    Start setup on the Zoom row

    Zoom row, choose Set up.

  4. 4

    Grant accessibility permission

    The macOS settings screen opens; switch on accessibility access for {{PRODUCT}}.

  5. 5

    Check the connection

    Go back to {{PRODUCT}}. Once it can read what it needs from Zoom, the Zoom row changes to enabled. There is no separate on/off switch for Zoom speaker labels.

Checking setup worked
  • System Settings > Privacy & Security > Accessibility shows the switch for {{PRODUCT}} turned on
  • Settings > Preferences > Speaker labels shows the Zoom row as enabled
  • participant display names appear in the transcript of a Zoom meeting recorded after setup

#About the accessibility permission

Accessibility is the macOS permission that allows one app to read and operate items on another app's screen. For Zoom speaker labels, it is used to read the participant names and speaking indicator shown in the Zoom desktop app.

This permission is never used to record the screen or audio, or to access the camera or microphone. Audio capture for transcription happens separately. For details see How transcription works.

You can check the permission's status under System Settings > Privacy & Security > Accessibility. Depending on your macOS version this screen may be called System Preferences and the items arranged differently. If the names do not match, search for “Accessibility” in the settings search field.

Revoking the permission stops speaker labels

Switching accessibility permission off stops Zoom speaker labels working, and the transcript goes back to showing “me” and “them”. If you do not want speaker labels, switch this permission off.

#Using it in a meeting

Start a meeting in the Zoom Workplace desktop app and begin transcribing in {{PRODUCT}} as usual. Where Zoom can identify who is speaking, that participant's Zoom display name appears above their speech in the transcript. Your own speech continues to show as “me”.

What can be identified, and how to think about telling participants, are covered in Speaker labels.

#If something is not working

Q. I cannot find “Speaker labels” in settings

A. Zoom speaker labels are a macOS-only feature at this time. First open Settings > Preferences > Speaker labels and check. If it is not shown, check that {{PRODUCT}} has updated to the latest version, and if necessary get the latest version from {{DOMAIN}} and reinstall.

Q. I granted accessibility but it still says “Set up”

A. Check the following in order.

  1. System Settings > Privacy & Security > Accessibility. Depending on your macOS version this may be called System Preferences.
  2. Check that {{PRODUCT}} is in the list and its switch is on.
  3. Go back to {{PRODUCT}} and reopen Settings > Preferences > Speaker labels.
  4. Zoom row does not change to enabled, quit {{PRODUCT}} completely and start it again.

If it is switched on in the list but still not recognised, switch it off and on again, then reopen {{PRODUCT}}. macOS sometimes fails to refresh the permission registration.

Q. Transcription works but no speaker names appear

A. Check the following.

  • The meeting was held in the Zoom Workplace desktop app. Speaker labels do not work in Zoom in a browser.
  • Settings > Preferences > Speaker labels shows the Zoom row as enabled.
  • {{PRODUCT}} was running and transcribing during the Zoom meeting.
  • That transcript was recorded after you set speaker labels up.

Some passages may have no speaker name — for example where several people join from a shared machine in a meeting room. The situations are listed under “What can and cannot be identified” in Speaker labels.

Q. The speaker name shown is wrong

A. Speaker labels use the participant name Zoom displays, as-is. If a participant has set a display name that is not their real name, that display name becomes the speaker name. Correct a wrong name by editing the note directly, or tell chat to replace it.

taking-notes/writing-your-own-notes.title: Writing your own notes
taking-notes/writing-your-own-notes.description: How to write your own notes during a meeting, with headings, bullet points and images.
taking-notes/writing-your-own-notes.html:
You can write notes in your own words while the meeting is going on. What you write here is treated as material for the summary note produced afterwards, and influences what it concentrates on. Recording the reasoning behind a decision, or a concern you noticed at the time — things a transcript alone does not capture — makes the note far more useful when you read it back.

AI-enhanced notesHow your notes feed into the summary→Shape your notes with templatesSpecifying the output structure in advance→

#Where to write

When a meeting starts, an input field for notes appears on the note screen. It is blank, with no set format or headings, so write in whatever order things occur to you. Even a single line marking something you want to be sure appears in the minutes changes how it is treated in the summary.

Typos and abbreviations are fine as they are

Typos, abbreviations only your company would understand, and sentences you never finished are all interpreted from context when the summary is generated. Rather than tidying as you go, prioritise getting the key points down without breaking the flow of the meeting.

#Using headings and formatting

If you want to specify the structure too, basic Markdown works.

Purpose How to type it
Heading Type # followed by a space at the start of the line (for example # Agenda, # Decisions)
Bullet point Type - or * at the start of the line
Checkbox [] at the start of the line
Bold **important** — type it like this
Italic *note* — type it like this

The same formatting is available from the keyboard.

  • Bold: CMD + B
  • Italic: CMD + I
  • Underline: CMD + U
  • Bold: Ctrl + B
  • Italic: Ctrl + I
  • Underline: Ctrl + U

Headings and bullet points also influence the structure of the final summary note. Setting up headings such as “Agenda”, “Decisions” and “Next actions” at the start of a meeting makes a summary that follows those divisions more likely.

If you want the same structure for every meeting, setting up a template is more reliable than typing the headings out each time.

#Examples of what to write

For notes during a live meeting, this level of detail is enough.

  • # Discussion points with “when the price change takes effect” underneath
  • “They want April; we are ready from June onwards”
  • [] with “resubmit the quote (by Friday this week)”

There is no need to write full sentences; they are turned into prose when the summary is generated.

#Pasting images

Visual material such as a diagram shared on screen during the meeting, or a photo of a whiteboard, can go into your notes too. Drag and drop a JPEG or PNG into the note input field, or copy and paste it.

Images are kept as material that fills in the context of the meeting. They are not converted into summary text, so adding a one-line description of the point of the diagram helps when you read it back later.

#You do not have to write anything

Writing notes steers the summary, but it is not required. If you write nothing, the summary is produced from the transcript and the calendar event alone. For meetings where you want to concentrate on the conversation, or where you are doing most of the talking, it is fine to take no notes at all.

If you realise after the meeting that you want a particular point covered more fully, you can add to your notes and then regenerate. The steps for regenerating are in AI-enhanced notes.

#If something is not working

  • The note input field does not appear: check that a meeting note is open. You cannot write notes from the home screen.
  • What I wrote is not reflected in the summary: after adding to your notes, the note has to be regenerated.
  • I cannot paste an image: JPEG and PNG are supported. For other formats, save the image again in a supported format and then paste it.

taking-notes/transcription.title: How transcription works
taking-notes/transcription.description: What starts and stops transcription, which audio is captured, and how to improve accuracy.
taking-notes/transcription.html:
{{PRODUCT}} transcribes meeting audio and uses that text to produce AI-enhanced notes. Transcription does not start on its own; it is triggered by you opening a note. This article explains when transcription starts and stops, which audio is captured, what you can do to improve accuracy, and how to get the finished text out.

AI-enhanced notesHow a summary note is produced from the transcript→Speaker labelsShowing who said what in the text→Customising transcriptionLanguage and proper noun (jargon) settings→Transcription problemsWhat to check when audio is not picked up→
What transcription requires

Transcription requires the desktop app (macOS / Windows). The web version only views and edits notes that already exist; it cannot record or transcribe. Install the desktop app on the computer you use for meetings and be signed in when you join.

#The four things that start transcription

{{PRODUCT}} starts capturing audio and transcribing only when you do one of the following. It never starts by itself.

  1. Click the notification. Clicking the notification shown before a meeting starts opens the video meeting URL and, at the same time, opens that meeting's note and begins transcribing.
  2. Open an event whose start time has passed, from the home screen. Opening a meeting from the home screen whose start time has already passed begins transcription at that moment.
  3. Click [+ New note]. This opens a new note from the button at the top right. Use this for an unplanned discussion that is not in your calendar.
  4. Leave the note for an upcoming event open. If you have the note for a meeting that is about to start already open, transcription begins automatically when the calendar start time arrives.

Put the other way round, a meeting whose note you have not opened is never transcribed. If a meeting has started but transcription does not appear to be running, check that you have that meeting's note (or a new note) open, and that the calendar start time has already passed.

#No recording bot joins

{{PRODUCT}} does not use a recording bot that joins the meeting as a participant. Processing runs on your own computer, taking sound from its system audio and microphone. No unfamiliar account appears in the participant list, and the meeting host does not need to allow a bot to join. Because of this, transcription happens only while the desktop app is running on your computer.

#Telling whether transcription is running

While a note is open, a moving green waveform bar at the bottom of the screen means audio is being captured. If the bar is not moving, no audio is arriving, so check your input device using the steps in Transcription problems.

To the left of the “Ask anything” chat field at the bottom of the screen is a small icon shaped like an audio waveform. Clicking it shows or hides the transcript panel, where the converted text scrolls past as it is produced.

While another app is in front, an indicator floats at the right edge of the screen showing a meeting is in progress. Click it to return to the meeting's note, and drag the handle at its base to move it.

Checking audio is being captured
  • the waveform bar at the bottom of the note moves in time with speech
  • new text keeps being added in the transcript panel
  • both your own speech (green) and the other party's (grey) appear

#What you can do in the transcript panel

Action What it does
Show / hide click the waveform icon to open and close the panel
Pause / resume stop and restart transcription temporarily without ending the meeting
Copy everything the copy icon at the top right of the panel copies the whole transcript to the clipboard
Copy or delete a block click any block of the transcript to copy or delete just that block
Search search the transcript for a particular word or phrase

Deleting by block is useful when unrelated small talk came up during the meeting, or when something was said that you do not want on the record. A deleted block is removed from the transcript.

#Reading the colours

Each block of the transcript changes colour and position according to where the sound came from.

  • Grey bubble (aligned left): captured from system audio. Normally the speech of participants other than you.
  • Green bubble (aligned right): captured from your microphone — that is, your own speech.

Speaker labels are not set up, this distinction is the only clue you have.

#What stops transcription

You can end transcription at any time with the stop button at the bottom of the screen. Beyond that, it stops automatically in the following situations.

  • When the meeting is judged to have ended. That judgement uses the length of the transcript, whether you are still using a meeting app (Zoom, Microsoft Teams, Google Meet and so on), and, for a meeting tied to a calendar, the scheduled end time.
  • When no new audio has been detected for fifteen minutes.
  • When the computer is put to sleep.

#A caveat for meetings not tied to a calendar

For a meeting linked to a calendar event, the scheduled end time is one of the signals used to decide it has ended. An unplanned discussion started from [+ New note] has no scheduled end time, so the only clue is whether the meeting app has stopped using the microphone.

As a result, if you carry on talking in the same room after hanging up, the audio never breaks, the fifteen-minute silence timer never fires, and transcription can keep going. For meetings not in your calendar, pressing the stop button when you finish is the surest approach.

#When automatic stopping does not work on macOS

On macOS, deciding automatically that a meeting has ended requires administrator rights on that Mac. On company-issued machines without administrator rights, automatic stopping does not work, so press the stop button yourself when the meeting ends.

#Back-to-back meetings

Going straight from one meeting into another can leave the meeting app holding the microphone through the gap. In that state the end of the first meeting cannot be detected, and the two meetings can end up joined into a single transcript. If you want a separate note for each meeting, press the stop button in between.

What to do between back-to-back meetings

Press stop when the meeting ends, then start again from the notification or a new note for the next one. That one extra step keeps your notes split by meeting.

#Resuming after it has ended

Even after a meeting has ended and the note has been generated, you can resume transcription in the same note. Open the transcript panel (the waveform icon to the left of the chat field) and click “Resume”, and new audio is appended to the existing transcript. Regenerate the note afterwards and the later material is reflected in the summary too.

#Which audio is captured

{{PRODUCT}} captures your computer's system audio and microphone input. System audio is the sound your computer is playing, which normally includes the speech of participants other than you. Microphone input is your own speech. Any call whose audio plays through the computer can be transcribed, including VoIP and internet calling apps. Those calls are not linked to a calendar, so start from [+ New note] and check that your audio device settings match the input and output the meeting is using.

Audio cannot be separated per app. What is captured is the system audio as a whole. If you play music or a video during a meeting, that sound is included in the transcript even if you have sent it to a different output device.

For the purpose of transcription, audio passes directly from your microphone and system audio to the transcription processor {{COMPANY}} engages. There is no mechanism that records or stores the call's audio or video itself, so a meeting's audio file cannot be retrieved afterwards. For how long transcript text is kept, see Automatic transcript deletion and Our security standards.

{{PRODUCT}} is also designed around transcribing a meeting as it happens. It cannot load and transcribe an audio file such as an MP3 recorded in advance.

About telling participants

There is no provision in Japanese law that generally prohibits a party to a conversation from recording a meeting they are in. At the same time, where recording or transcription acquires personal information, the Act on the Protection of Personal Information requires the purpose of use to be promptly notified to the individual or made public, unless it has been published in advance. Saying at the start of the meeting that it is being recorded makes that requirement easier to satisfy and reduces misunderstandings with participants. Sample wording and how to approach it in practice are covered in How far you can rely on AI meeting notes (a guide for teams).

Meetings where sensitive personal information may come up

Medical history, health check results, disability, beliefs and criminal records are treated as “sensitive personal information”, and acquiring them requires the individual's consent as a rule. In meetings where these are likely to be discussed — an occupational health consultation or an HR interview, say — obtain the consent of the person speaking in advance, or use pause in the transcript panel to stop recording. If something has already been recorded, you can select the relevant block and delete it.

#Telling speakers apart

Speaker labels puts participants' display names in the transcript instead of “me” and “them”. Which meeting tools are supported, what setup is needed, and what can be identified are covered in Speaker labels.

Where speaker labels are unavailable or not set up, the transcript shows only “me” and “them”. “Me” corresponds to microphone input and “them” to system audio. Even so, who said what is often inferred from the surrounding context and reflected in the note; if a name is wrong you can correct it directly in the note or tell chat to fix it.

#Improving accuracy

Transcription accuracy depends heavily on the quality of the incoming sound and on what vocabulary you have registered. Check these three things.

  1. Register proper nouns. Company names, product names, in-house terminology and colleagues' names go into your personal jargon list under language settings in Settings. If an administrator has set workspace-level jargon, that applies too. The steps are in Customising transcription.
  2. Match your audio device settings. The input and output devices your meeting app uses must match the device {{PRODUCT}} is taking sound from. Also check the microphone input level is not too low.
  3. Use a headset where it helps. This suppresses background noise and sound from the speakers looping back into the microphone. It makes the most difference in shared office space and in meetings where several people join from the same room.

#Exporting the transcript

Transcript text can be copied from the panel and pasted into other tools.

  1. Open the meeting's note and click the waveform icon to the left of the chat field at the bottom of the screen to open the transcript panel.
  2. To copy the whole thing, click the copy icon at the top right of the panel.
  3. If you only need part of it, click the block you want and then the copy icon that appears.
  4. Unwanted blocks can be removed from the transcript using the delete icon that appears in the same way.

To pass a whole note to another tool, use the steps in Exporting notes.

#If something is not working

  • Transcription does not start: check that a note is open and that the calendar start time has passed. If it still does not start, check your audio device settings and restart the app. Detailed steps are in Transcription problems.
  • Two meetings ended up in one transcript: this is likely because the meeting app kept hold of the microphone. Press the stop button between meetings next time.
  • It does not stop when the meeting ends: automatic stopping does not work on macOS without administrator rights. End it manually with the stop button.

If only the other party's voice is missing, system audio may not be being captured. Where to check depends on your operating system.

System Settings > Privacy & Security and check that {{PRODUCT}} is allowed under “Screen & System Audio Recording”. Depending on your macOS version this item may be shown as “Screen Recording” only. Just after changing the permission you may be asked to restart the app.

Settings > System > Sound and check that the output (the other party's voice, i.e. system audio) is pointed at the device actually playing sound. Selecting a USB microphone as the output makes it impossible to capture participants' audio separately. If that does not help, turn off “Audio enhancements” in the output device's properties.

Checking audio is being captured the waveform bar at the bottom of the note moves in time with speech new text keeps being added in the transcript panel both your own speech (green) and the other party's (grey) appear # What you can do in the transcript panel Action What it does Show / hide click the waveform icon to open and close the panel Pause / resume stop and restart transcription temporarily without ending the meeting Copy everything the copy icon at the top right of the panel copies the whole transcript to the clipboard Copy or delete a block click any block of the transcript to copy or delete just that block Search search the transcript for a particular word or phrase Deleting by block is useful when unrelated small talk came up during the meeting, or when something was said that you do not want on the record. A deleted block is removed from the transcript. # Reading the colours Each block of the transcript changes colour and position according to where the sound came from. Grey bubble (aligned left) : captured from system audio. Normally the speech of participants other than you. Green bubble (aligned right) : captured from your microphone — that is, your own speech. Speaker labels are not set up, this distinction is the only clue you have. # What stops transcription You can end transcription at any time with the stop button at the bottom of the screen. Beyond that, it stops automatically in the following situations. When the meeting is judged to have ended. That judgement uses the length of the transcript, whether you are still using a meeting app (Zoom, Microsoft Teams, Google Meet and so on), and, for a meeting tied to a calendar, the scheduled end time. When no new audio has been detected for fifteen minutes. When the computer is put to sleep. # A caveat for meetings not tied to a calendar For a meeting linked to a calendar event, the scheduled end time is one of the signals used to decide it has ended. An unplanned discussion started from [+ New note] has no scheduled end time, so the only clue is whether the meeting app has stopped using the microphone. As a result, if you carry on talking in the same room after hanging up, the audio never breaks, the fifteen-minute silence timer never fires, and transcription can keep going. For meetings not in your calendar, pressing the stop button when you finish is the surest approach. # When automatic stopping does not work on macOS On macOS, deciding automatically that a meeting has ended requires administrator rights on that Mac. On company-issued machines without administrator rights, automatic stopping does not work, so press the stop button yourself when the meeting ends. # Back-to-back meetings Going straight from one meeting into another can leave the meeting app holding the microphone through the gap. In that state the end of the first meeting cannot be detected, and the two meetings can end up joined into a single transcript. If you want a separate note for each meeting, press the stop button in between. What to do between back-to-back meetings Press stop when the meeting ends, then start again from the notification or a new note for the next one. That one extra step keeps your notes split by meeting. # Resuming after it has ended Even after a meeting has ended and the note has been generated, you can resume transcription in the same note. Open the transcript panel (the waveform icon to the left of the chat field) and click “Resume”, and new audio is appended to the existing transcript. Regenerate the note afterwards and the later material is reflected in the summary too. # Which audio is captured {{PRODUCT}} captures your computer's system audio and microphone input. System audio is the sound your computer is playing, which normally includes the speech of participants other than you. Microphone input is your own speech. Any call whose audio plays through the computer can be transcribed, including VoIP and internet calling apps. Those calls are not linked to a calendar, so start from [+ New note] and check that your audio device settings match the input and output the meeting is using. Audio cannot be separated per app. What is captured is the system audio as a whole. If you play music or a video during a meeting, that sound is included in the transcript even if you have sent it to a different output device. For the purpose of transcription, audio passes directly from your microphone and system audio to the transcription processor {{COMPANY}} engages. There is no mechanism that records or stores the call's audio or video itself, so a meeting's audio file cannot be retrieved afterwards. For how long transcript text is kept, see Automatic transcript deletion and Our security standards . {{PRODUCT}} is also designed around transcribing a meeting as it happens. It cannot load and transcribe an audio file such as an MP3 recorded in advance. About telling participants There is no provision in Japanese law that generally prohibits a party to a conversation from recording a meeting they are in. At the same time, where recording or transcription acquires personal information, the Act on the Protection of Personal Information requires the purpose of use to be promptly notified to the individual or made public, unless it has been published in advance. Saying at the start of the meeting that it is being recorded makes that requirement easier to satisfy and reduces misunderstandings with participants. Sample wording and how to approach it in practice are covered in How far you can rely on AI meeting notes (a guide for teams) . Meetings where sensitive personal information may come up Medical history, health check results, disability, beliefs and criminal records are treated as “sensitive personal information”, and acquiring them requires the individual's consent as a rule. In meetings where these are likely to be discussed — an occupational health consultation or an HR interview, say — obtain the consent of the person speaking in advance, or use pause in the transcript panel to stop recording. If something has already been recorded, you can select the relevant block and delete it. # Telling speakers apart Speaker labels puts participants' display names in the transcript instead of “me” and “them”. Which meeting tools are supported, what setup is needed, and what can be identified are covered in Speaker labels . Where speaker labels are unavailable or not set up, the transcript shows only “me” and “them”. “Me” corresponds to microphone input and “them” to system audio. Even so, who said what is often inferred from the surrounding context and reflected in the note; if a name is wrong you can correct it directly in the note or tell chat to fix it. # Improving accuracy Transcription accuracy depends heavily on the quality of the incoming sound and on what vocabulary you have registered. Check these three things. Register proper nouns . Company names, product names, in-house terminology and colleagues' names go into your personal jargon list under language settings in Settings. If an administrator has set workspace-level jargon, that applies too. The steps are in Customising transcription . Match your audio device settings . The input and output devices your meeting app uses must match the device {{PRODUCT}} is taking sound from. Also check the microphone input level is not too low. Use a headset where it helps . This suppresses background noise and sound from the speakers looping back into the microphone. It makes the most difference in shared office space and in meetings where several people join from the same room. # Exporting the transcript Transcript text can be copied from the panel and pasted into other tools. Open the meeting's note and click the waveform icon to the left of the chat field at the bottom of the screen to open the transcript panel. To copy the whole thing, click the copy icon at the top right of the panel. If you only need part of it, click the block you want and then the copy icon that appears. Unwanted blocks can be removed from the transcript using the delete icon that appears in the same way. To pass a whole note to another tool, use the steps in Exporting notes . # If something is not working Transcription does not start : check that a note is open and that the calendar start time has passed. If it still does not start, check your audio device settings and restart the app. Detailed steps are in Transcription problems . Two meetings ended up in one transcript : this is likely because the meeting app kept hold of the microphone. Press the stop button between meetings next time. It does not stop when the meeting ends : automatic stopping does not work on macOS without administrator rights. End it manually with the stop button. If only the other party's voice is missing, system audio may not be being captured. Where to check depends on your operating system. macOS Windows System Settings > Privacy & Security and check that {{PRODUCT}} is allowed under “Screen & System Audio Recording”. Depending on your macOS version this item may be shown as “Screen Recording” only. Just after changing the permission you may be asked to restart the app. Settings > System > Sound and check that the output (the other party's voice, i.e. system audio) is pointed at the device actually playing sound. Selecting a USB microphone as the output makes it impossible to capture participants' audio separately. If that does not help, turn off “Audio enhancements” in the output device's properties.

getting-more-from-your-notes/chatting-wi.title: Asking your notes questions (chat)
getting-more-from-your-notes/chatting-wi.description: Asking questions across past meetings, rewriting notes, and attaching files to supply context.
getting-more-from-your-notes/chatting-wi.html:
Chat lets you ask questions about your meeting notes and transcripts and get answers on the spot. You can ask about a single meeting, or about many past meetings at once. This article covers how the scope is decided, rewriting notes, attaching files, and how chat history is handled.

Note

Chat is a desktop app (macOS / Windows) feature. The web version in a browser only views and edits notes that are already saved; chat and transcription are not available there.

Recipes (saved instructions)Save instructions you use often and run them repeatedly→Choosing an AI modelWhen to use the standard model and when to use the reasoning model→Actions from chat (workflows)Sending email and creating calendar events→

#Where to open chat

In the desktop app, a chat input field is always visible at the bottom of the screen. Open it from the home screen and every saved note is in scope; open it with an individual meeting showing and only that meeting is. You can also open chat from a folder, or from the record screen for a person or a company.

#Choosing the scope (context)

What chat looks at is determined by the screen you open it from. There is no need to switch the transcript in and out of scope each time.

Where you open chat What is in scope Typical use
Home screen all saved notes finding something when you cannot remember which meeting it came up in
An individual meeting that meeting's note and transcript asking about that meeting before, during or after it; rewriting the note once it has ended
A folder the notes in that folder analysing a team's or a project's meetings together
A person or company record meetings with that party following the history with a particular client
Several meetings you have selected only the meetings you chose specifying the meetings you want to compare yourself

To select several meetings, use the checkbox that appears to the left of a meeting title when you hover over it.

How far back your notes go depends on your plan. The free plan covers the last 30 days; the Team and Enterprise plans cover all of them.

Check
  • you opened chat from the screen you intended (chat on an individual meeting does not look at any other note)
  • if you want to compare several meetings, they are ticked
  • the meeting you are looking for falls within the period your plan covers

#Using it before, during and after a meeting

Different ways of asking suit different moments.

Before a meeting

  • getting an overview of the day's schedule
  • drawing out the points to raise, as preparation for a meeting about to start
  • checking what was decided at the last meeting with the same person or on the same project

During a meeting

  • catching up on the discussion so far when you join late
  • checking the decisions and take-aways so far
  • asking for an explanation of a technical term or some background

After a meeting

  • finding a particular passage, such as something decided or a figure
  • reviewing how much you spoke and how you asked questions
  • working out what to do next

Across several meetings

  • spotting recurring points of discussion or patterns of dissatisfaction
  • finding something when you cannot remember which meeting it came up in
  • summarising the position by folder or by client

#Rewriting a note from chat

You can rewrite the text of a note from chat. Phrasing your request as a rewrite — “rewrite this”, “fix this” — triggers the rewrite behaviour. Naming a heading or section in the note limits it to that part.

Common uses are:

  • expanding a passage, or cutting it back to the essentials
  • correcting a misspelled name, or reassigning an owner
  • translating the note into another language

Selecting the passage you want changed before sending your instruction to chat makes that selection the target. If the result is not what you meant, follow up with another instruction.

#Attaching files to supply context

When the meeting data alone is not enough, you can add files from the attach button in the input field. Passing in material circulated beforehand, a specification, or a proposal you received means the answer takes that content into account. For the limits on attachments, see File size limits.

Check before attaching confidential material

The contents of a file you attach are passed to AI processing in order to generate the answer. Where the material is covered by a non-disclosure agreement with a client, contains unannounced HR information, or contains customers' personal data, please check in advance whether your internal rules and your contracts permit it to be processed by an external service. As for use in training: on the free and Personal plans this is on by default and can be switched off at any time under Settings → Preferences → Data and sharing. On the Team and Enterprise plans it is not used for training. The settings are explained in AI models and training data.

Uploaded material is processed only to generate notes and chat answers within that workspace. It is not provided to other users or other organisations. It remains your responsibility, as the person uploading, to confirm that you hold the necessary rights in the material or have the rights holder's permission.

LegislationCopyright Act, Article 30(1) (reproduction for private use)

This provides that a person may reproduce a work where the purpose is use within a limited scope such as personally or within the family. Business use by a company or organisation does not fall within that scope. When uploading material received from outside your company to {{PRODUCT}}, please check that internal use is within what has been permitted.

#Save instructions you use often as recipes

If you ask the same thing repeatedly, saving the wording as a recipe lets you call it up just by typing / in the input field. How to create and share them is covered in Recipes (saved instructions), and how to word them in Writing effective recipes.

#How chat history is handled

Chat exchanges are visible only to you. Sharing a note with other members never exposes to them the chat you had about that note.Actions from chat (workflows) — a draft created that way is likewise invisible to anyone else until you actually send it.

To delete a chat thread, hover over it in the history list and choose the bin icon. A deleted thread cannot be recovered.

#What data chat can see

Chat can see only the meeting data stored in {{PRODUCT}}, files you have attached, and material you have added to a folder. It does not look at your email inbox, your task manager, or notes on your own machine. It cannot answer about anything that was not said in a meeting or is not in the record.

#If something is not working

When you cannot find what you are looking for

  1. Widen the scope. Switch from an individual meeting to chat on a folder or the home screen and try again.
  2. Check the period of notes you can see. On the free plan, notes older than the last 30 days are out of scope.
  3. Check that where you opened chat gives the scope you intended. Chat on an individual meeting does not look at any other note.
  4. Check the meeting's transcript was saved. For a meeting with no transcript, only what is written in the note can be consulted. For details see How transcription works.

When the chat input field does not appear

You may have the note open in a browser. The web version only views and edits notes, so reopen it in the desktop app (macOS / Windows).

When an answer does not match the facts

AI summaries and answers can contain errors. Speech may be misheard, speakers confused, or facts transposed in the course of summarising. For anything where accuracy matters — confirming decisions, anything contractual, amounts, dates — check it against the original transcript before relying on it.

#Related articles

Recipes (saved instructions)Saving an instruction and calling it up→Writing effective recipesGetting consistent output→Dictation vs transcriptionWhat the microphone icon does→AI models and training dataThe training setting→
