getting-more-from-your-notes/dictation-v.title: Dictation vs transcription
getting-more-from-your-notes/dictation-v.description: Chat dictation and meeting transcription are different things. When to use each, and how they are billed.
getting-more-from-your-notes/dictation-v.html:
The microphone icon in the chat input field and the transcription that records a meeting look similar, and are easily confused. This article explains what each does, which to use, and how to tell when you have used the wrong one.

Note

Dictation and transcription are both desktop app (macOS / Windows) features. The web version in a browser only views and edits notes that are already saved; neither is available there.

#Which to use, at a glance

Dictation Transcription
Purpose typing a question into chat with your voice recording what is said in a meeting and producing a note
Where you use it the microphone icon in the chat input field at the bottom of the screen “+ New note” at the top right, or starting from a notification or calendar event
Audio covered a short question you speak yourself what meeting participants say, plus system audio
Expected length a single sentence, a few to a few dozen seconds a whole meeting
Result what you said becomes text and is sent to chat a transcript is saved, and a note is generated when it ends
Records a new meeting no yes

Remember it as: dictation for asking about past meetings, transcription for recording a conversation that is about to happen.

#Chat dictation

At the right of the chat input field at the bottom of the desktop app is a microphone icon. It is there to let you speak a question rather than type it, and it does not start recording a meeting.

Use it when:

  • you want to ask chat about a meeting that has already been recorded
  • speaking is quicker than typing a long question
  • your hands are full and the keyboard is awkward

#How to dictate

  1. Choose the microphone icon in the chat input field.
  2. Audio capture begins. Two icons are shown while it is listening.
  3. When you have finished speaking, choose the tick icon. What you said becomes text and is sent to chat exactly as if you had typed it.
  4. To abandon it without sending, choose the × icon. Nothing is sent to chat.

Dictation is meant for short questions. It is not suited to capturing a long conversation, so use transcription to record a meeting or discussion. For everything chat can do, see Asking your notes questions (chat).

Improving recognition accuracy

Proper nouns such as company and product names can be misheard in dictation too. Registering terms you use often in the dictionary in advance makes them more likely to be recognised, in transcription as well. How to set this up is in Customising transcription.

#Starting meeting transcription

Transcription starts only when you do one of the following. Do nothing and no meeting is recorded.

  1. click the notification shown when a call is detected
  2. open an event whose start time has passed, from the home screen
  3. click “+ New note” at the top right of the screen
  4. leave the note for an upcoming event open (it starts automatically when the start time arrives)

The conditions are set out in detail in How transcription works. To record an unplanned discussion that is not in your calendar, use the third option, a new note.

Check

After starting from a new note, check the following.

  • three green bars appear vertically at the bottom of the screen
  • the bars move with the volume (if they move, audio capture and transcription are running)
  • selecting the bars shows the state of transcription

If the green bars do not appear after choosing a new note, transcription has not started. Check microphone permission, the permission needed to capture system audio, and your input device selection. The steps are in Transcription problems.

#Telling participants

Transcription records what is said in a meeting. Quite apart from any legal obligation, saying at the start of the meeting that it is being recorded makes problems less likely later. How to set internal rules, and wording you can use at the start of a meeting, are explained in How far you can rely on AI meeting notes (a guide for teams). Dictation is an action for entering your own question, so it is not covered by that notice.

#Usage and billing

What you say when dictating is treated as chat input. It is not saved as a meeting note or transcript, so it does not appear in your notes list. Transcripts are saved as notes and are subject to retention settings and automatic deletion. Automatic deletion is “off (do not delete automatically)” by default, and a period can be set in workspace settings. The periods available and what deletion covers are in Automatic transcript deletion.

#If something is not working

You meant to ask a question but a meeting recording started

You may have chosen a new note. Check the green bars at the bottom of the screen and stop the recording. You can delete the unwanted note. What happens to a deleted note is covered in Deleting and restoring notes.

You meant to record but nothing was kept

You may have used dictation from the microphone icon. Dictation is for sending a question; it does not create a meeting record. Start again from a new note.

Nothing happens when you choose the microphone icon

Check that {{PRODUCT}} has microphone permission from the operating system. If another app has exclusive use of the microphone, quit that app and try again.

#Related articles

Asking your notes questions (chat)Using chat generally→How transcription worksWhen audio is captured→Transcription problemsWhat to do when audio is not captured→

getting-more-from-your-notes/recipes.title: Recipes (saved instructions)
getting-more-from-your-notes/recipes.description: How to build and share saved instructions you can run again and again.
getting-more-from-your-notes/recipes.html:
A recipe saves the instructions you type into chat every time. Work with a fixed output — formatting minutes, copying into a daily report, filling in an interview scorecard — becomes a matter of picking a name. This article covers calling up recipes, creating them, and sharing and editing them. How to word the instructions themselves, with examples you can use as-is, is covered in Writing effective recipes.

Note

Recipes are called from chat, and chat is available in the desktop app (macOS / Windows). How chat's scope is decided is covered in Asking your notes questions (chat).

Writing effective recipesHow instructions are structured, with examples→Asking your notes questions (chat)Chat basics→Shape your notes with templatesSetting the format of the note itself→

#What recipes suit

They suit work that produces the same shape of output repeatedly. For example:

  • formatting minutes for internal circulation, or a daily report for your manager
  • pulling just the take-aways and decisions out of recent meetings
  • summarising trends in requests across meetings with several customers
  • building a list of things to verify, or of defects, from development meetings
  • drafting an internal procedure from support enquiry records

#Calling up a recipe

Type a forward slash / in the chat input field and the available recipes are listed — those provided out of the box, those you have made, and those shared by members of the same workspace. Keep typing part of a name to narrow it down.

Opening the recipes tab from the sidebar menu shows the whole list at once.

#Finding recipes

The recipes tab is divided into sections.

  • Recommended: recipes provided by {{PRODUCT}} together with ones contributed by users. A good starting point when you want ideas for how to analyse something.
  • My recipes: the ones you have made.
  • Workspace recipes: ones published by members of the same workspace.

The search field searches the body of the instructions as well as the recipe name. Search by the words of the situation you have in mind — “daily report”, “assessment”, and so on.

#Creating a recipe

  1. 1

    Open the creation screen

    Type / in the chat input field, or open the recipes tab from the sidebar and choose “Create recipe”.

  2. 2

    Give it a name

    This name is the shortcut you use to call it from chat. Choose something that makes its purpose clear, such as “Minutes (internal circulation)”.

  3. 3

    Write the instructions

    The more specifically you say what to extract and what format to produce, the more consistent the result. How to decide the structure, Japanese-specific choices (polite or plain form, orthography, number formatting), and examples you can save and use as-is are in Writing effective recipes.

  4. 4

    Choose where it is used

    Choosing “a single meeting” makes it appear in chat on an individual meeting, usable both during and after it. Choosing “several meetings” makes it appear on the home screen, in folders, in person and company records, and when several meetings are selected — and not in chat on an individual meeting. A recipe can only be one or the other. To use the same instructions in both situations, create them as two separate recipes.

  5. 5

    Specify an AI model (optional)

    Under advanced settings you can specify which AI model runs the recipe. What you can specify depends on your plan. How to choose, and which plans this applies to, are in Choosing an AI model. Left unspecified, it runs on automatic selection.

  6. 6

    Save it and set its visibility

    A saved recipe can be kept to yourself, published to your workspace, or shared by link. Choosing the scope is covered in the next section.

Check
  • the name alone makes clear which situation the recipe is for
  • you chose whichever of “a single meeting” and “several meetings” matches the screen you want to use it on
  • the instructions specify the output's headings, number of items and tone

#Sharing scope

A recipe's visibility has three levels.

Setting Who can see it
Private only the person who created it
Within the workspace members of the same workspace
Anyone with the link everyone who receives the link

Someone who receives a shared recipe can run it against their own notes, save it as their own, or make an edited version for themselves. They cannot change the author's version. Sharing a recipe also never exposes your meeting notes or transcripts to them.

Check before sharing outside your company

Recipe instructions often contain things you would not want to leave your company — company and product names, team structures, assessment criteria, commercial terms. Choosing “anyone with the link” means everyone who receives that link can read the instructions in full. Write any recipe that might go to someone outside your company without internal specifics in it.

#Building on someone else's recipe (remix)

Recipes made by other people show a “Remix” button. This makes a copy you can edit. It does not appear on your own recipes, since you can edit those directly.

A remix lets you change the settings as well as the instructions. If a shared recipe is set for “several meetings” and you want it on an individual meeting, remix it and switch it to “a single meeting”. The original is unaffected.

#Editing and deleting

To edit

  1. Open the recipe from My recipes.
  2. Choose the pencil icon on the detail screen to enter edit mode.
  3. Make your changes.
  4. Choose “Save”.

To delete

  1. Open the recipe from My recipes.
  2. Choose the pencil icon to enter edit mode.
  3. Choose the bin icon at the bottom left.

#Instructions cannot use variables

Recipes are static templates. Variables, merge fields and substituting values at run time are not supported. The instructions you saved are sent exactly as they are, every time.

To vary the conditions by project or by role, create separate recipes with the conditions written in. If, say, sales and engineering interviews have different assessment criteria, set up “Interview scorecard (sales)” and “Interview scorecard (engineering)” as two recipes.

#If something is not working

The recipe does not appear in the list

Check whether it is set to “a single meeting” or “several meetings”. It does not appear in situations other than its setting. To change the setting of a shared recipe, remix it first and then switch.

The output comes out differently every time

Short instructions do not pin the format down. State the order of headings, the tone, the length per item and the table columns explicitly in the instructions. How to word them is explained in Writing effective recipes.

Output contains things that were not said in the meeting

Only the meeting data and attached material can be consulted. Asking for anything beyond that can lead to content being filled in. Put a rule in your instructions saying “do not write anything that is not in the record”.

I want to stop a shared recipe being visible outside the company

Change the visibility setting. Note, though, that copies already remixed remain with the people who made them. Rewrite instructions containing anything sensitive before sharing.

#Related articles

Writing effective recipesStructure, tone and example instructions→Choosing an AI modelSpecifying a model for a recipe→Actions from chat (workflows)Turning output into email or a calendar event→

getting-more-from-your-notes/model-selec.title: Choosing an AI model
getting-more-from-your-notes/model-selec.description: The difference between the standard and reasoning models, which to use when, and how to think about time and cost.
getting-more-from-your-notes/model-selec.html:
By default, chat and recipes choose an AI model automatically according to the scope and the question. On some plans you can also specify the standard or reasoning model yourself. This article covers what each is like, how to choose, and what you can specify.

Team plan Enterprise plan

Note

Choosing a model manually is available on the Team and Enterprise plans. The free plan only has automatic selection. What automatic selection does, and which tasks suit which model, are the same on every plan.

About the models available

Which AI models are available in {{PRODUCT}}, and how they are combined, may change as provision changes. This article describes them by function — “standard model” and “reasoning (thinking) model” — rather than by individual model name. For the options actually available to you, see the model selector in the app.

#Automatic selection

Leave model selection on “automatic” and the model is chosen according to where you opened chat and what you asked. For most purposes, automatic is fine.

You would switch manually when you want a fuller answer and are willing to wait, or when you want the work finished quickly.

#The standard model

The standard model is a general-purpose model for everyday work. It responds quickly and suits short questions and routine output.

It is well suited to:

  • asking a short question about a meeting
  • pulling take-aways out of a discussion
  • summarising what was said, briefly
  • drafting a short email or message

#The reasoning (thinking) model

The reasoning model works through its thinking in steps before answering. It suits producing long documents and analysis that cross-references several sources. It takes longer to respond than the standard model.

With the reasoning model, a line such as “thought for N seconds” appears above the answer. Open it and you can see the order in which it reached its conclusion. This helps when you want to trace the basis for a judgement, or verify output before using it internally.

It is well suited to:

  • comparing several meetings to draw out common themes or trends
  • working out an approach from what several people have said
  • setting out the advantages and concerns of each option
  • checking the reasoning towards a conclusion, rather than the conclusion itself

#What each plan can specify

Plan Model selection
Free plan automatic only
Team plan automatic, or choose the standard or reasoning model manually
Enterprise plan automatic, or choose the standard or reasoning model manually. Some models cannot be chosen until an administrator enables them

#Choosing by task

The longer and more complex the output, the more the reasoning model suits. For short checks and fixed-format output, the standard model means less waiting.

What you want to do Model that suits
Summarise one meeting standard model
Extract decisions and next actions standard model
Write a short message based on a discussion standard model
Find “how was that decided?” within one meeting standard model
Draw out trends across several meetings reasoning model
Build a proposed approach from what several people said reasoning model
Compare advantages and concerns to produce a discussion document reasoning model
Check the reasons and assumptions behind a proposal reasoning model

The same thinking applies when specifying a model for a recipe. How to specify it is in the creation steps in Recipes (saved instructions), and how to make the tone and format consistent through the instructions is in Writing effective recipes.

#Processing time and usage

Because the reasoning model works through steps before answering, it takes longer than the standard model — tens of seconds is not unusual. Using the standard model when you need a quick check and the reasoning model when you are settling in to produce a document keeps frustration with waiting down.

In general, the more meetings involved and the longer the output requested, the more computation is needed. Selecting only the meetings you need before running something produces a faster and more focused result than leaving the scope set to the whole home screen while asking for a long document. How to narrow the scope is explained in Asking your notes questions (chat).

#Administrator restrictions

On the Enterprise plan, some models are disabled by default. While disabled they cannot be chosen even though they appear in the model selector. To use one, an administrator enables it under Settings > Workspace > Data security.

Administrators have this as a separate setting because data handling can differ between models.

Check

Before asking an administrator to enable one, consider the following.

  • whether the task really requires that model (the choice between standard and reasoning may be enough)
  • whether the meetings involved contain client information or sensitive personal information
  • whether that model is covered by an arrangement under which the provider retains no logs

#About sending data to external model providers

{{PRODUCT}} stores data in a Japanese region by default. Some processing for AI summarisation and transcription may, however, be delegated to providers overseas. In that case data including meeting content is sent to that provider, which raises the question of cross-border transfer of personal data.

{{COMPANY}} selects only providers where it can confirm contractually that the data sent is not used to train models, where the retention period is stated, and which have arrangements allowing supervision as a processor.

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 25 (supervision of processors)

This provides that where the handling of personal data is delegated in whole or in part, the delegating party must exercise necessary and appropriate supervision over the processor. On business plans, the contracting company is the delegating party and {{COMPANY}} the processor. Where {{COMPANY}} uses an external model provider, that is a sub-delegation and subject to equivalent supervision.

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 28 (restriction on provision to third parties in foreign countries)

This governs providing personal data to a third party in a foreign country. It applies even where provision accompanies delegation. {{COMPANY}} provides data only to providers that have put in place arrangements meeting the standards set by Personal Information Protection Commission rules, and periodically confirms the measures those providers implement and the legal regime of the destination country.

For some models, an arrangement under which the provider retains no data (zero data retention) does not apply, and input and output logs may be retained for a period for purposes such as abuse monitoring. Whether your organisation uses such a model is for an administrator to decide through the setting above.

Whether data is used to improve {{PRODUCT}}'s own AI models is a separate setting. On the free and Personal plans it is on by default and can be switched off at any time under Settings → Preferences → Data and sharing. On the Team and Enterprise plans it is not used for training. For details see AI models and training data, and for storage location and cross-border transfer generally see Security and privacy FAQs.

#Frequently asked questions

Q. I do not know which model to choose

A. Leave the setting on “automatic”. The model is chosen according to the scope and the question. It is simplest to switch to the reasoning model manually only when step-by-step deliberation is needed, or when you want to see the thinking.

Q. Automatic is the only option available

A. The free plan only has automatic selection. To choose a model manually you need to move to a paid plan from Settings > Billing. For what the plans include, see Plans and billing.

Q. A model in the selector cannot be selected

A. On the Enterprise plan, some models are disabled by default. Ask an administrator to enable it under Settings > Workspace > Data security. On the free plan, you need to move to a paid plan.

Q. The reasoning model is slow to answer

A. Because the reasoning model works through steps before answering, it takes longer than the standard model. For a short check, switch to the standard model. Narrowing down the meetings involved also reduces the time.

Q. The same instructions produce different tone with different models

A. Models differ in their output tendencies. To keep tone and format consistent, state the polite or plain form, the order of headings, and the length per item explicitly in the instructions. How to word them is explained in Writing effective recipes.

#Related articles

getting-more-from-your-notes/workflows-i.title: Actions from chat (workflows)
getting-more-from-your-notes/workflows-i.description: Sending email and creating calendar events from chat, the scope of the permissions, and checking before you run them.
getting-more-from-your-notes/workflows-i.html:
Some of the work that follows a meeting can be done straight from chat: drafting and sending a follow-up email, posting a message to Slack, and creating an event in Google Calendar. In every case a draft appears on screen, and nothing is sent to the external service until you have reviewed it and told it to go ahead.

Note

This feature is available in the desktop app (macOS / Windows). You need to have connected whichever of Gmail, Slack and Google Calendar you intend to use. Microsoft 365 mail and calendar are not supported at this time.

Always check the content before sending

This feature has AI produce a draft from the meeting record. The wrong recipient, an incorrect date or figure, or content that was not actually agreed in the meeting can all creep in. Sending, posting and creating an event cannot be undone. Read the recipients and the body again before you go ahead. The points to check are collected under “Checklist before sending” in this article.

Asking your notes questions (chat)Chat basics and scope→Writing follow-up emailsThe feature that prepares post-meeting email automatically→Slack integrationSetting up automatic posting of notes to a channel→

#What you can do

Action Connection required Currently supported
Drafting and sending email Gmail Google accounts only
Drafting and sending a Slack message Slack channels, group DMs, direct messages
Finding free time and creating an event Google Calendar only people within the same Google Workspace domain

#Setting up connections

  1. 1

    Open the integrations screen

    Settings > Integrations. Connections are added and removed from this screen.

  2. 2

    Connect the services you will use

    Connect whichever of Gmail, Slack and Google Calendar you will use. Email and calendar actions need Gmail and Google Calendar; posting messages needs Slack.

  3. 3

    Check which account you are connecting

    A connection is tied to your individual account. Email is sent from the account you connected, Slack messages are posted in your name, and events are created in your calendar. Connecting a shared organisational account makes it impossible to tell who did what, so connect a personal account. If you keep work and personal accounts separate, check here which one you are connecting.

Understand what it can access before connecting

Once connected, {{PRODUCT}} operates the external service with your permissions. The mail you can read, the channels you are in and the calendars you can see become the material for producing drafts. It never accesses more than you can — but by the same token, anything you can see may be consulted. You can disconnect at any time from Settings > Integrations. Disconnecting stops new actions running, but messages already sent and events already created are not undone.

#How it works

  1. 1

    Ask in chat

    Open chat and write what you want done. Be specific about recipients, the channel to post to, attendees, and the times you would prefer. What is consulted depending on which screen you open chat from is covered in Asking your notes questions (chat).

  2. 2

    Review the draft

    An editable draft appears in the chat. Check the content and the destination and correct anything that needs it. For an event, you can pick one of the suggested times or change the date, time and duration directly. Times that clash with another event are flagged.

  3. 3

    Tell it to go ahead

    If everything is right, choose “Send” or “Create event”. If you discard the draft, nothing is left on the external service. Where “Save as draft” is offered for an email, choosing it saves it to your Gmail drafts without sending.

#Drafting and sending email

Tell chat what kind of email you want, to whom, and what to include. The draft is produced from the meetings in the current scope together with relevant context from the connected Gmail account.

Before sending you can edit the recipients, CC, BCC, subject and body. If you have a signature set in Gmail, you can choose whether to include it. Where something needs filling in, a conspicuous placeholder may be inserted. Replace every placeholder with the real content before sending. Email is sent only after you choose “Send”.

Where saving to Gmail drafts and applying labels is offered, you can save as a draft and apply an existing or new label. The first time you use this, Gmail may ask for additional permissions. Saving as a draft does not send anything.

Examples of how to ask:

Draft an email to everyone who attended this meeting, thanking them and
confirming what was decided. Polite form, no more than three lines of
preamble. Separate our actions from what we are asking of them, and put
a deadline on each request.

Turn today's discussion into an internal report email to the department head.
Plain form, conclusion first, background as no more than five bullet points.

From these three sales meetings, write the weekly customer status email.
Use a heading per customer and make the outstanding concerns explicit.

If you make the same kind of request repeatedly, saving the conditions as a recipe saves rewriting them each time. How to build the instructions is in Writing effective recipes.

How this differs from email prepared automatically after a meeting

For some external meetings, a suggested follow-up email is prepared automatically once the meeting ends. That is a separate feature, described in Writing follow-up emails. With actions from chat, you decide when a draft is made and what goes into it.

#Messages to Slack

Meeting content can be turned into an internal update, a progress report or a list of next actions and posted to a Slack channel, group DM or direct message. Specify the destination in what you ask chat.

Before posting, both the destination and the message are shown, and both can be edited. Posting happens in the name of the connected Slack account, and only after you have reviewed it. If you specify a destination that includes people outside your company through Slack Connect, a warning is shown before sending.

  • You can post to channels, group DMs and direct messages.
  • Only destinations you can access within the connected Slack workspace are available.
  • Where channel names are similar and more than one could match, write the exact name including #.
  • For a group DM or direct message, name the people.
  • Where suggestions appear, type at least two characters after @ or # and then choose. People you choose are notified, and channels you choose appear as links.

Examples of how to ask:

Post the key points of this meeting to #project-hokuriku. A summary of no
more than three lines, plus the take-aways as bullets with owners.

Post an internal report to #sales-share. Three headings: “What they asked
for”, “Concerns” and “Next actions”. Use companies' full legal names.

Send Tanaka-san a direct message with what was decided today and just the
parts he is responsible for.

#Finding free time and creating an event

Chat can consult Google Calendar, check what is already scheduled, and draft a new event. Tell it the attendees, roughly when, and how long.

Before it is created, an editable draft of the event is shown. You can check the title, attendees, date and time, description, location and video meeting details. Adjust it by picking one of the suggested times, entering a different time, or moving the event in the calendar view and changing its length. Times that clash with another event are marked, so you can see what the clash is before proceeding. Choose “Create event” and it is added to the connected Google Calendar, with attendees notified by Google Calendar.

Where not everyone is free, you are shown the best available options and whose schedule clashes. No event is created until you pick a time and review the draft.

Examples of how to ask:

Set up a 30-minute meeting next week with me and the owners of this
meeting's take-aways. Afternoons preferred.

Set up a one-hour working session with Sato-san and Suzuki-san on Tuesday
afternoon next week. Title it “XX project — specification review”.

Check whether a review meeting for this project is already scheduled.
If not, find options this week and draft one.

#What information is consulted

The following is consulted in order to carry out an action.

  • the notes and transcripts of the meetings in the selected scope
  • relevant Gmail context, when drafting email
  • the Slack information needed to identify the destination
  • the calendar information needed to check availability and avoid clashes

All of it within the permissions of the person who connected. Chat history is visible only to you, as explained in Asking your notes questions (chat), and drafts for external actions are likewise invisible to anyone else until actually sent. For data handling generally, see Security and privacy FAQs.

#About sending personal data to external services

The email and messages sent by this feature will normally contain personal data — attendees' names, what they said, the names of contacts at client companies. The destination services (Gmail, Slack, Google Calendar) are not processors to whom {{COMPANY}} has delegated the handling of personal data; they are separate providers contracted by you or your organisation. The flow of data created by these actions therefore has to be accounted for on your side, separately from how it is handled inside {{PRODUCT}}.

Before sending a note containing personal data outside, please check it against your company's personal data handling rules and whether it falls within the purposes of use you have specified. Take particular care where the recipients include people outside your company.

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 27(1) (restriction on provision to third parties)

This provides that personal data must not, as a rule, be provided to a third party without the individual's prior consent. Paragraph 5 of the same Article treats provision accompanying delegation within the scope necessary to achieve the purpose of use as not constituting “provision to a third party”. For actions that send messages or events from chat to an external service, lawfulness has to be secured by the business handling the personal information that performs the action — in most cases the user's employer.

Points to watch when sending email outside your company are in Writing follow-up emails, and how to think about sharing scope is in Sharing controls.

#Checklist before sending

Drafts are produced on the assumption that you will review and correct them.

Check
  • the recipients, destination channel and attendee list are as you intended
  • no unreplaced placeholders remain
  • the destination does not include anyone outside your company
  • names, company names, dates, times, time zones and durations are correct
  • nothing that was not actually agreed in the meeting is written as settled
  • owners and deadlines match what was agreed in the meeting
  • links, attachments, location and video meeting details are correct
  • no internal abbreviations or internal nicknames remain in text going outside
  • the tone and level of formality suit the recipient

If anything is wrong, edit the draft directly or tell chat what to change.

#If something is not working

Q. No draft appears, or it says it could not be created

A. Check the desktop app is on the latest version and that the action is enabled for your account. Then check under Settings > Integrations that the service you need is connected. How you phrase the request matters too: rather than “what should I say?”, be explicit about the action — “draft an email to X”. If it says processing was interrupted, ask again in the same chat. That happens if generation was stopped partway, another message was sent while the draft was being produced, the connection dropped, or the app was quit before it finished.

Q. It says a connection is required

A. Follow the prompt shown in chat, or connect Gmail, Slack or Google Calendar from Settings > Integrations. Once connected, go back to the same chat and ask again.

Q. The Slack destination cannot be found

A. For a channel, give the exact name including #. For a group DM or direct message, name the people. Also check that the destination is inside the connected Slack workspace and that you have access to it.

Q. An event cannot be created

A. Check that Google Calendar is connected, that permission to create events has been granted, and that a writable calendar is selected. If you have changed permission settings, disconnecting and reconnecting sometimes resolves it.

Q. Can anything be sent without confirmation?

A. No. This feature always includes a review step. Sending email, posting to Slack and creating an event happen only after you have reviewed the draft and told it to go ahead.

Q. Can I use it with Microsoft 365 mail and calendar?

A. Not at this time. Email and calendar actions require Gmail and Google Calendar to be connected.

getting-more-from-your-notes/writing-eff.title: Writing effective recipes
getting-more-from-your-notes/writing-eff.description: How to structure instructions, and how to specify tone and formatting, so the output you want comes out consistently.
getting-more-from-your-notes/writing-eff.html:
A recipe is a set of instructions you write once and get the same shape of output from every time. The shorter the instructions, though, the more the output varies. This article covers how to build the instructions, which specifications matter most when writing in Japanese, and how to test and refine them — ending with examples you can save and use as they are.

Note

Creating, saving, sharing and deleting recipes is covered in Recipes (saved instructions). This article deals only with what to put in the instructions field on the creation screen.

#Decide the shape first

Recipes are either for “a single meeting” or for “several meetings”, and which you are building changes how the instructions are written. The difference, and how to choose, are in the creation steps in Recipes (saved instructions).

What matters when writing is that the input your instructions assume matches the input actually supplied. Instructions that say “this meeting” in a recipe for several meetings leave it unclear which meeting is meant, and the output becomes unstable. Conversely, “compare the meetings with each other” in a single-meeting recipe has nothing to compare against. For several meetings, open with something that assumes a set, such as “from the records of the selected meetings”.

#The basic structure of an instruction

For consistent output, this order is easiest to work with.

  1. Define the job: start by saying who uses the document, in what situation, and for what. Naming the reader settles the tone and the level of detail.
  2. Background: write in the information you would otherwise explain every time — company, product, team structure, the history of a project.
  3. Rules: list the conditions you want observed. This is the main thing that keeps the output from drifting.
  4. Output format: specify the order of headings, the table columns, the number of items, and the length of each.
  5. Example output: where the format matters, paste in a real example, however short.

An example opening:

A meeting has just finished and a follow-up email to the attendees is needed.
Your job is to write an external-facing email setting out the decisions and
next actions. The readers are the client contact and their manager.

When writing rules, imagine you are addressing someone who has just joined. Assumptions that are second nature internally do not carry across unless you write them down. Expressions such as “in the usual format” or “summarise appropriately” mean different things to different people, and do not work as instructions.

#Tips for instructions in Japanese

Japanese documents involve many formal choices that English does not. Unless you specify them, a different choice is made every time, so set them down as rules in the recipe.

#Specify polite or plain form

State whether to write in polite form (desu/masu) or plain form (da/de aru). Without it, the two can end up mixed within a single document. Deciding by purpose — polite form for external documents, plain form for internal records and analysis notes — removes the question.

You can specify the degree of honorific language too. Rules such as “do not use doubled honorifics” or “do not overuse sasete-itadaku” make external text easier to read.

- Write in polite form (desu/masu).
- Avoid excessive honorifics. Use “sasete-itadaku” at most once per email.
- Write only the internal note at the end (the remarks section) in plain form.

#Standardise internal terms and loanwords

Where more than one word refers to the same thing, specify which to use. Decide too whether to use a katakana loanword or its Japanese equivalent.

- Standardise on the following:
  “顧客” (do not use “クライアント” or “お客さん”)
  “持ち帰り事項” (do not use “ToDo” or “アクションアイテム”)
  “見込み案件” (do not use “パイプライン”)
- Include the long vowel mark (“サーバー”, “ユーザー”).
- Expand internal abbreviations (such as short names for meetings) to the
  official name before writing.

#Keep proper nouns consistent

In speech, company and personal names get shortened, and transcription of them varies. Writing the correct form into the instructions makes them consistent in the output.

- Write company names in full. Do not drop the position of “株式会社”.
  e.g. “〇〇商事” → “株式会社〇〇商事”
- Add the honorific “さん” to personal names, and do not also give job titles.
- Replace product names referred to by short forms during the meeting with
  the official names below.
  “新版” → “〇〇 2.0” / “旧システム” → “〇〇 販売管理”
- Where the correct form of a proper noun cannot be confirmed, quote it as
  spoken rather than guessing, and append “【表記要確認】”.

Proper nouns that recur during meetings are better registered in the dictionary at the transcription stage, which saves correcting them in the instructions. How to set that up is in Customising transcription.

#Decide the granularity of bullet points

Without a specified granularity, bullet lists end up mixing one-line items with long paragraphs. Decide the number of items, the characters or sentences per item, and how deep the nesting goes.

- Use a single level of bullets; do not nest.
- Keep each item to one sentence, within 60 full-width characters.
- Use between three and seven items. Beyond seven, break with a heading.
- Do not end on a noun; write the full predicate.

#Decide the format of numbers and units

Specify the format for amounts, periods, headcounts and dates to match your internal documentation standards.

- Use half-width numerals with a separator every three digits (1,200,000円).
- Append “円” to amounts and always state whether tax is included. Where the
  meeting did not say, write “（税区分の記載なし）”.
- Write dates in the form “2026年4月1日”, with the day of the week in brackets.
- Write periods in the form “4月1日〜4月30日”.
- Use “%” for proportions, to one decimal place.
- Do not supply figures that were not stated in the meeting, or estimate them.

#Make it lead with the conclusion

Japanese meetings often work through the background before arriving at a conclusion, and summarising them as they stand puts the conclusion at the end. Where the reader is a decision-maker or a busy manager, specify the order explicitly.

- Put a “結論” heading at the top with the conclusion alone, in no more than
  three sentences. Do not put background or preamble before it.
- Follow the conclusion with “理由”, in no more than three points.
- Put the history and the detail of the discussion in a later “補足” section.
- Where the meeting did not settle on a conclusion, write “未確定” under the
  “結論” heading and give the reason in one sentence.

#Write the background once

The advantage of a recipe is that you can write in the background you would otherwise explain every time. Including the following keeps the quality of the output steady.

  • what your company does and who its main customers are
  • product names, feature names, and the terms used internally
  • for a development team, the languages and architecture in use
  • your own role and what you want this document to achieve
  • colleagues' names and what they are responsible for
  • the background and history of each project

Another approach is to create a “company background” recipe containing only that context, run it at the start of a chat, and then use other recipes in the same thread.

#Include an example of the output

For documents where the format matters, pasting in one real example is more reliable than listing rules. Paste an email you wrote previously, the format of your internal minutes, or the heading structure of a report straight into the instructions.

Follow this format exactly.

---
件名: 【〇〇案件】本日の打ち合わせの御礼と確認事項

株式会社〇〇
〇〇様

お世話になっております。〇〇株式会社の〇〇です。
本日はお時間をいただきありがとうございました。

本日決定した事項は以下のとおりです。
・（項目）
・（項目）

次回までの宿題は以下のとおりです。
・弊社: （内容）（〇月〇日まで）
・貴社: （内容）（〇月〇日まで）

引き続きよろしくお願いいたします。
---

#Work within the data available

A recipe can only see the meeting data stored in {{PRODUCT}} and the material you attach. The scope is described in detail in Asking your notes questions (chat).

What causes trouble when writing instructions is assuming information outside that scope. Asking it to “list the outstanding tasks”, for instance, will not work, because it cannot tell which are already finished. Unless someone said in the meeting that something was done, there is nothing to distinguish them by. Attach whatever material is needed, and include a rule against filling in what is not in the record.

- Do not write anything that is not in the meeting record.
- Where something is unclear, write “記録なし” and do not fill it in.
- Do not supplement explanations with general knowledge.

#Try it and fix it

Instructions are never finished in one go. Accuracy improves by writing, testing, finding where it broke down, and adding a rule to prevent that.

Choosing “Preview” on the recipe editing screen runs it against one meeting or folder as a test. Look at the result, fix the instructions, run it again, and you can compare the effect of the change on the spot.

Only make rules for what actually broke

Trying to specify everything from the start makes the instructions too long to manage. Add rules only for the problems you actually hit. Adding one rule at a time against a concrete symptom — “the conclusion always ends up last”, “honorifics on names are inconsistent”, “extra table columns keep appearing” — produces shorter, more effective instructions in the end.

Check

Before saving the instructions, check the following.

  • the reader is named at the top
  • polite or plain form is specified
  • heading names and order, table columns and the number of items are concrete
  • the format of numbers, dates and amounts is specified
  • there is a rule against filling in what is not in the record
  • the opening of the instructions matches whether the recipe is for one meeting or several

#Differences between models

Even with the tone specified in the instructions, output tendencies vary by model. The longer and more complex the document, the more the reasoning model suits; for a quick check during a meeting or a routine list, the standard model means less waiting. What you can specify and how to choose are in Choosing an AI model. Try the same recipe on both models and pick whichever is closer to your own documents.

#Examples: for a single meeting

Instructions you can save and use as they are. Rewrite company names, department names and assessment criteria to match your own situation. Each is structured the same way: explain the purpose at the top, list the rules to observe, then specify the output format at the end.

#Formatting minutes for internal circulation

Produce minutes for internal circulation. The readers are members of the same
department who did not attend, and their manager.

Rules:
- Write in polite form (desu/masu).
- Put “決定事項” first, then “議論の要点” and “持ち帰り事項” in that order.
- Under decisions, write only what was actually decided. Proposals still under
  consideration go under the discussion points.
- Make the take-aways a three-column table: owner / item / deadline. Where no
  deadline was stated, write “未定” rather than inventing a date.
- Use the form of speakers' names used in the meeting (honorific “さん” throughout).
- Write amounts with half-width numerals and “円”, and dates as “YYYY年M月D日”.
- Do not write anything not discussed in the meeting. Where unclear, write “記録なし”.

Output format:
## 会議名 / 日時 / 出席者
## 決定事項
## 議論の要点
## 持ち帰り事項（表）

#Turning sales notes into a daily report

From the record of this sales meeting, produce text to paste into the sales
daily report. The reader is my manager.

Rules:
- Write concisely in plain form (da/de aru). No more than two sentences per item.
- Always produce these headings, in this order: 訪問先 / 面談者 / 目的 /
  先方の反応 / 課題 / 次のアクション.
- Base the customer's reaction on what was said, not on my inference. Where
  nothing was said on a point, write “言及なし”.
- For likelihood of winning and amounts, write only figures the customer
  stated. Do not write our own projections.
- Include our owner and the planned date under next actions.

#Drafting a visit report email

Draft an email thanking them for today's meeting and confirming what was
discussed. The recipients are the attendees from the other company.

Rules:
- Output in the order subject, salutation, body, closing.
- Write in polite form. Do not use excessive (doubled) honorifics.
- Open with one sentence of thanks and get to the point. No more than three
  lines of preamble.
- Summarise what was decided as three to six bullets, one line each.
- Separate what we will do from what we are asking of them.
- Give an explicit date for any request with a deadline. Where the meeting
  gave no date, write “【要確認】” and leave it blank.
- This goes outside the company, so use official names rather than internal
  abbreviations or nicknames.

#A report for the department head from a weekly meeting

A longer example, with the background and rules written out in full.

The weekly departmental meeting has just finished. Your job is to produce,
from the record of this meeting, the weekly report submitted to the department
head, who did not attend.

Background:
- This department handles B2B order processing.
- “案件” means a deal before it is won; “契約” means one already signed.
- There are three owners (Tanaka, Sato, Suzuki).

Rules:
- Write in polite form.
- Open with “今週の結論” in no more than three sentences. Do not put the
  background first.
- Then use the headings “進捗”, “懸案” and “来週の予定”, in that order.
- Use bullets under each heading: one sentence per item, within 60 full-width
  characters, three to seven items.
- Half-width numerals; amounts with thousands separators and “円”, stating the
  tax treatment.
- Write dates in the form “2026年4月1日”.
- Add “さん” to personal names. Write company names in full.
- Do not supply figures or projections that were not stated in the meeting.
  Where nothing was said, write “言及なし”.
- For each concern, state the owner and whether a decision is required.

#A review of a one-to-one

Organise the record of a one-to-one I held as the manager into a review for
next time. This will not be shared with the other person.

Rules:
- Clearly separate “what they said” from “my impression”. Always mark the
  impressions with “（解釈）”.
- Quote what they said they were struggling with, close to their own words.
- Where they mentioned changes since last time, pull those passages out.
- Finish with two or three lines on whether I talked for too long, and on the
  balance between questions and explanation.
- Do not write anything amounting to a performance or HR judgement.

#A recruitment interview scorecard

From the interview record, draft a scorecard. This is for a mid-career sales
hire.

Rules:
- Use four criteria: 経験の適合 / 課題解決の進め方 / 顧客との関係構築 /
  入社後に想定される立ち上がり.
- For each, quote one or two things the candidate said as evidence, then give
  two or three lines of assessment. Quotes should follow what was actually
  said rather than paraphrasing the gist.
- Where nothing relevant was said, write “確認できず” and propose one question
  to ask at the next interview.
- Do not write a hire/no-hire decision. Do not touch on age, family
  circumstances, place of origin or anything else that must not form part of
  the selection criteria.

#Examples: for several meetings

In recipes covering several meetings, include an instruction to keep a record of which meeting each statement came from, so you can trace back to the original note later.

#A summary to attach to an approval request

From the records of the selected meetings, produce a summary of how the matter
was considered, to attach to an approval request. The reader is the approver,
who attended none of the individual meetings.

Rules:
- Give the conclusion first, in one paragraph of no more than three sentences.
- Then set out “検討の経緯” chronologically, each item beginning with the date
  of the meeting.
- Present “検討した選択肢” as a table with the columns 案 / 主な利点 /
  主な懸念 / 会議での扱い.
- For amounts, periods and headcounts, give only figures stated in the
  meetings, with the date of the source meeting in brackets.
- End with the unresolved points as bullets.
- Do not supply conjecture or general observations. Do not write anything that
  is not in the record.

#Building an incident timeline

From the records of the selected meetings, produce a timeline of the incident
response. The readers are the development and operations teams, who were not
involved in the response.

Rules:
- Organise it into five parts: 検知 / 一次対応 / 原因の切り分け / 恒久対応 /
  未完了の作業.
- Format each line as 時刻 / 事象 / 誰が対応したか. Where no time was stated in
  the meeting, write “時刻不明” and preserve only the ordering.
- Separate confirmed facts about the cause from hypotheses. Mark hypotheses
  with “（仮説）”.
- Put the preventive measures agreed in the meeting into a table with owners
  and deadlines.
- Do not write anything assessing individual responsibility.

#Organising customer requests for product development

From the records of the selected customer meetings, organise the requests made
of the product. The reader is a product developer who did not attend the
meetings.

Rules:
- Write in plain form.
- Classify requests into four: 機能の追加 / 既存機能の改善 / 不具合の指摘 /
  運用上の相談. Leave anything that fits none of them unclassified.
- For each request, always give:
  customer name (official) / the gist of what was said / the date of the
  meeting it was said in / the reason the customer gave
- Where the same request comes from several customers, combine it into one
  item and list the customer names together.
- Do not apply your own prioritisation. Order simply by how often each came up.
- Do not guess at feature names or specifications that do not appear in the
  record.

#If something is not working

The format changes every time you run it

Either the output format is not specified, or the specification is abstract. Write the heading names and order, the table columns, the number of items and the length per item as concrete figures.

Some of the rules are not being followed

Where the rules are very long, instructions towards the end can be applied less reliably. Move the important rules to the top, or split the recipe in two and run them in stages.

Expressions that should not leave the company appear

State a rule replacing internal abbreviations and nicknames with official names. In recipes for external use, include a rule saying “do not output names used only internally”.

I want different conditions per project

Recipes do not support variables, so create separate recipes with the conditions written in. For details see Recipes (saved instructions).

getting-more-from-your-notes/writing-eff.text: A recipe is a set of instructions you write once and get the same shape of output from every time. The shorter the instructions, though, the more the output varies. This article covers how to build the instructions, which specifications matter most when writing in Japanese, and how to test and refine them — ending with examples you can save and use as they are. Note Creating, saving, sharing and deleting recipes is covered in Recipes (saved instructions) . This article deals only with what to put in the instructions field on the creation screen. # Decide the shape first Recipes are either for “a single meeting” or for “several meetings”, and which you are building changes how the instructions are written. The difference, and how to choose, are in the creation steps in Recipes (saved instructions) . What matters when writing is that the input your instructions assume matches the input actually supplied. Instructions that say “this meeting” in a recipe for several meetings leave it unclear which meeting is meant, and the output becomes unstable. Conversely, “compare the meetings with each other” in a single-meeting recipe has nothing to compare against. For several meetings, open with something that assumes a set, such as “from the records of the selected meetings”. # The basic structure of an instruction For consistent output, this order is easiest to work with. Define the job : start by saying who uses the document, in what situation, and for what. Naming the reader settles the tone and the level of detail. Background : write in the information you would otherwise explain every time — company, product, team structure, the history of a project. Rules : list the conditions you want observed. This is the main thing that keeps the output from drifting. Output format : specify the order of headings, the table columns, the number of items, and the length of each. Example output : where the format matters, paste in a real example, however short. An example opening: A meeting has just finished and a follow-up email to the attendees is needed. Your job is to write an external-facing email setting out the decisions and next actions. The readers are the client contact and their manager. When writing rules, imagine you are addressing someone who has just joined. Assumptions that are second nature internally do not carry across unless you write them down. Expressions such as “in the usual format” or “summarise appropriately” mean different things to different people, and do not work as instructions. # Tips for instructions in Japanese Japanese documents involve many formal choices that English does not. Unless you specify them, a different choice is made every time, so set them down as rules in the recipe. # Specify polite or plain form State whether to write in polite form (desu/masu) or plain form (da/de aru). Without it, the two can end up mixed within a single document. Deciding by purpose — polite form for external documents, plain form for internal records and analysis notes — removes the question. You can specify the degree of honorific language too. Rules such as “do not use doubled honorifics” or “do not overuse sasete-itadaku” make external text easier to read. - Write in polite form (desu/masu). - Avoid excessive honorifics. Use “sasete-itadaku” at most once per email. - Write only the internal note at the end (the remarks section) in plain form. # Standardise internal terms and loanwords Where more than one word refers to the same thing, specify which to use. Decide too whether to use a katakana loanword or its Japanese equivalent. - Standardise on the following: “顧客” (do not use “クライアント” or “お客さん”) “持ち帰り事項” (do not use “ToDo” or “アクションアイテム”) “見込み案件” (do not use “パイプライン”) - Include the long vowel mark (“サーバー”, “ユーザー”). - Expand internal abbreviations (such as short names for meetings) to the official name before writing. # Keep proper nouns consistent In speech, company and personal names get shortened, and transcription of them varies. Writing the correct form into the instructions makes them consistent in the output. - Write company names in full. Do not drop the position of “株式会社”. e.g. “〇〇商事” → “株式会社〇〇商事” - Add the honorific “さん” to personal names, and do not also give job titles. - Replace product names referred to by short forms during the meeting with the official names below. “新版” → “〇〇 2.0” / “旧システム” → “〇〇 販売管理” - Where the correct form of a proper noun cannot be confirmed, quote it as spoken rather than guessing, and append “【表記要確認】”. Proper nouns that recur during meetings are better registered in the dictionary at the transcription stage, which saves correcting them in the instructions. How to set that up is in Customising transcription . # Decide the granularity of bullet points Without a specified granularity, bullet lists end up mixing one-line items with long paragraphs. Decide the number of items, the characters or sentences per item, and how deep the nesting goes. - Use a single level of bullets; do not nest. - Keep each item to one sentence, within 60 full-width characters. - Use between three and seven items. Beyond seven, break with a heading. - Do not end on a noun; write the full predicate. # Decide the format of numbers and units Specify the format for amounts, periods, headcounts and dates to match your internal documentation standards. - Use half-width numerals with a separator every three digits (1,200,000円). - Append “円” to amounts and always state whether tax is included. Where the meeting did not say, write “（税区分の記載なし）”. - Write dates in the form “2026年4月1日”, with the day of the week in brackets. - Write periods in the form “4月1日〜4月30日”. - Use “%” for proportions, to one decimal place. - Do not supply figures that were not stated in the meeting, or estimate them. # Make it lead with the conclusion Japanese meetings often work through the background before arriving at a conclusion, and summarising them as they stand puts the conclusion at the end. Where the reader is a decision-maker or a busy manager, specify the order explicitly. - Put a “結論” heading at the top with the conclusion alone, in no more than three sentences. Do not put background or preamble before it. - Follow the conclusion with “理由”, in no more than three points. - Put the history and the detail of the discussion in a later “補足” section. - Where the meeting did not settle on a conclusion, write “未確定” under the “結論” heading and give the reason in one sentence. # Write the background once The advantage of a recipe is that you can write in the background you would otherwise explain every time. Including the following keeps the quality of the output steady. what your company does and who its main customers are product names, feature names, and the terms used internally for a development team, the languages and architecture in use your own role and what you want this document to achieve colleagues' names and what they are responsible for the background and history of each project Another approach is to create a “company background” recipe containing only that context, run it at the start of a chat, and then use other recipes in the same thread. # Include an example of the output For documents where the format matters, pasting in one real example is more reliable than listing rules. Paste an email you wrote previously, the format of your internal minutes, or the heading structure of a report straight into the instructions. Follow this format exactly. --- 件名: 【〇〇案件】本日の打ち合わせの御礼と確認事項 株式会社〇〇 〇〇様 お世話になっております。〇〇株式会社の〇〇です。 本日はお時間をいただきありがとうございました。 本日決定した事項は以下のとおりです。 ・（項目） ・（項目） 次回までの宿題は以下のとおりです。 ・弊社: （内容）（〇月〇日まで） ・貴社: （内容）（〇月〇日まで） 引き続きよろしくお願いいたします。 --- # Work within the data available A recipe can only see the meeting data stored in {{PRODUCT}} and the material you attach. The scope is described in detail in Asking your notes questions (chat) . What causes trouble when writing instructions is assuming information outside that scope. Asking it to “list the outstanding tasks”, for instance, will not work, because it cannot tell which are already finished. Unless someone said in the meeting that something was done, there is nothing to distinguish them by. Attach whatever material is needed, and include a rule against filling in what is not in the record. - Do not write anything that is not in the meeting record. - Where something is unclear, write “記録なし” and do not fill it in. - Do not supplement explanations with general knowledge. # Try it and fix it Instructions are never finished in one go. Accuracy improves by writing, testing, finding where it broke down, and adding a rule to prevent that. Choosing “Preview” on the recipe editing screen runs it against one meeting or folder as a test. Look at the result, fix the instructions, run it again, and you can compare the effect of the change on the spot. Only make rules for what actually broke Trying to specify everything from the start makes the instructions too long to manage. Add rules only for the problems you actually hit. Adding one rule at a time against a concrete symptom — “the conclusion always ends up last”, “honorifics on names are inconsistent”, “extra table columns keep appearing” — produces shorter, more effective instructions in the end. Figure Screenshot: preview on the recipe editing screen The instructions field on the left, the test run's result on the right, and a field at the top for choosing the meeting to run against. Check Before saving the instructions, check the following. the reader is named at the top polite or plain form is specified heading names and order, table columns and the number of items are concrete the format of numbers, dates and amounts is specified there is a rule against filling in what is not in the record the opening of the instructions matches whether the recipe is for one meeting or several # Differences between models Even with the tone specified in the instructions, output tendencies vary by model. The longer and more complex the document, the more the reasoning model suits; for a quick check during a meeting or a routine list, the standard model means less waiting. What you can specify and how to choose are in Choosing an AI model . Try the same recipe on both models and pick whichever is closer to your own documents. # Examples: for a single meeting Instructions you can save and use as they are. Rewrite company names, department names and assessment criteria to match your own situation. Each is structured the same way: explain the purpose at the top, list the rules to observe, then specify the output format at the end. # Formatting minutes for internal circulation Produce minutes for internal circulation. The readers are members of the same department who did not attend, and their manager. Rules: - Write in polite form (desu/masu). - Put “決定事項” first, then “議論の要点” and “持ち帰り事項” in that order. - Under decisions, write only what was actually decided. Proposals still under consideration go under the discussion points. - Make the take-aways a three-column table: owner / item / deadline. Where no deadline was stated, write “未定” rather than inventing a date. - Use the form of speakers' names used in the meeting (honorific “さん” throughout). - Write amounts with half-width numerals and “円”, and dates as “YYYY年M月D日”. - Do not write anything not discussed in the meeting. Where unclear, write “記録なし”. Output format: ## 会議名 / 日時 / 出席者 ## 決定事項 ## 議論の要点 ## 持ち帰り事項（表） # Turning sales notes into a daily report From the record of this sales meeting, produce text to paste into the sales daily report. customising/customising-transcription.title: Customising transcription
customising/customising-transcription.description: Registering technical terms and company names, default speaker names, and transcript display settings.
customising/customising-transcription.html:
In meetings full of company names, department names, product names and industry phrasing, registering the terms in advance improves the chance of them being transcribed correctly. You register them under Settings > Preferences > Language. There are two kinds: your own terms, which apply to your meetings, and shared terms, which apply across the workspace.

Registering helps most for words you can see would otherwise be misheard. Registering large numbers of ordinary Japanese words, or normal dictionary words, barely changes accuracy.

There is no need to register your own company name or the names of people attending the meeting — those come from the meeting's own information. Names of other companies mentioned in conversation, contacts at client companies, and external product names, on the other hand, are worth registering.

#What is worth registering for Japanese meetings

In Japanese speech, the common failure is the right sound written with the wrong characters. Registering words like these in advance means fewer corrections when you read the transcript back.

Type Example to register Typical error without it
Department names 品質保証部 the same reading written with different characters, such as “品質補償部”
Personal names (external, executives) 山田, 齋藤, 渡邊 replaced by a different surname with the same reading; old-form characters modernised
Names of internal documents and forms ＱＣ工程表, 日程遵守率 inconsistent spellings such as “QC工程票” or “日程順守率”
Product and project names project names, code names transcribed as ordinary nouns
Industry terms and abbreviations abbreviations used day to day on the ground turned into a different, similar-sounding word
Internal terms mixing English names that mix Japanese and English word boundaries fall differently from what you expect

Register proper nouns in the form actually spoken in meetings. If documents say “株式会社〇〇” but people say “〇〇さん” in conversation, register the spoken form.

In meetings that mix Japanese and English, the language setting itself affects the result too. See also Multi-language support.

#Registering your own terms

Your own terms apply only to your meetings.

  1. Settings > Preferences > Language.
  2. Your terms field, type the word you want to register.
  3. Enter to confirm.

You can register up to 30. Because the number is limited, the efficient approach is to register words in the order they actually cause errors.

If shared terms have already been registered at workspace level, you can see them by opening “View terms applied to everyone in this workspace” below your own list. Those apply automatically, so there is no need to register them again yourself.

#Registering terms for the whole workspace

Workspace terms apply to the transcripts of every member of that workspace. Words that should come out the same way no matter who in the organisation records the meeting — department names, your own product names — belong here.

Only workspace administrators can add and remove them.Settings > Workspace > General and edit them under Language. Members can view the list but not edit it. Up to 50 can be registered.

Shared terms are visible to every member

Any member of the workspace can see the list of workspace terms. Registering a project name or code name shared only within a limited group, or the name of an individual at a client company, can therefore make that fact known more widely than intended. Choose what you register on the basis that it will be seen.

#Examples

  • Registering your own service name spelled “Blokk” makes it less likely to be transcribed as “block”.
  • Registering a project name spelled like “Projekt DolFin” makes it less likely to be transcribed as “project dolphin”.
  • Registering a company name such as “Tekto” makes it less likely to be broken into similar-sounding words.

The same thinking applies in Japanese. If the same word comes out wrong in the same way meeting after meeting, that word is a candidate for registration.

#What registering does not do

  • Word replacement: registering makes a word more likely to be recognised when it is spoken. It is not a feature that mechanically replaces one word in the transcript with another. A similar-sounding word can still survive.
  • Blocks of text: each term is passed to transcription individually. Registering a long sentence or paragraph changes nothing unless that sentence is spoken exactly.
  • Expanding abbreviations: abbreviations are transcribed as spoken. They are not expanded to the full name in the transcript. To check what an abbreviation means, asking chat during or after the meeting is quicker.

#When it takes effect

Registered terms take effect from the transcripts of meetings recorded afterwards. Transcripts already recorded are never rewritten retrospectively. Where a past meeting has many errors, edit the transcript directly or check the content through chat.

#Speaker names and transcript display

The speaker names shown in a transcript are decided by a different mechanism from term registration. By default, speech captured from system audio and speech captured from your microphone are only distinguished by colour, with no names attached. Attaching the meeting tool's display names to speech requires setup such as a browser extension. Which meeting tools are supported, and the steps, are in Speaker labels.

On-screen actions during a meeting — showing and hiding the transcript panel, pausing and resuming, copying and searching — are described in How transcription works.

#If something is not working

If recognition does not improve after registering terms, the underlying audio may not be good enough. Check the microphone selection, system audio permission, and the distance between microphone and speaker along with background noise first. The steps are in Transcription problems.

toc.text: What is worth registering for Japanese meetings
Registering terms for the whole workspace

customising/customising-transcription.text: In meetings full of company names, department names, product names and industry phrasing, registering the terms in advance improves the chance of them being transcribed correctly. You register them under Settings > Preferences > Language . There are two kinds: your own terms, which apply to your meetings, and shared terms, which apply across the workspace. Registering helps most for words you can see would otherwise be misheard. Registering large numbers of ordinary Japanese words, or normal dictionary words, barely changes accuracy. There is no need to register your own company name or the names of people attending the meeting — those come from the meeting's own information. Names of other companies mentioned in conversation, contacts at client companies, and external product names, on the other hand, are worth registering. # What is worth registering for Japanese meetings In Japanese speech, the common failure is the right sound written with the wrong characters. Registering words like these in advance means fewer corrections when you read the transcript back. Type Example to register Typical error without it Department names 品質保証部 the same reading written with different characters, such as “品質補償部” Personal names (external, executives) 山田, 齋藤, 渡邊 replaced by a different surname with the same reading; old-form characters modernised Names of internal documents and forms ＱＣ工程表, 日程遵守率 inconsistent spellings such as “QC工程票” or “日程順守率” Product and project names project names, code names transcribed as ordinary nouns Industry terms and abbreviations abbreviations used day to day on the ground turned into a different, similar-sounding word Internal terms mixing English names that mix Japanese and English word boundaries fall differently from what you expect Register proper nouns in the form actually spoken in meetings. If documents say “株式会社〇〇” but people say “〇〇さん” in conversation, register the spoken form. In meetings that mix Japanese and English, the language setting itself affects the result too. See also Multi-language support . # Registering your own terms Your own terms apply only to your meetings. Settings > Preferences > Language . Your terms field, type the word you want to register. Enter to confirm. Figure Screenshot: your own terms under Settings > Preferences > Language Registered terms shown as tags below the input field. You can register up to 30. Because the number is limited, the efficient approach is to register words in the order they actually cause errors. If shared terms have already been registered at workspace level, you can see them by opening “View terms applied to everyone in this workspace” below your own list. Those apply automatically, so there is no need to register them again yourself. # Registering terms for the whole workspace Workspace terms apply to the transcripts of every member of that workspace. Words that should come out the same way no matter who in the organisation records the meeting — department names, your own product names — belong here. Only workspace administrators can add and remove them. Settings > Workspace > General and edit them under Language . Members can view the list but not edit it. Up to 50 can be registered. Figure Screenshot: shared terms under Settings > Workspace > General The list of terms an administrator can edit, with the field for adding more. Shared terms are visible to every member Any member of the workspace can see the list of workspace terms. Registering a project name or code name shared only within a limited group, or the name of an individual at a client company, can therefore make that fact known more widely than intended. Choose what you register on the basis that it will be seen. # Examples Registering your own service name spelled “Blokk” makes it less likely to be transcribed as “block”. Registering a project name spelled like “Projekt DolFin” makes it less likely to be transcribed as “project dolphin”. Registering a company name such as “Tekto” makes it less likely to be broken into similar-sounding words. The same thinking applies in Japanese. If the same word comes out wrong in the same way meeting after meeting, that word is a candidate for registration. # What registering does not do Word replacement : registering makes a word more likely to be recognised when it is spoken. It is not a feature that mechanically replaces one word in the transcript with another. A similar-sounding word can still survive. Blocks of text : each term is passed to transcription individually. Registering a long sentence or paragraph changes nothing unless that sentence is spoken exactly. Expanding abbreviations : abbreviations are transcribed as spoken. They are not expanded to the full name in the transcript. To check what an abbreviation means, asking chat during or after the meeting is quicker. # When it takes effect Registered terms take effect from the transcripts of meetings recorded afterwards. Transcripts already recorded are never rewritten retrospectively.
