consent-security-privacy/getting-consent.title: How far you can rely on AI meeting notes (a guide for teams)
consent-security-privacy/getting-consent.description: What Japanese law permits for recording and transcription, how to write internal rules, and wording to use at the start of a meeting.
consent-security-privacy/getting-consent.html:
We are often asked whether consent has to be obtained from everyone present before recording and transcribing a meeting. Under Japanese law, the answer depends on the situation. This article separates what the law actually requires from practices that are not required but strongly advisable, and then gives wording you can use as-is, a draft internal policy, and a basis for deciding which meetings to avoid.

Please note

This article is general information compiled by {{COMPANY}} and is not legal advice. For decisions on a specific matter, consult your own legal department or a lawyer.

Note

What {{PRODUCT}} records is an online meeting you join on a computer. The desktop app (macOS / Windows) or a browser on your computer (Chrome / Edge) captures the audio your computer plays and your microphone audio on the device itself, so everything in this article assumes that scope. Telephone calls, in-person discussions not involving a computer, and recording bots that join meetings are outside {{PRODUCT}}'s scope.

About telling people you are recordingThe notice shown when recording starts, and how to tell people→Security and privacy FAQsStorage location, cross-border transfer, disclosure requests→Use in healthcare, finance and professional servicesAdditional considerations by sector→How transcription worksWhen audio is captured→

#The starting point: Japan has no general prohibition on recording

Many overseas help articles state flatly that consent must be obtained from everyone before recording. That reflects the all-party consent regime adopted in some US states and does not describe Japanese law. Japan has neither a law generally prohibiting a party to a conversation from recording a conversation they are in, nor a law generally requiring consent from everyone present before recording.

The “Wiretapping Act” often cited in this context governs compulsory measures by investigative authorities.

LegislationAct on Wiretapping for Criminal Investigation, Article 1 (purpose) / Article 3 (wiretap warrants)

This Act sets out the requirements and procedure for the compulsory measure of intercepting telecommunications, carried out by a public prosecutor or judicial police officer under a warrant issued by a judge. What it governs is interception by investigative authorities; it does not apply to a participant recording a meeting they are in.

As for the Telecommunications Business Act, which protects the secrecy of communications, what it protects is “communications being handled by a telecommunications carrier”.

LegislationTelecommunications Business Act, Article 4 (protection of secrecy)

This provides that the secrecy of communications being handled by a telecommunications carrier must not be violated, and imposes confidentiality obligations on people engaged in the telecommunications business, both during and after their employment. The {{PRODUCT}} desktop app captures the audio your computer plays and your microphone audio inside the computer. Because {{COMPANY}} does not sit in the meeting service's communication path intercepting the call, we take the view that capturing meeting audio does not itself constitute a violation prohibited by this provision.

#Being lawful and avoiding trouble are different things

Even where recording does not fall foul of a criminal prohibition, civil liability can still arise depending on how and why it is done. The trend in the case law is that audio recorded by one party to a conversation without telling the other is, as a rule, admissible in civil proceedings. That is a ruling that it can be used as evidence, not a guarantee that the recording was lawful in all respects. Disseminating recorded audio beyond its purpose, for example, is territory where a tort claim for invasion of privacy can succeed.

LegislationCivil Code, Article 709 (damages in tort) / Article 710 (damages for non-pecuniary loss)

A person who intentionally or negligently infringes another's rights or legally protected interests is liable in damages. Article 710 makes emotional harm compensable. Invasion of privacy is litigated through these provisions.

The level of risk in different situations can be set out as follows.

Situation Assessment
Recording a meeting you are taking part in recording by a party; as a rule not unlawful
Recording a conversation between others that you are not part of, without telling them you are not a party, and the risk of a tort claim for invasion of privacy is considerably higher
Leaving a computer in a meeting room while you step out, continuing to record the conversation in your absence you cease to be a party, so this is assessed much like recording between third parties above
Publishing or circulating recorded audio or notes beyond their purpose separately from the act of recording, invasion of privacy or defamation can arise
Recording employees' conversations on an ongoing basis and using it for monitoring this has to be balanced against workers' privacy and personal interests

Do not use {{PRODUCT}} to record conversations you are not part of.

#What the law actually requires

What requires “consent” is not recording as such, but particular aspects of how the personal information acquired is handled. The “legal obligation” rows in the table below are the parts where failure can lead to sanctions or civil liability.

Strength Requirement Basis
Legal obligation Where recording or transcription acquires personal information, promptly notify the individual of the purpose of use or make it public, unless the purpose has been published in advance Act on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 21(1)
Legal obligation Do not acquire information by deception or other improper means, such as recording without telling participants Act on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 20(1)
Legal obligation Where you acquire information expecting it to contain sensitive personal information such as medical history or a criminal record, obtain the individual's prior consent as a rule Act on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 20(2)
Legal obligation Where audio, transcripts or notes acquired are provided to a third party, obtain the individual's prior consent as a rule (with exceptions such as delegation and joint use) Act on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 27(1) and (5)
Legal obligation Where monitoring covers employees, put appropriate arrangements in place as part of security control measures and supervision of employees Act on the Protection of Personal Information, Articles 23 and 24
Legal obligation Where the handling of personal data is delegated to an external service, exercise necessary and appropriate supervision over that processor Act on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 25
Strongly recommended Say at the start of the meeting that it is being recorded and transcribed, and display it in the meeting chat too reducing civil risk, maintaining trust
Strongly recommended Be able to stop recording where a participant objects as above
Recommended For meetings with external attendees, give notice of recording in the invitation as well dispute prevention
Custom / optional Obtain explicit individual consent from every participant not a general obligation under Japanese law. Done at the other party's request or under internal rules

#Specifying the purpose of use and notifying or publishing it

Meeting audio, transcript text, AI-enhanced notes and speaker names can readily be cross-referenced with attendees' names and calendar invitations, so they normally constitute personal information. A company that records has to decide what it acquires this personal information for and how it will be used, and put that where the individual can find it.

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 21(1) (notification of the purpose of use on acquisition)

When personal information is acquired, the purpose of use must be promptly notified to the individual or made public, unless it has been published in advance. The familiar practice of a call centre announcing “this call is being recorded for quality purposes” is, in substance, less a procedure for obtaining permission to record than a way of meeting this requirement while also preventing disputes.

The purpose of use must be specified “as far as possible” (Article 17(1)). Wording such as “for our business activities” is not considered specific enough, so write it at a level the individual can predict — “producing minutes of meetings”, “sharing the content with employees who could not attend”.

#Do not record without telling participants

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 20(1) (proper acquisition)

This provides that personal information must not be acquired by deception or other improper means. Continuing to record and transcribe without telling participants at all risks amounting to such “improper means”. Announcing at the start of a meeting, and the notice {{PRODUCT}} shows when you start recording (for you to paste into the meeting chat), are the practical measures that address this.

#Where sensitive personal information may be discussed

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 20(2) (proper acquisition) / Article 2(3) (definition of sensitive personal information)

Personal information containing race, creed, social status, medical history, criminal record, the fact of having suffered harm from a crime, or the descriptions prescribed by Cabinet Order (disability, the results of health check-ups, guidance, diagnosis or dispensing by a doctor or similar, criminal proceedings, juvenile protection proceedings) is sensitive personal information, and acquiring it requires the individual's prior consent as a rule.

The person whose consent is needed here is the individual speaking. A workspace administrator or the meeting's host cannot consent on their behalf. Note that a statement amounting only to inference — “A seems unwell” — is not treated as sensitive personal information, but if a specific condition is recorded, as in “A is on leave with X”, that part is treated as medical history.

For personal data containing sensitive personal information, a leak is reportable to the Personal Information Protection Commission even if it affects a single individual. That is the point on which the design of a meeting-recording process usually turns.

#Passing data to third parties

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 27(1) and (5) (restriction on provision to third parties)

Providing personal data to a third party requires the individual's prior consent as a rule. However, provision accompanying delegation within the scope necessary to achieve the purpose of use, provision accompanying a business succession, and joint use meeting the stated requirements are treated as not involving a “third party”.

{{COMPANY}} provides {{PRODUCT}} as a party to whom the customer (the contracting company) has delegated the handling of personal data, and that relationship is not provision to a third party. Sending a note to an external service through an integration (a chat tool or CRM, say) is different: the destination is not {{COMPANY}}'s processor but a separate provider, so it can constitute provision to a third party. Before enabling an integration, check it against your company's personal data handling rules and the purposes of use you have specified.

#Recording meetings involving employees on an ongoing basis

The Personal Information Protection Commission's guideline Q&A sets out four points to bear in mind when monitoring employees who handle personal data.

  1. specify the purpose of the monitoring in advance, set it down in internal rules, and make it clear to employees
  2. designate who is responsible for carrying out the monitoring and what authority they have
  3. establish the rules for how it is done in advance, and make sure those operating it understand them
  4. check that it is being carried out properly, in accordance with those rules

Notifying and consulting a labour union, and informing employees, are also regarded as desirable. Where rules on recording and transcribing meetings apply across the company, they may need to go into the work rules.

LegislationLabour Standards Act, Article 89 (duty to prepare and file) / Article 90 (procedure for preparation)

An employer who regularly employs ten or more workers must prepare work rules and file them. Provisions applying to all workers at the workplace belong in the work rules. When preparing or amending them, the employer must hear the opinion of the union representing a majority of workers at that workplace, or, failing that, a person representing a majority of the workers.

Prohibiting covert recording in the workplace through the work rules is generally considered possible in itself. There is, however, a strong body of opinion questioning the validity of a blanket prohibition extending to recording done by a victim of harassment to preserve evidence, and treating it as a disciplinary matter. If you include a blanket prohibition, check how exceptions should be handled with your legal department.

#Wording you can use as-is

Adapt the wording below as needed, replacing the company name, storage location and who can see it.

#Spoken announcement at the start (internal meetings, standard)

Today's meeting is being recorded with {{PRODUCT}} to produce the minutes, and will be transcribed and summarised automatically. The record will be stored in 〔location〕 and can be seen by 〔attendees / project members〕. If that is a problem for anyone, please say so now.

#Spoken announcement at the start (meetings with external attendees)

One thing before we begin. We will be recording today's discussion so that we have an accurate record, and it will be transcribed and summarised automatically. We use the record solely to confirm internally what was discussed, and we are happy to share the minutes if you would like them. If you would prefer we did not record, please just say so and we will stop.

#Spoken announcement at the start (short version for regular meetings)

This meeting is being recorded and transcribed with {{PRODUCT}}. Let me know if that is a problem.

#For posting in meeting chat (one line)

This meeting is being recorded and transcribed to produce the minutes. Please let us know if that is a problem.

{{PRODUCT}} never posts to the meeting chat by itself. When you start recording, {{PRODUCT}} shows a short notice in Japanese and English; press Copy and paste it into the meeting chat (see About telling people you are recording). Tell people who join partway through out loud as well.

#A line to add to the meeting invitation

[Please note] This meeting is expected to be recorded and transcribed by AI in order to produce the minutes. The record will be used only to confirm what was discussed, and we are happy to share it on request. If you would prefer we did not record, please tell us on the day or reply in advance.

For recurring meeting invitations, putting this line in the body template removes the burden of announcing it out loud every time. For meetings with external attendees, telling them at the invitation stage rather than on the day makes it easier for them to decide.

#Wording for a first sales meeting

Thank you for making the time today. One thing I should mention: we use an AI recording and automatic summary tool so that we can pass on what was discussed accurately within our company. We use the record only to confirm internally what was discussed and to prepare our proposal, and we do not provide it to anyone outside. It is retained for 〔　〕 months, after which it is deleted automatically. If you would prefer we did not record, we will stop now — please just say.

#Draft internal policy

A template for setting this down as an internal policy. Adapt it in the light of your own work rules and labour procedures.

Article 1 (Purpose) The purpose of this policy is to set out how the meeting recording and automatic transcription tool (the “Tool”) is to be used at this company, so as to reconcile efficiency in our work with the proper protection of meeting participants' privacy and personal information.

Article 2 (Purposes of use) The Tool is used for the following purposes. It must not be used for any other purpose. (1) producing and sharing the minutes of meetings (2) sharing the content with employees unable to attend (3) recording how business decisions were arrived at

Article 3 (Prior announcement) 1. Before starting to record, an employee using the Tool (a “User”) must inform all participants in the meeting that recording and transcription will take place, the purpose, where the record will be stored, and who will be able to see it. 2. For meetings with external attendees, notice that recording will take place shall so far as possible also be given when the meeting is convened. 3. Where a participant objects to recording, the User shall stop recording and, where necessary, delete the record of that meeting.

Article 4 (Prohibited acts) A User must not: (1) record a conversation they are not taking part in (2) begin recording without giving the announcement, or continue recording contrary to it (3) use the Tool in a way intended to keep participants from noticing that they are being recorded (4) use a record for any purpose other than those in Article 2, or provide it to anyone outside those entitled to see it (5) use the Tool for the purpose of personnel evaluation, attendance management or any other monitoring of an individual employee

Article 5 (Handling of sensitive personal information) The Tool shall as a rule not be used in meetings where health, medical history, creed or other sensitive personal information is expected to be discussed (occupational health consultations, HR interviews and the like). Where its use is unavoidable, the individual's prior consent must be obtained.

Article 6 (Retention period and deletion) Records shall be retained for 〔　〕 months from the date of creation and deleted promptly thereafter. Where a participant asks for deletion, the responsible manager shall decide whether to delete, having confirmed whether the record is needed for business purposes.

Article 7 (Responsible manager) The manager responsible for use of the Tool shall be 〔department / position〕, who shall issue and suspend accounts, set viewing permissions, and check compliance with this policy.

Article 8 (Treatment as monitoring) The company does not use the Tool as a means of monitoring individual employees. Where use of the Tool is reviewed, this shall be carried out under the responsibility of the responsible manager, having first made the purpose and method clear to employees.

#Which meetings to use it for, and which to avoid

The law draws no uniform line, but meetings where a record is likely to cause harm share common features. Use the table below as a starting point for drawing your own line when rolling this out.

Kind of meeting Guidance Why
Regular progress meetings, project meetings fine to use there is a strong business need for a record, and little likelihood of sensitive personal information arising
External sales meetings, regular client meetings fine to use, having announced it give notice in the invitation and at the start, and make sure the other party is able to decline
Recruitment interviews judge carefully obtain the candidate's consent and define internally how far it may be used as an assessment record. Stop on the spot if the conversation turns to health or beliefs
Performance reviews, disciplinary interviews avoid disciplinary history and health are likely to come up, and the existence of a record itself has a chilling effect on those involved. Where a record is needed, use HR's prescribed form
Labour negotiations, consultations with a union avoid given the nature of negotiation, recording at one party's discretion bears directly on trust between the parties. Agree in advance whether recording is permitted
Occupational health consultations, health consultations, leave and return-to-work interviews do not use health check results and guidance from a doctor are sensitive personal information, and acquiring them requires the individual's consent
Meetings with a lawyer or tax accountant do not use, or check in advance this engages professional confidentiality obligations and the protection of the client's secrets. For details see Use in healthcare, finance and professional services
Healthcare or care consultations with a patient or service user present do not use clinical information is sensitive personal information, and conformity with healthcare sector guidelines also needs separate consideration
Internal whistleblowing, interviews at a harassment contact point do not use protecting the person reporting comes first. The scope of the record and how it is stored should follow your whistleblowing policy
Board meetings, investment and M&A discussions set it out specifically in internal rules record retention duties and the scope of disclosure are constrained by the Companies Act and by contract. Follow your legal department's judgement

Where the conversation turns to something sensitive partway through a meeting, stop recording and start again once the topic has moved on. Part of a transcript cannot be deleted on its own, so if something that should not be kept has been recorded, delete the whole note. How to do that is explained in Deleting notes.

#When a participant says no

If someone asks you not to record, stop there and then. Being able to stop when an objection is raised is what keeps the announcement from being a formality.

Options after stopping include:

  1. not transcribing that meeting and recording it with typed notes instead
  2. pausing only for the sensitive part of the agenda and recording the rest
  3. writing up the key points afterwards as you understood them, and asking the other party to confirm them

If you are asked to delete something already recorded, delete the whole note. Part of a transcript cannot be deleted on its own. A note can be permanently deleted by its owner or an admin. How to delete is covered in Deleting notes.

#Steps for writing internal rules

Deciding the rules at rollout saves each user making the judgement every time. In practice this order works well.

  1. 1

    Write out the purposes of use

    List the purposes you will actually use it for — producing minutes, sharing with those who could not attend, recording how decisions were made. This is what corresponds to specifying the purpose of use under the Act on the Protection of Personal Information and to what goes in your privacy policy.

  2. 2

    Decide which meetings it is not used for

    Start from the table under “Which meetings to use it for, and which to avoid” and add to or cut from it to suit your own circumstances. Turn what you decide into the articles of an internal policy.

  3. 3

    Decide how the announcement is made

    Decide which of a spoken announcement, pasting the notice into the meeting chat, and standard wording in the invitation are mandatory.

  4. 4

    Decide the retention period

    Decide how long notes and imported emails and chat should be kept, and have an admin set it under Settings → Workspace → General → Data retention. The choices are 6, 12, 24 or 36 months, or keep forever; the default is 12 months. See Automatic transcript deletion for details.

  5. 5

    Decide how notes are shared

    New notes start out private. Decide which notes go into folders and who they are shared with. There are no public links that let people outside the organisation open a note. See Sharing controls.

  6. 6

    Inform employees

    Where this involves amending the work rules, carry out the opinion-hearing procedure under Article 90 of the Labour Standards Act.

  7. 7

    Check how it is being used

    This corresponds to the fourth point in the guideline Q&A on monitoring. The responsible manager periodically checks that it is being used in accordance with the rules.

Check
  • the purposes of use are documented and reflected in the privacy policy or internal rules
  • the meetings it is not used for are listed and communicated
  • which announcement methods (spoken, meeting chat, invitation) are mandatory has been decided
  • the data retention period has been checked and changed if needed
  • how notes are placed in folders and shared, and whether they may be exported to outside services, have been decided
  • whether the work rules need amending has been checked

For what administrators can do, see also Making recording notices a rule in your organisation (for admins).

The desktop app (macOS / Windows) or a browser on your computer (Chrome / Edge) captures the audio your computer plays and your microphone audio on the device itself, so everything in this article assumes that scope. Telephone calls, in-person discussions not involving a computer, and recording bots that join meetings are outside {{PRODUCT}}'s scope. About telling people you are recording The notice shown when recording starts, and how to tell people → Security and privacy FAQs Storage location, cross-border transfer, disclosure requests → Use in healthcare, finance and professional services Additional considerations by sector → How transcription works When audio is captured → # The starting point: Japan has no general prohibition on recording Many overseas help articles state flatly that consent must be obtained from everyone before recording. That reflects the all-party consent regime adopted in some US states and does not describe Japanese law. Japan has neither a law generally prohibiting a party to a conversation from recording a conversation they are in, nor a law generally requiring consent from everyone present before recording. The “Wiretapping Act” often cited in this context governs compulsory measures by investigative authorities. Legislation Act on Wiretapping for Criminal Investigation, Article 1 (purpose) / Article 3 (wiretap warrants) This Act sets out the requirements and procedure for the compulsory measure of intercepting telecommunications, carried out by a public prosecutor or judicial police officer under a warrant issued by a judge. What it governs is interception by investigative authorities; it does not apply to a participant recording a meeting they are in. As for the Telecommunications Business Act, which protects the secrecy of communications, what it protects is “communications being handled by a telecommunications carrier”. Legislation Telecommunications Business Act, Article 4 (protection of secrecy) This provides that the secrecy of communications being handled by a telecommunications carrier must not be violated, and imposes confidentiality obligations on people engaged in the telecommunications business, both during and after their employment. The {{PRODUCT}} desktop app captures the audio your computer plays and your microphone audio inside the computer. Because {{COMPANY}} does not sit in the meeting service's communication path intercepting the call, we take the view that capturing meeting audio does not itself constitute a violation prohibited by this provision. # Being lawful and avoiding trouble are different things Even where recording does not fall foul of a criminal prohibition, civil liability can still arise depending on how and why it is done. The trend in the case law is that audio recorded by one party to a conversation without telling the other is, as a rule, admissible in civil proceedings. That is a ruling that it can be used as evidence, not a guarantee that the recording was lawful in all respects. Disseminating recorded audio beyond its purpose, for example, is territory where a tort claim for invasion of privacy can succeed. Legislation Civil Code, Article 709 (damages in tort) / Article 710 (damages for non-pecuniary loss) A person who intentionally or negligently infringes another's rights or legally protected interests is liable in damages. Article 710 makes emotional harm compensable. Invasion of privacy is litigated through these provisions. The level of risk in different situations can be set out as follows. Situation Assessment Recording a meeting you are taking part in recording by a party; as a rule not unlawful Recording a conversation between others that you are not part of, without telling them you are not a party, and the risk of a tort claim for invasion of privacy is considerably higher Leaving a computer in a meeting room while you step out, continuing to record the conversation in your absence you cease to be a party, so this is assessed much like recording between third parties above Publishing or circulating recorded audio or notes beyond their purpose separately from the act of recording, invasion of privacy or defamation can arise Recording employees' conversations on an ongoing basis and using it for monitoring this has to be balanced against workers' privacy and personal interests Do not use {{PRODUCT}} to record conversations you are not part of. # What the law actually requires What requires “consent” is not recording as such, but particular aspects of how the personal information acquired is handled. The “legal obligation” rows in the table below are the parts where failure can lead to sanctions or civil liability. Strength Requirement Basis Legal obligation Where recording or transcription acquires personal information, promptly notify the individual of the purpose of use or make it public, unless the purpose has been published in advance Act on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 21(1) Legal obligation Do not acquire information by deception or other improper means, such as recording without telling participants Act on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 20(1) Legal obligation Where you acquire information expecting it to contain sensitive personal information such as medical history or a criminal record, obtain the individual's prior consent as a rule Act on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 20(2) Legal obligation Where audio, transcripts or notes acquired are provided to a third party, obtain the individual's prior consent as a rule (with exceptions such as delegation and joint use) Act on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 27(1) and (5) Legal obligation Where monitoring covers employees, put appropriate arrangements in place as part of security control measures and supervision of employees Act on the Protection of Personal Information, Articles 23 and 24 Legal obligation Where the handling of personal data is delegated to an external service, exercise necessary and appropriate supervision over that processor Act on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 25 Strongly recommended Say at the start of the meeting that it is being recorded and transcribed, and display it in the meeting chat too reducing civil risk, maintaining trust Strongly recommended Be able to stop recording where a participant objects as above Recommended For meetings with external attendees, give notice of recording in the invitation as well dispute prevention Custom / optional Obtain explicit individual consent from every participant not a general obligation under Japanese law. Done at the other party's request or under internal rules # Specifying the purpose of use and notifying or publishing it Meeting audio, transcript text, AI-enhanced notes and speaker names can readily be cross-referenced with attendees' names and calendar invitations, so they normally constitute personal information. A company that records has to decide what it acquires this personal information for and how it will be used, and put that where the individual can find it. Legislation Act on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 21(1) (notification of the purpose of use on acquisition) When personal information is acquired, the purpose of use must be promptly notified to the individual or made public, unless it has been published in advance. The familiar practice of a call centre announcing “this call is being recorded for quality purposes” is, in substance, less a procedure for obtaining permission to record than a way of meeting this requirement while also preventing disputes. The purpose of use must be specified “as far as possible” (Article 17(1)). Wording such as “for our business activities” is not considered specific enough, so write it at a level the individual can predict — “producing minutes of meetings”, “sharing the content with employees who could not attend”. # Do not record without telling participants Legislation Act on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 20(1) (proper acquisition) This provides that personal information must not be acquired by deception or other improper means. Continuing to record and transcribe without telling participants at all risks amounting to such “improper means”. Announcing at the start of a meeting, and the notice {{PRODUCT}} shows when you start recording (for you to paste into the meeting chat), are the practical measures that address this. # Where sensitive personal information may be discussed Legislation Act on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 20(2) (proper acquisition) / Article 2(3) (definition of sensitive personal information) Personal information containing race, creed, social status, medical history, criminal record, the fact of having suffered harm from a crime, or the descriptions prescribed by Cabinet Order (disability, the results of health check-ups, guidance, diagnosis or dispensing by a doctor or similar, criminal proceedings, juvenile protection proceedings) is sensitive personal information, and acquiring it requires the individual's prior consent as a rule. The person whose consent is needed here is the individual speaking . A workspace administrator or the meeting's host cannot consent on their behalf. Note that a statement amounting only to inference — “A seems unwell” — is not treated as sensitive personal information, but if a specific condition is recorded, as in “A is on leave with X”, that part is treated as medical history. For personal data containing sensitive personal information, a leak is reportable to the Personal Information Protection Commission even if it affects a single individual . That is the point on which the design of a meeting-recording process usually turns. # Passing data to third parties Legislation Act on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 27(1) and (5) (restriction on provision to third parties) Providing personal data to a third party requires the individual's prior consent as a rule. However, provision accompanying delegation within the scope necessary to achieve the purpose of use, provision accompanying a business succession, and joint use meeting the stated requirements are treated as not involving a “third party”. {{COMPANY}} provides {{PRODUCT}} as a party to whom the customer (the contracting company) has delegated the handling of personal data, and that relationship is not provision to a third party. Sending a note to an external service through an integration (a chat tool or CRM, say) is different: the destination is not {{COMPANY}}'s processor but a separate provider, so it can constitute provision to a third party. Before enabling an integration, check it against your company's personal data handling rules and the purposes of use you have specified. # Recording meetings involving employees on an ongoing basis The Personal Information Protection Commission's guideline Q&A sets out four points to bear in mind when monitoring employees who handle personal data. specify the purpose of the monitoring in advance, set it down in internal rules, and make it clear to employees designate who is responsible for carrying out the monitoring and what authority they have establish the rules for how it is done in advance, and make sure those operating it understand them check that it is being carried out properly, in accordance with those rules Notifying and consulting a labour union, and informing employees, are also regarded as desirable. Where rules on recording and transcribing meetings apply across the company, they may need to go into the work rules. Legislation Labour Standards Act, Article 89 (duty to prepare and file) / Article 90 (procedure for preparation) An employer who regularly employs ten or more workers must prepare work rules and file them. Provisions applying to all workers at the workplace belong in the work rules. When preparing or amending them, the employer must hear the opinion of the union representing a majority of workers at that workplace, or, failing that, a person representing a majority of the workers. Prohibiting covert recording in the workplace through the work rules is generally considered possible in itself. There is, however, a strong body of opinion questioning the validity of a blanket prohibition extending to recording done by a victim of harassment to preserve evidence, and treating it as a disciplinary matter. If you include a blanket prohibition, check how exceptions should be handled with your legal department. # Wording you can use as-is Adapt the wording below as needed, replacing the company name, storage location and who can see it. # Spoken announcement at the start (internal meetings, standard) Today's meeting is being recorded with {{PRODUCT}} to produce the minutes, and will be transcribed and summarised automatically. The record will be stored in 〔location〕 and can be seen by 〔attendees / project members〕. If that is a problem for anyone, please say so now. # Spoken announcement at the start (meetings with external attendees) One thing before we begin. We will be recording today's discussion so that we have an accurate record, and it will be transcribed and summarised automatically. We use the record solely to confirm internally what was discussed, and we are happy to share the minutes if you would like them. If you would prefer we did not record, please just say so and we will stop. # Spoken announcement at the start (short version for regular meetings) This meeting is being recorded and transcribed with {{PRODUCT}}. Let me know if that is a problem. # For posting in meeting chat (one line) This meeting is being recorded and transcribed to produce the minutes. Please let us know if that is a problem. {{PRODUCT}} never posts to the meeting chat by itself. When you start recording, {{PRODUCT}} shows a short notice in Japanese and English; press Copy and paste it into the meeting chat (see About telling people you are recording ). Tell people who join partway through out loud as well. # A line to add to the meeting invitation [Please note] This meeting is expected to be recorded and transcribed by AI in order to produce the minutes. The record will be used only to confirm what was discussed, and we are happy to share it on request. If you would prefer we did not record, please tell us on the day or reply in advance. For recurring meeting invitations, putting this line in the body template removes the burden of announcing it out loud every time. For meetings with external attendees, telling them at the invitation stage rather than on the day makes it easier for them to decide. # Wording for a first sales meeting Thank you for making the time today. One thing I should mention: we use an AI recording and automatic summary tool so that we can pass on what was discussed accurately within our company. We use the record only to confirm internally what was discussed and to prepare our proposal, and we do not provide it to anyone outside. It is retained for 〔 〕 months, after which it is deleted automatically. If you would prefer we did not record, we will stop now — please just say. # Draft internal policy A template for setting this down as an internal policy. Adapt it in the light of your own work rules and labour procedures. Article 1 (Purpose) The purpose of this policy is to set out how the meeting recording and automatic transcription tool (the “Tool”) is to be used at this company, so as to reconcile efficiency in our work with the proper protection of meeting participants' privacy and personal information. Article 2 (Purposes of use) The Tool is used for the following purposes. It must not be used for any other purpose. (1) producing and sharing the minutes of meetings (2) sharing the content with employees unable to attend (3) recording how business decisions were arrived at Article 3 (Prior announcement) 1. Before starting to record, an employee using the Tool (a “User”) must inform all participants in the meeting that recording and transcription will take place, the purpose, where the record will be stored, and who will be able to see it. 2. For meetings with external attendees, notice that recording will take place shall so far as possible also be given when the meeting is convened. 3. Where a participant objects to recording, the User shall stop recording and, where necessary, delete the record of that meeting. Article 4 (Prohibited acts) A User must not: (1) record a conversation they are not taking part in (2) begin recording without giving the announcement, or continue recording contrary to it (3) use the Tool in a way intended to keep participants from noticing that they are being recorded (4) use a record for any purpose other than those in Article 2, or provide it to anyone outside those entitled to see it (5) use the Tool for the purpose of personnel evaluation, attendance management or any other monitoring of an individual employee Article 5 (Handling of sensitive personal information) The Tool shall as a rule not be used in meetings where health, medical history, creed or other sensitive personal information is expected to be discussed (occupational health consultations, HR interviews and the like). Where its use is unavoidable, the individual's prior consent must be obtained. Article 6 (Retention period and deletion) Records shall be retained for 〔 〕 months from the date of creation and deleted promptly thereafter. Where a participant asks for deletion, the responsible manager shall decide whether to delete, having confirmed whether the record is needed for business purposes. Article 7 (Responsible manager) The manager responsible for use of the Tool shall be 〔department / position〕, who shall issue and suspend accounts, set viewing permissions, and check compliance with this policy. Article 8 (Treatment as monitoring) The company does not use the Tool as a means of monitoring individual employees. Where use of the Tool is reviewed, this shall be carried out under the responsibility of the responsible manager, having first made the purpose and method clear to employees. # Which meetings to use it for, and which to avoid The law draws no uniform line, but meetings where a record is likely to cause harm share common features. Use the table below as a starting point for drawing your own line when rolling this out. Kind of meeting Guidance Why Regular progress meetings, project meetings fine to use there is a strong business need for a record, and little likelihood of sensitive personal information arising External sales meetings, regular client meetings fine to use, having announced it give notice in the invitation and at the start, and make sure the other party is able to decline Recruitment interviews judge carefully obtain the candidate's consent and define internally how far it may be used as an assessment record. Stop on the spot if the conversation turns to health or beliefs Performance reviews, disciplinary interviews avoid disciplinary history and health are likely to come up, and the existence of a record itself has a chilling effect on those involved. Where a record is needed, use HR's prescribed form Labour negotiations, consultations with a union avoid given the nature of negotiation, recording at one party's discretion bears directly on trust between the parties. Agree in advance whether recording is permitted Occupational health consultations, health consultations, leave and return-to-work interviews do not use health check results and guidance from a doctor are sensitive personal information, and acquiring them requires the individual's consent Meetings with a lawyer or tax accountant do not use, or check in advance this engages professional confidentiality obligations and the protection of the client's secrets. For details see Use in healthcare, finance and professional services Healthcare or care consultations with a patient or service user present do not use clinical information is sensitive personal information, and conformity with healthcare sector guidelines also needs separate consideration Internal whistleblowing, interviews at a harassment contact point do not use protecting the person reporting comes first. The scope of the record and how it is stored should follow your whistleblowing policy Board meetings, investment and M&A discussions set it out specifically in internal rules record retention duties and the scope of disclosure are constrained by the Companies Act and by contract. Follow your legal department's judgement Where the conversation turns to something sensitive partway through a meeting, stop recording and start again once the topic has moved on. Part of a transcript cannot be deleted on its own, so if something that should not be kept has been recorded, delete the whole note. How to do that is explained in Deleting notes . # When a participant says no If someone asks you not to record, stop there and then. Being able to stop when an objection is raised is what keeps the announcement from being a formality. Options after stopping include: not transcribing that meeting and recording it with typed notes instead pausing only for the sensitive part of the agenda and recording the rest writing up the key points afterwards as you understood them, and asking the other party to confirm them If you are asked to delete something already recorded, delete the whole note. Part of a transcript cannot be deleted on its own. A note can be permanently deleted by its owner or an admin. How to delete is covered in Deleting notes . # Steps for writing internal rules Deciding the rules at rollout saves each user making the judgement every time. In practice this order works well. 1 Write out the purposes of use List the purposes you will actually use it for — producing minutes, sharing with those who could not attend, recording how decisions were made. This is what corresponds to specifying the purpose of use under the Act on the Protection of Personal Information and to what goes in your privacy policy. 2 Decide which meetings it is not used for Start from the table under “Which meetings to use it for, and which to avoid” and add to or cut from it to suit your own circumstances. Turn what you decide into the articles of an internal policy. 3 Decide how the announcement is made Decide which of a spoken announcement, pasting the notice into the meeting chat, and standard wording in the invitation are mandatory. 4 Decide the retention period Decide how long notes and imported emails and chat should be kept, and have an admin set it under Settings → Workspace → General → Data retention. The choices are 6, 12, 24 or 36 months, or keep forever; the default is 12 months. See Automatic transcript deletion for details. 5 Decide how notes are shared New notes start out private. Decide which notes go into folders and who they are shared with. There are no public links that let people outside the organisation open a note. See Sharing controls . 6 Inform employees Where this involves amending the work rules, carry out the opinion-hearing procedure under Article 90 of the Labour Standards Act. 7 Check how it is being used This corresponds to the fourth point in the guideline Q&A on monitoring. The responsible manager periodically checks that it is being used in accordance with the rules. Check the purposes of use are documented and reflected in the privacy policy or internal rules the meetings it is not used for are listed and communicated which announcement methods (spoken, meeting chat, invitation) are mandatory has been decided the data retention period has been checked and changed if needed how notes are placed in folders and shared, and whether they may be exported to outside services, have been decided whether the work rules need amending has been checked For what administrators can do, see also Making recording notices a rule in your organisation (for admins) . # Related articles About telling people you are recording The notice shown when recording starts, and how to tell people → Telling people you are recording (for individuals) Copying the notice, and sample wording → Automatic transcript deletion Setting a retention period → Sharing controls Default sharing scope and sharing outside the organisation → Use in healthcare, finance and professional services How sector-specific regulation applies → Security and privacy FAQs Storage location, cross-border transfer, disclosure requests →

consent-security-privacy/medical-informa.html:
Healthcare institutions, financial institutions, law and tax practices, and government bodies ask us how {{PRODUCT}} relates to their sector's regulation and guidelines. This article sets out, for each of four sectors, the scope within which {{PRODUCT}} can be used and what you need to check when considering it.

Note

What {{PRODUCT}} records is an online meeting you join on a computer, using the desktop app (macOS / Windows) or a browser (Chrome / Edge). Face-to-face exchanges in a consulting room and telephone calls are out of scope. Read this on the basis of online meetings joined from a computer, such as internal hospital meetings and case conferences.

Please note

This article is general information compiled by {{COMPANY}} and is not legal advice. Whether your organisation may use it is for your organisation's responsible officer to determine, in the light of the applicable rules, industry guidelines and regulators' guidance.

How far you can rely on AI meeting notesThe lawfulness of recording, and writing internal rules→Our security standardsWhat our security control measures cover→AI models and training dataThe setting for whether data is used for training→Security and privacy FAQsStorage location, cross-border transfer, responding to audits→

#A common starting point: {{COMPANY}} acts as a processor

The starting point common to all four sectors is the relationship between {{COMPANY}} and your organisation.

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 27(5)(i) (restriction on provision to third parties) / Article 25 (supervision of processors)

Provision accompanying delegation of the handling of personal data within the scope necessary to achieve the purpose of use does not constitute “provision to a third party”. The delegating party, meanwhile, has a duty to exercise necessary and appropriate supervision over the processor. When you use {{PRODUCT}}, your organisation is the delegating party and {{COMPANY}} the processor.

Adopting {{PRODUCT}} is therefore, for your organisation, a question of selecting and managing an external processor. {{COMPANY}} does not handle personal data beyond the scope agreed in its contract with you. For use in evaluating and improving the service, which an organisation's admin can switch off, see AI models and training data. The information your organisation needs to select and assess a processor is available as documentation on request, through your account contact or {{SUPPORT_EMAIL}}.

#Use in healthcare institutions

{{PRODUCT}} can be used to produce the minutes of internal hospital meetings, case conferences and committees. Where clinical information such as medical records is involved, there are additional points to consider.

#Clinical information is sensitive personal information

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 2(3) (definition of sensitive personal information) / Article 20(2) (proper acquisition)

Personal information containing race, creed, social status, medical history, criminal record, the fact of having suffered harm from a crime, or the descriptions prescribed by Cabinet Order (disability, the results of health check-ups, guidance, diagnosis or dispensing by a doctor or similar, criminal proceedings, juvenile protection proceedings) is sensitive personal information. Acquiring it requires the individual's prior consent, except where a statutory exception applies.

A patient's medical history and clinical information fall within this. The consent must come from the patient themselves; the meeting's host or an administrator cannot consent on their behalf.

It also affects the threshold for reporting a breach. For personal data containing sensitive personal information, a leak is reportable to the Personal Information Protection Commission even if it affects a single individual (Article 7(i) of the Enforcement Regulations). Decide whether to record meetings involving clinical information on the basis of that reporting threshold.

#The three-ministry, two-guideline framework

Where a healthcare institution uses an external information processing service, two guidelines have to be followed. Together they are known as the “three-ministry, two-guideline” framework.

Applies to Title Issued by
What healthcare institutions must observe Guidelines on the Safe Management of Medical Information Systems, version 6.0 Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare
What service providers must observe Guidelines on Safe Management for Providers of Information Systems and Services Handling Medical Information, version 2.0 (revised March 2025) Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry; Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications

{{COMPANY}} provides documentation setting out how it addresses the provider-side requirements, individually to healthcare institutions. Please contact your account representative when considering adoption.

Where specific clinical information will be handled in {{PRODUCT}}, we recommend confirming with your institution's medical information systems security officer and carrying out a risk assessment.

#About the Next-Generation Medical Infrastructure Act

The Next-Generation Medical Infrastructure Act (formally the Act on Anonymously Processed Medical Information and Pseudonymously Processed Medical Information to Contribute to Medical Research and Development, Act No. 28 of 2017) establishes a framework for the secondary use of medical information in research and development. Medical information is provided to nationally accredited operators and used in anonymised or pseudonymised form.

{{PRODUCT}} is not an accredited operator under that Act, and is not a service that collects or processes medical information under its framework. What {{PRODUCT}} does is help produce the minutes created in the course of a healthcare institution's own work. If you are considering secondary use of medical information for research, check the separate procedures under that Act's framework.

Questions about overseas medical privacy law

We are sometimes asked about compliance with HIPAA in the United States. That is US law and does not apply directly to healthcare institutions in Japan, where the position is governed by the Act on the Protection of Personal Information together with the three-ministry, two-guideline framework described above. Customers who are US healthcare institutions considering a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) should contact their account representative.

#Use in financial institutions

Financial institutions use {{PRODUCT}} too. There are three things to check when considering it.

#FISC security guidelines

The Center for Financial Industry Information Systems (FISC) publishes its “Security Guidelines on Computer Systems for Financial Institutions” (currently in its 14th edition). These are an industry self-regulatory standard rather than law, but they are referred to as a de facto standard in financial institutions' system procurement. {{COMPANY}} provides financial institution customers with documentation setting out how it addresses the relevant items.

#Managing external processors

Where a financial institution outsources systems, it has to comply with the provisions on managing external processors in the supervisory guidelines for its sector (the Comprehensive Supervisory Guidelines for Major Banks, and equivalents). In addition, the Personal Information Protection Commission and Financial Services Agency's “Guidelines on the Protection of Personal Information in the Financial Sector” require security control measures and processor management going beyond the general law. {{COMPANY}} provides the information needed for your risk assessment and processor review.

#Position under the Act on the Protection of Personal Information

As set out above, {{COMPANY}} acts as a party to whom your company has delegated the handling of personal data, and that relationship is not provision to a third party. The security control measures {{COMPANY}} implements as a processor are described in Our security standards.

#Use in law firms and tax accountancy practices

For the professions, the central question is whether using an external service is consistent with confidentiality obligations.

#The confidentiality provisions

LegislationAttorney Act, Article 23 (right and duty of confidentiality)

This provides that an attorney, or a person who was an attorney, has both the right and the duty to preserve secrets learned in the course of their duties.

LegislationPenal Code, Article 134(1) (disclosure of secrets)

This provides the penalty (imprisonment for up to six months or a fine of up to ¥100,000) where a doctor, pharmacist, pharmaceuticals distributor, midwife, attorney, defence counsel, notary, or a person formerly in such a position, discloses without justifiable grounds a person's secret learned in the course of their work. It is a status offence with a limited class of subjects, and neither a SaaS provider nor its employees fall within it. It does apply to the attorney or doctor using {{PRODUCT}}, so care is needed when it is used in the professions or in healthcare.

LegislationCertified Public Tax Accountant Act, Article 38 (duty of confidentiality) / Article 54 (duty of confidentiality of employees)

Article 38 provides for the tax accountant themselves, and Article 54 for their employees and other staff, that secrets learned in the course of their work must not be disclosed to others or used for their own purposes without justifiable grounds.

#Is outsourcing “disclosure”?

What these provisions prohibit is “disclosing” a secret. Delegating processing to an external provider bound by confidentiality, within the scope necessary to carry out the work, is generally understood not to amount to disclosure. It is the same analysis as a practice using clerical staff, a translation company or a cloud storage provider.

That does presuppose, however, that the secret is properly protected at the processor. {{COMPANY}} is bound by confidentiality under its terms of service and under individual non-disclosure agreements, and does not use customers' data for anything other than providing the service to them and, unless an organisation's admin has switched it off, evaluating and improving the service. It is never used to train AI models.

#What we recommend in practice

  1. explain in your engagement letter with the client that external cloud services are used, and obtain their agreement in advance
  2. {{PRODUCT}} never uses customer data for training AI models, on any plan. If you also want to rule out its use for evaluating and improving the service, have your organisation's admin switch that off in settings
  3. follow the information management rules and guidance of your bar association or tax accountants' association
  4. start by using it for internal meetings and training rather than for recording client meetings themselves

Note that {{COMPANY}} does not practise law, and {{PRODUCT}} does not provide legal advice.

#Use by government and local authorities

When government bodies procure cloud services, they are as a rule to procure from services on the ISMAP (Information system Security Management and Assessment Program) cloud service list. ISMAP is administered by the Digital Agency, the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, and the National center of Incident readiness and Strategy for Cybersecurity (NISC).

{{PRODUCT}} is not currently on the ISMAP cloud service list. If you are considering use by a government body, check the procurement requirements first. In procurements where ISMAP registration is not mandatory, customers assess {{PRODUCT}} against their own criteria, with documentation on {{COMPANY}}'s security controls provided.

#Recommended settings common to all four sectors

In any of these sectors, checking the following settings at rollout prevents records reaching further than intended.

Setting Recommended state Reference
Starting a recording leave “Start recording automatically” off (the default) and start each recording deliberately. When it is on, recording starts without a confirmation when the call of a scheduled meeting starts How transcription works
Use for training and service improvement data is never used to train AI models, on any plan. If needed, an admin switches off its use for evaluating and improving the service in settings AI models and training data
Default sharing scope new notes start private. Place notes in folders or share links to them only where needed Sharing controls
Data retention period the default is 12 months. Have an admin choose 6, 12, 24 or 36 months, or keep forever, to match the period the business actually requires Automatic transcript deletion
External integrations permit only those used for work and disable the rest Integrations overview

Where the conversation turns to something sensitive partway through a meeting, stop recording. Part of a transcript cannot be deleted on its own, so if something that should not be kept has been recorded, delete the whole note.

Check
  • meetings where sensitive personal information may arise are documented as meetings it is not used for
  • the data retention period has been checked (the default is 12 months; an admin can change it)
  • how notes are shared, and how exports to outside services are used, have been checked
  • the documentation needed for processor review has been requested from {{COMPANY}}

#Certifications and third-party assessments

People in each sector ask us which certifications we hold. This help centre collects the nature of each scheme and {{COMPANY}}'s position in the table under “Certifications and third-party assessments” in Our security standards. Please refer to that table.

Note that none of the three-ministry, two-guideline framework, the FISC guidelines or the Next-Generation Medical Infrastructure Act has a third-party conformity certification scheme. We therefore cannot describe ourselves as “certified” or “compliant” in relation to them, and instead provide documentation setting out how we address the relevant items.

#If something is not working

  • If your IT department asks you to complete a security questionnaire: email {{SUPPORT_EMAIL}} with the form and the deadline. We will tell you what we can answer and what documentation we can provide.
  • If you need material to explain the service to a regulator: there is material we can provide in writing on {{COMPANY}}'s security control measures as a processor, where data is stored, and any sub-processing. Please speak to your account representative.
  • If sensitive personal information has ended up in a record: move the note to the trash and delete it permanently (part of a transcript cannot be deleted on its own). How to delete is covered in Deleting notes.
