consent-security-privacy/medical-informa.text: Healthcare institutions, financial institutions, law and tax practices, and government bodies ask us how {{PRODUCT}} relates to their sector's regulation and guidelines. This article sets out, for each of four sectors, the scope within which {{PRODUCT}} can be used and what you need to check when considering it. Note What {{PRODUCT}} records is an online meeting you join on a computer, using the desktop app (macOS / Windows) or a browser (Chrome / Edge). Face-to-face exchanges in a consulting room and telephone calls are out of scope. Read this on the basis of online meetings joined from a computer, such as internal hospital meetings and case conferences. Please note This article is general information compiled by {{COMPANY}} and is not legal advice. Whether your organisation may use it is for your organisation's responsible officer to determine, in the light of the applicable rules, industry guidelines and regulators' guidance. How far you can rely on AI meeting notes The lawfulness of recording, and writing internal rules → Our security standards What our security control measures cover → AI models and training data The setting for whether data is used for training → Security and privacy FAQs Storage location, cross-border transfer, responding to audits → # A common starting point: {{COMPANY}} acts as a processor The starting point common to all four sectors is the relationship between {{COMPANY}} and your organisation. Legislation Act on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 27(5)(i) (restriction on provision to third parties) / Article 25 (supervision of processors) Provision accompanying delegation of the handling of personal data within the scope necessary to achieve the purpose of use does not constitute “provision to a third party”. The delegating party, meanwhile, has a duty to exercise necessary and appropriate supervision over the processor. When you use {{PRODUCT}}, your organisation is the delegating party and {{COMPANY}} the processor. Adopting {{PRODUCT}} is therefore, for your organisation, a question of selecting and managing an external processor. {{COMPANY}} does not handle personal data beyond the scope agreed in its contract with you. For use in evaluating and improving the service, which an organisation's admin can switch off, see AI models and training data . The information your organisation needs to select and assess a processor is available as documentation on request, through your account contact or {{SUPPORT_EMAIL}}. # Use in healthcare institutions {{PRODUCT}} can be used to produce the minutes of internal hospital meetings, case conferences and committees. Where clinical information such as medical records is involved, there are additional points to consider. # Clinical information is sensitive personal information Legislation Act on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 2(3) (definition of sensitive personal information) / Article 20(2) (proper acquisition) Personal information containing race, creed, social status, medical history, criminal record, the fact of having suffered harm from a crime, or the descriptions prescribed by Cabinet Order (disability, the results of health check-ups, guidance, diagnosis or dispensing by a doctor or similar, criminal proceedings, juvenile protection proceedings) is sensitive personal information. Acquiring it requires the individual's prior consent, except where a statutory exception applies. A patient's medical history and clinical information fall within this. The consent must come from the patient themselves; the meeting's host or an administrator cannot consent on their behalf. It also affects the threshold for reporting a breach. For personal data containing sensitive personal information, a leak is reportable to the Personal Information Protection Commission even if it affects a single individual (Article 7(i) of the Enforcement Regulations). Decide whether to record meetings involving clinical information on the basis of that reporting threshold. # The three-ministry, two-guideline framework Where a healthcare institution uses an external information processing service, two guidelines have to be followed. Together they are known as the “three-ministry, two-guideline” framework. Applies to Title Issued by What healthcare institutions must observe Guidelines on the Safe Management of Medical Information Systems, version 6.0 Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare What service providers must observe Guidelines on Safe Management for Providers of Information Systems and Services Handling Medical Information, version 2.0 (revised March 2025) Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry; Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications {{COMPANY}} provides documentation setting out how it addresses the provider-side requirements, individually to healthcare institutions. Please contact your account representative when considering adoption. Where specific clinical information will be handled in {{PRODUCT}}, we recommend confirming with your institution's medical information systems security officer and carrying out a risk assessment. # About the Next-Generation Medical Infrastructure Act The Next-Generation Medical Infrastructure Act (formally the Act on Anonymously Processed Medical Information and Pseudonymously Processed Medical Information to Contribute to Medical Research and Development, Act No. 28 of 2017) establishes a framework for the secondary use of medical information in research and development. Medical information is provided to nationally accredited operators and used in anonymised or pseudonymised form. {{PRODUCT}} is not an accredited operator under that Act, and is not a service that collects or processes medical information under its framework. What {{PRODUCT}} does is help produce the minutes created in the course of a healthcare institution's own work. If you are considering secondary use of medical information for research, check the separate procedures under that Act's framework. Questions about overseas medical privacy law We are sometimes asked about compliance with HIPAA in the United States. That is US law and does not apply directly to healthcare institutions in Japan, where the position is governed by the Act on the Protection of Personal Information together with the three-ministry, two-guideline framework described above. Customers who are US healthcare institutions considering a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) should contact their account representative. # Use in financial institutions Financial institutions use {{PRODUCT}} too. There are three things to check when considering it. # FISC security guidelines The Center for Financial Industry Information Systems (FISC) publishes its “Security Guidelines on Computer Systems for Financial Institutions” (currently in its 14th edition). These are an industry self-regulatory standard rather than law, but they are referred to as a de facto standard in financial institutions' system procurement. {{COMPANY}} provides financial institution customers with documentation setting out how it addresses the relevant items. # Managing external processors Where a financial institution outsources systems, it has to comply with the provisions on managing external processors in the supervisory guidelines for its sector (the Comprehensive Supervisory Guidelines for Major Banks, and equivalents). In addition, the Personal Information Protection Commission and Financial Services Agency's “Guidelines on the Protection of Personal Information in the Financial Sector” require security control measures and processor management going beyond the general law. {{COMPANY}} provides the information needed for your risk assessment and processor review. # Position under the Act on the Protection of Personal Information As set out above, {{COMPANY}} acts as a party to whom your company has delegated the handling of personal data, and that relationship is not provision to a third party. The security control measures {{COMPANY}} implements as a processor are described in Our security standards . # Use in law firms and tax accountancy practices For the professions, the central question is whether using an external service is consistent with confidentiality obligations. # The confidentiality provisions Legislation Attorney Act, Article 23 (right and duty of confidentiality) This provides that an attorney, or a person who was an attorney, has both the right and the duty to preserve secrets learned in the course of their duties. Legislation Penal Code, Article 134(1) (disclosure of secrets) This provides the penalty (imprisonment for up to six months or a fine of up to ¥100,000) where a doctor, pharmacist, pharmaceuticals distributor, midwife, attorney, defence counsel, notary, or a person formerly in such a position, discloses without justifiable grounds a person's secret learned in the course of their work. It is a status offence with a limited class of subjects, and neither a SaaS provider nor its employees fall within it. It does apply to the attorney or doctor using {{PRODUCT}}, so care is needed when it is used in the professions or in healthcare. Legislation Certified Public Tax Accountant Act, Article 38 (duty of confidentiality) / Article 54 (duty of confidentiality of employees) Article 38 provides for the tax accountant themselves, and Article 54 for their employees and other staff, that secrets learned in the course of their work must not be disclosed to others or used for their own purposes without justifiable grounds. # Is outsourcing “disclosure”? What these provisions prohibit is “disclosing” a secret. Delegating processing to an external provider bound by confidentiality, within the scope necessary to carry out the work, is generally understood not to amount to disclosure. It is the same analysis as a practice using clerical staff, a translation company or a cloud storage provider. That does presuppose, however, that the secret is properly protected at the processor. {{COMPANY}} is bound by confidentiality under its terms of service and under individual non-disclosure agreements, and does not use customers' data for anything other than providing the service to them and, unless an organisation's admin has switched it off, evaluating and improving the service. It is never used to train AI models. # What we recommend in practice explain in your engagement letter with the client that external cloud services are used, and obtain their agreement in advance {{PRODUCT}} never uses customer data for training AI models , on any plan. If you also want to rule out its use for evaluating and improving the service, have your organisation's admin switch that off in settings follow the information management rules and guidance of your bar association or tax accountants' association start by using it for internal meetings and training rather than for recording client meetings themselves Note that {{COMPANY}} does not practise law, and {{PRODUCT}} does not provide legal advice. # Use by government and local authorities When government bodies procure cloud services, they are as a rule to procure from services on the ISMAP (Information system Security Management and Assessment Program) cloud service list. ISMAP is administered by the Digital Agency, the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, and the National center of Incident readiness and Strategy for Cybersecurity (NISC). {{PRODUCT}} is not currently on the ISMAP cloud service list. If you are considering use by a government body, check the procurement requirements first. In procurements where ISMAP registration is not mandatory, customers assess {{PRODUCT}} against their own criteria, with documentation on {{COMPANY}}'s security controls provided. # Recommended settings common to all four sectors In any of these sectors, checking the following settings at rollout prevents records reaching further than intended. Setting Recommended state Reference Starting a recording leave “Start recording automatically” off (the default) and start each recording deliberately. When it is on, recording starts without a confirmation when the call of a scheduled meeting starts How transcription works Use for training and service improvement data is never used to train AI models, on any plan. If needed, an admin switches off its use for evaluating and improving the service in settings AI models and training data Default sharing scope new notes start private. Place notes in folders or share links to them only where needed Sharing controls Data retention period the default is 12 months. Have an admin choose 6, 12, 24 or 36 months, or keep forever, to match the period the business actually requires Automatic transcript deletion External integrations permit only those used for work and disable the rest Integrations overview Where the conversation turns to something sensitive partway through a meeting, stop recording. Part of a transcript cannot be deleted on its own, so if something that should not be kept has been recorded, delete the whole note. Check meetings where sensitive personal information may arise are documented as meetings it is not used for the data retention period has been checked (the default is 12 months; an admin can change it) how notes are shared, and how exports to outside services are used, have been checked the documentation needed for processor review has been requested from {{COMPANY}} # Certifications and third-party assessments People in each sector ask us which certifications we hold. This help centre collects the nature of each scheme and {{COMPANY}}'s position in the table under “Certifications and third-party assessments” in Our security standards . Please refer to that table. Note that none of the three-ministry, two-guideline framework, the FISC guidelines or the Next-Generation Medical Infrastructure Act has a third-party conformity certification scheme. We therefore cannot describe ourselves as “certified” or “compliant” in relation to them, and instead provide documentation setting out how we address the relevant items. # If something is not working If your IT department asks you to complete a security questionnaire : email {{SUPPORT_EMAIL}} with the form and the deadline. We will tell you what we can answer and what documentation we can provide. If you need material to explain the service to a regulator : there is material we can provide in writing on {{COMPANY}}'s security control measures as a processor, where data is stored, and any sub-processing. Please speak to your account representative. If sensitive personal information has ended up in a record : move the note to the trash and delete it permanently (part of a transcript cannot be deleted on its own). How to delete is covered in Deleting notes . # Related articles How far you can rely on AI meeting notes The lawfulness of recording, sample announcements, and a draft internal policy → Our security standards Security control measures and the certifications we hold → AI models and training data Whether data is used for training, and how to change it → Security and privacy FAQs Storage location, cross-border transfer, disclosure requests, audits →

consent-security-privacy/model-training.title: AI models and training data
consent-security-privacy/model-training.description: Why your data is not used to train AI models, how it may be used to evaluate and improve the service and how to switch that off, and the legal position.
consent-security-privacy/model-training.html:
{{PRODUCT}} does not use the meeting audio, transcripts, notes, uploaded material or chat exchanges it holds to train AI models. That is the same on every plan. {{COMPANY}} may, however, use customer data to evaluate and improve the service, unless an organisation's admin has switched that off. This article covers what your data is used for, how to switch off its use for evaluation and improvement, and how it is analysed legally.

Note

{{PRODUCT}} does not use customer data to train AI models. The AI providers we delegate processing to (Anthropic, OpenAI and Google) also state in their terms that data sent through their APIs is not used for training by default. An organisation's admin can switch off use for evaluating and improving the service in settings.

Security and privacy FAQsWhere data is stored, and transfer overseas→Choosing a modelSwitching the model used in chat→Our security standardsWhat our security control measures cover→

#What {{PRODUCT}} uses your data for

The uses of the data we hold fall into three groups.

Use What it covers Can it be stopped?
Providing the features processing needed to provide {{PRODUCT}}'s features: transcription, writing notes and summaries, extracting information, answering chat questions, search and so on No, it is needed to provide the service
Evaluating and improving the service use to evaluate and improve {{PRODUCT}}'s quality, such as checking that notes and extracted information reflect the meeting correctly. Not used to train AI models Yes, an organisation's admin can switch it off in settings
Training AI models not used to train {{PRODUCT}}'s own models or those of outside AI providers Not done

Data is sent to outside AI providers only as far as is needed to provide the features. Under each provider's API terms (for Google, the paid API), data sent through the API is not used for model training by default. How long each provider keeps API data is set by its own terms; {{COMPANY}} has no special arrangement with them for keeping no data at all (zero data retention).

#Use for evaluating and improving the service

{{COMPANY}} may use customers' meeting data to check and improve {{PRODUCT}}'s quality, for example to evaluate whether notes and extracted information reflect the meeting correctly. This happens only where the organisation's admin has not switched it off.

  • It is not used to train AI models
  • When {{COMPANY}} staff look at your data, it is recorded in your organisation's audit log, which admins can see under Settings → Workspace → Audit log

#Switching off use for evaluation and improvement

Use for evaluation and improvement is a workspace setting. Only a workspace admin can change it.

#How an admin switches it off

  1. 1

    Open settings

    Sign in to {{PRODUCT}} and open Settings.

  2. 2

    Find the item

    In the workspace settings, find the item for use in evaluating and improving the service.

  3. 3

    Switch it off

    Switch it off and save. The change takes effect within 30 days.

#For members

There is no setting for an individual user to exclude only their own notes. If you want use for evaluation and improvement stopped, speak to your workspace admin. Your data is never used to train AI models, whatever the setting.

#After it is switched off

Once switched off, the change takes effect within 30 days, and from then on the workspace's data is not used for evaluation and improvement. Data taken out for evaluation before then is also deleted within that period.

Note

Because data is not used to train AI models, there is never any need to remove it from a trained model.

#The models we use

{{PRODUCT}} uses a combination of models to generate summary notes. The models come from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google (all in the United States), and transcription also uses services from ElevenLabs and AssemblyAI (United States). Different models suit different kinds of meeting and purposes, so {{COMPANY}} evaluates them continuously and switches between them.

The chat screen shows the name of the model used for the answer.

At present you cannot connect your own model to {{PRODUCT}}. Transcription and summarisation use models selected by {{COMPANY}}. We are considering it as a feature for business customers, but there is no timetable.

#The position under the Act on the Protection of Personal Information

Under the Act, using meeting data for training AI models or for evaluating and improving the service raises two questions: whether it falls within the purpose of use, and whether it falls within the scope of the delegation. We take them in turn.

#Relationship to the purpose of use

Meeting audio, transcripts, notes and speaker names can readily be cross-referenced with attendees' names and calendar information, so they normally constitute personal information.

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 17(1) (specifying the purpose of use) / Article 18(1) (restriction by purpose of use)

When handling personal information, the purpose of use must be specified as far as possible, and handling it beyond the scope necessary to achieve that purpose requires the individual's consent as a rule. Where meeting data is used to train AI models, wording such as “to improve our service” is likely to be insufficiently specific, so {{COMPANY}} does not use meeting data to train AI models, and states use for evaluating and improving the service as a separate purpose of use that an organisation's admin can switch off.

The purposes of use are set out in full in our Privacy policy.

#Data held under delegation

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 27(5)(i) (restriction on provision to third parties) / Article 25 (supervision of processors)

Provision of personal data accompanying delegation within the scope necessary to achieve the purpose of use does not constitute provision to a third party. A processor, meanwhile, cannot handle that personal data beyond the scope of the work delegated to it, and the delegating party has a duty of supervision over the processor.

For meeting data held in {{PRODUCT}}, {{COMPANY}} acts as a party to whom the customer has delegated its handling. {{COMPANY}} does not use customers' meeting data to train AI models. Use for evaluating and improving the service takes place under the contract with the customer, and only where the organisation's admin has not switched it off.

#Sending data to external model providers

Where data is sent to an external model provider, {{COMPANY}} selects only providers meeting the following conditions.

  1. their API terms state that data sent is not used to train their models by default
  2. their terms state how long data is retained
  3. arrangements allow supervision of the processor under Article 25 of the Act on the Protection of Personal Information

The model providers {{PRODUCT}} uses are located in the United States, so customers' personal data is transferred abroad (to the United States). The rules on cross-border transfer apply even where the provision accompanies delegation, so {{COMPANY}} complies with Article 28 of the Act. The destination countries, their legal regimes, the measures taken, and how information is provided on request are set out under “Provision to third parties in foreign countries” in our Privacy policy. For the key points only, see Security and privacy FAQs.

#The position under copyright law

Material used in a meeting, and speech such as a lecture or presentation, can contain third parties' copyright works.

LegislationCopyright Act, Article 30-4 (use not for the purpose of enjoying the thoughts or sentiments expressed in a work)

This provides that where the purpose is not to enjoy, oneself or through others, the thoughts or sentiments expressed in a work, it may be used to the extent considered necessary. Item (ii) of that Article covers use for “information analysis”, which includes use for machine learning. The Article has a proviso, however: it does not apply where use “would unreasonably prejudice the interests of the copyright holder in light of the nature and purpose of the work and the manner of its use”.

That said, being permitted under copyright law and being permitted under contract and under the Act on the Protection of Personal Information are separate questions. Meeting records contain participants' personal data, business secrets, and information covered by non-disclosure agreements with clients. What governs the handling of those is not copyright law but the Act on the Protection of Personal Information and the contract between the customer and {{COMPANY}}.

{{COMPANY}} therefore does not use customer data to train AI models, whatever the copyright position.

#If something is not working

  • There is no training on/off item in my settings: {{PRODUCT}} does not use customer data to train AI models, so there is no such item. The setting for use in evaluating and improving the service can be changed only by a workspace admin.
  • An internal review asks for an explanation that data is not used for training: use what this article says in your answer. If you need it in writing, contact {{PRIVACY_EMAIL}}.
  • I want a particular meeting excluded from evaluation and improvement: there is no per-meeting setting. Have it switched off for the whole workspace, or delete the note concerned. How to delete is covered in Deleting notes.

#Related articles

consent-security-privacy/our-security-st.title: Our security standards
consent-security-privacy/our-security-st.description: Encryption, access control, the certifications we hold, and our policy on disclosing third-party assessments.
consent-security-privacy/our-security-st.html:
This explains how {{COMPANY}} protects the data held in {{PRODUCT}}, following the categories of security control measures required by the Act on the Protection of Personal Information. You can use it as background material for your IT department's processor assessment or for answering security questionnaires.

Note

Within this help centre, the detail of each category of security control measure, and the certifications and third-party assessments we hold, are collected in this article.

{{COMPANY}} has established a basic policy on the handling of personal data, put handling rules in place covering each stage from acquisition to deletion, and implements the measures below.

#Organisational security measures

  • We designate a person responsible for the handling of personal data, and make the scope of authority and responsibility clear
  • We identify which employees handle personal data and the categories of personal data they handle
  • We keep records of system use, of the granting, changing and removal of permissions, and of data taken out, so that handling can be reviewed
  • We have reporting arrangements in place for where a breach of the handling rules, or an indication of one, is identified
  • We review handling periodically and report the results to the responsible person
  • We have documented procedures for a leak of personal data, including the deadlines for reporting and notification. The process is described under “If a leak occurs” in Security and privacy FAQs

#Personnel security measures

  • We have confidentiality agreements with all employees. The obligation continues after employment ends
  • We provide training on the handling of personal data on joining and periodically thereafter
  • Permissions are granted only to the extent needed for the work, and are reviewed promptly on transfer or departure

We handle the secrecy of communications in line with the framework of the Telecommunications Business Act.

LegislationTelecommunications Business Act, Article 4 (protection of secrecy) / Article 179 (penalties)

The secrecy of communications being handled by a telecommunications carrier must not be violated, and people engaged in the telecommunications business owe confidentiality obligations both during and after their employment. Breach carries penalties. We treat the parts of {{PRODUCT}} that mediate exchanges between users — sharing and notification features — as subject to that provision. {{COMPANY}}'s officers and employees do not acquire, use or disclose information subject to the secrecy of communications learned in the course of their work, except where required by law or where there is other justifiable cause.

{{COMPANY}} keeps the position of each feature it provides under review against the Telecommunications Business Act and the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications' “Manual on Entry into the Telecommunications Business (Supplement)”. Where we provide a feature that mediates messages between users, we complete the necessary procedures, including the filing required by Article 16 of that Act.

#Physical security measures

  • {{PRODUCT}}'s servers are housed in data centres with entry controls, monitoring, and redundant power and air conditioning
  • Disk encryption and screen locking are mandatory on devices used for work
  • We have procedures for carrying equipment or electronic media containing personal data
  • When equipment and electronic media are disposed of, data is erased by a method that prevents recovery

#Technical security measures

Category Detail
Encryption in transit communication between devices and servers is encrypted with TLS
Encryption at rest stored data is held encrypted
Access control users of information systems handling personal data are identified and authenticated, and permissions are limited to what the work requires
Authentication sign-in goes through {{PRODUCT}} ID, with a Google account or an email address and password. {{PRODUCT}} ID supports two-step verification with codes from an authenticator app (TOTP) and backup codes, which each user can turn on; it is required for signing in to {{COMPANY}}'s own admin tools. If you sign in with Google, use Google's 2-Step Verification as well
Logging records of system use and access are captured and retained for a period
Vulnerability management the software we use is kept up to date, and we check continuously for known vulnerabilities
Protection against unauthorised access mechanisms to prevent unauthorised external access are in place and monitored
Note

The precise scope of access control, the monitoring methods, and the detail of measures preventing unauthorised access are not set out in this article, because publishing them could prejudice security. The Enforcement Order of the Act on the Protection of Personal Information permits such matters to be excluded from what is published. Where detail is needed for a processor assessment, we explain it individually on the basis of a non-disclosure agreement.

#Understanding the external environment

Where personal data is handled in a foreign country, the data protection regime of that country has to be understood and necessary and appropriate measures taken. {{PRODUCT}}'s database, application hosting and backups are in the Tokyo region. Transcription (including live captions) and AI processing such as writing notes and summaries, extracting information and answering chat questions are delegated to providers in the United States (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, ElevenLabs and AssemblyAI) and take place in the United States. PostHog, which we use for usage analytics, is also a US provider.

In that case, {{COMPANY}} documents three things.

  1. the name of the country where processing is delegated
  2. an understanding of that country's personal data protection regime, including any regime governing government access to data
  3. the measures taken in the light of that understanding. These include encryption in transit and at rest, checking that each provider's API terms exclude the data we send from model training by default, and checking how long each provider keeps that data

The names of the destination countries, an outline of the measures the destination providers take, and how often and by what means {{COMPANY}} verifies them, are provided on request. The list of countries and the measures taken are published under “Provision to third parties in foreign countries” in our Privacy policy.

#Managing processors and sub-processors

Where {{COMPANY}} delegates the handling of personal data externally, we set criteria for selecting the processor, establish by contract the security measures to be implemented and the conditions for sub-processing, and review their handling periodically. The same conditions are imposed on sub-processing.

For customers' meeting data, {{COMPANY}} acts as a party to whom the customer has delegated the handling of personal data. As part of supervising us as a processor, we recommend customers review this article. If your organisation needs contractual terms on how we process data, contact {{PRIVACY_EMAIL}}.

#Certifications and third-party assessments

The table below sets out the nature of each scheme and {{COMPANY}}'s position. {{COMPANY}} does not currently hold any certification or third-party assessment. For schemes not held, you cannot write “compliant”, “equivalent” or “meets the criteria”.

Scheme Nature Status
ISMS certification (ISO/IEC 27001 / JIS Q 27001) third-party certification against the international standard for information security management systems not held
ISO/IEC 27017 a standard on controls specific to cloud services, held in addition to ISMS certification not held
ISO/IEC 27018 a code of practice for protecting personal information in the cloud not held
Privacy Mark a domestic scheme in which JIPDEC certifies conformity with JIS Q 15001 not held
SOC 2 Type II report a report in which an audit firm expresses an opinion on the operation of internal controls over a period. Not a certification not held
ISMAP the security assessment scheme for government information systems. Anyone can check registration on the public list at the ISMAP portal not currently on the cloud service list

For schemes not held, we say: “we do not currently hold this. We will update this page as the position changes.” Whatever the certification position, the specific controls we implement — encryption, access control, logging, vulnerability management, incident response, processor management — are described in the sections of this article, and we are happy to answer your security questionnaire or individual questions. If you need more to go on, contact {{SUPPORT_EMAIL}}.

#Our policy on publishing incidents

Where an event amounting to a leak of personal data occurs, for personal data {{COMPANY}} handles on its own account (such as account information) we report it to the Personal Information Protection Commission and notify the individuals concerned under Article 26 of the Act on the Protection of Personal Information. For meeting data we handle on a customer's behalf, we notify the customer promptly and provide the information they need to report it and to notify the individuals concerned. The procedure is described in Security and privacy FAQs.

#Reporting vulnerabilities

If you become aware of a vulnerability in {{PRODUCT}}, contact {{SECURITY_EMAIL}}.

consent-security-privacy/security-privac.html:
These are the questions users and IT teams ask us most often about security and privacy in {{PRODUCT}}. Use them for pre-adoption review, processor selection, and explaining the service internally. For anything specific, write to {{SUPPORT_EMAIL}}.

Note

This article gives short answers. The detail of each category of security control measure and the certifications we hold are in Our security standards, and the detail of provision to third parties in foreign countries (cross-border transfer), including the destination countries, is in our Privacy policy.

Our security standardsThe detail of our security control measures→How far you can rely on AI meeting notesThe lawfulness of recording, and announcements→AI models and training dataWhether data is used for training→Use in healthcare, finance and professional servicesSector-specific regulation→

#Where data is stored, and transfer overseas

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 28(1) (restriction on provision to third parties in foreign countries)

Providing personal data to a third party in a foreign country requires the individual's prior consent as a rule. Without consent, the destination must either be a country recognised as having a level of protection equivalent to Japan's, or a party that has put in place arrangements meeting the standards set by Personal Information Protection Commission rules.These rules apply to provision accompanying delegation too. Article 27(5), which sets out the exceptions to the restriction on provision to third parties (delegation, business succession, joint use), is not among the exclusions from Article 28.

Q. Where is data stored?

A. The meeting notes, transcripts and account information held in {{PRODUCT}} are stored in a database in the Tokyo region. Application hosting and the encrypted backups are in the Tokyo region too. Stored data is held encrypted, and communication between devices and servers is encrypted too. Transcription and AI processing, however, are carried out by providers in the United States (see “Is personal data transferred overseas?” below).

If a recording could not be uploaded, the desktop app keeps its audio on your computer so it can be sent again. Protect the device with disk encryption and screen locking.

Q. Can we specify the storage region?

A. Not at present, on a per-customer basis. If you have a requirement here, speak to your account representative.

Q. Is personal data transferred overseas?

A. Yes. Transcription (including live captions) and AI processing such as writing notes and summaries, extracting information and answering chat questions are delegated to providers located in the United States (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, ElevenLabs and AssemblyAI), and the processing takes place there. PostHog (United States), which we use for usage analytics, also receives users' account details and records of how the app is used. Personal data is therefore transferred abroad.

There are three points worth understanding.

  1. The cross-border rules apply even where the provision accompanies delegation. Delegation within Japan is analysed as not constituting provision to a third party, but that exception does not operate where the recipient is a third party in a foreign country.
  2. The test is not where data is stored. Saying “the servers are in Japan, so there is no cross-border transfer” is not accurate; what matters is whether personal data is provided to a third party in a foreign country. Sending data to an inference API can be such a provision.
  3. {{COMPANY}} relies on having arrangements in place, not on consent. Obtaining individual consent from every meeting participant is impractical, so we provide data only to providers that have put in place arrangements meeting the standards set by Personal Information Protection Commission rules.

A comparison of the approaches, how often we verify destinations, what happens if we stop providing data, and the scope of information provided to individuals are set out under “Provision to third parties in foreign countries” in our Privacy policy. To request that information, contact {{PRIVACY_EMAIL}}.

Q. Where can I see the destination countries?

A. The destination country is the United States. The names of the destination countries, and the measures taken in the light of an understanding of those countries' regimes, are listed in our Privacy policy. For how {{COMPANY}} goes about that, see the “Understanding the external environment” section of Our security standards.

Q. Can we use it at overseas offices?

A. {{PRODUCT}} can be used from outside Japan. This article and the related ones are, however, written on the basis of Japanese law. If you need to address regulation specific to a location outside Japan, speak to your account representative.

#Requests relating to individuals' rights

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 33 (disclosure) / Article 34 (correction) / Article 35 (cessation of use) / Article 38 (fees)

An individual may request disclosure of retained personal data, its correction, addition or deletion, the cessation of its use, its erasure or the cessation of provision to third parties, and disclosure of records of provision to third parties. For disclosure, the individual may specify provision by electromagnetic record. Under Article 35(5), cessation of use may also be requested where there is no longer a need to use the data or where a leak has occurred. Fees may be charged only for notification of the purpose of use and for disclosure, not for correction or cessation of use.

Q. How do you handle disclosure, correction and cessation-of-use requests?

A. Write to {{PRIVACY_EMAIL}} with documentation confirming your identity. We accept requests from statutory representatives and from authorised agents.

Disclosure is made by provision of an electromagnetic record as a rule — either a download within {{PRODUCT}} or an email attachment. Tell us if you would prefer it on paper.

For requests for notification of the purpose of use and for disclosure, we may charge a fee reflecting our actual costs. No fee is charged for correction or cessation-of-use requests.

Q. Can I export all my own data?

A. Yes. You can download your own data in one go from Settings. Workspace admins can export the whole organisation's notes (Markdown) and data (JSON), and the data about one person (JSON). Much of a disclosure request can be handled by yourself this way.

Where you need disclosure of personal data not included in an export, write to {{PRIVACY_EMAIL}} marking it as a disclosure request.

Q. I want to change my name or email address

A. You can change it yourself in account settings. The steps are in Changing your account and email address. For fields you cannot change yourself, contact {{PRIVACY_EMAIL}}. No fee is charged for correction requests.

Q. A meeting participant has asked me to delete what they said

A. Part of a transcript cannot be deleted on its own. Move the meeting's note to the trash and delete it permanently (a note's owner or an admin can do this). The steps are in Deleting notes.

If everything {{PRODUCT}} has gathered about that person has to go, an admin can delete everything about the person from their person page; the person is then recorded so that later meetings do not rebuild them. Notes and transcripts that mention the person are not deleted by this, so delete those notes too if the request requires it.

Note that for meeting data held in {{PRODUCT}}, the authority to decide on deletion rests with the customer (the contracting company). A request from a meeting participant should as a rule be made to the organisation that created the record.

Q. How do I delete my account and all my data?

A. In the app, go to Settings → Profile → Delete account. The deletion takes place 30 days after you ask, and you can cancel it until then. Meetings placed in the organisation's folders and the like stay as the organisation's records. A whole organisation can be deleted by an admin in settings, with a 30-day grace period. If you cannot reach the app, contact {{SUPPORT_EMAIL}} and we will process it. For details see Deleting your account.

#If a leak occurs

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 26(1) and (2) (reporting leaks)

Where a leak, loss or damage of personal data occurs that is likely to substantially harm individuals' rights and interests, reporting to the Personal Information Protection Commission and notification of the individuals are required. For personal data handled under delegation, a processor is relieved of its own reporting duty once it has notified the delegating party. The Enforcement Regulations define four categories of reportable event: where sensitive personal information is involved, where there is a risk of financial harm, where the act was for an improper purpose, and where more than 1,000 individuals are affected. Each includes events that “may have” occurred.

Q. What are your arrangements for reporting a leak?

A. Where a leak, loss or damage of personal data occurs (including where it may have), {{COMPANY}} follows the Act on the Protection of Personal Information and its Enforcement Regulations.

  • For personal data handled under delegation from a customer (such as meeting data): we notify the customer promptly after becoming aware (as a guide, within roughly three to five days). That notification relieves {{COMPANY}} of its own duty to report to the Commission. A contract can also provide that {{COMPANY}} reports on the customer's behalf.
  • For personal data {{COMPANY}} handles on its own account: we make a prompt initial report to the Personal Information Protection Commission and submit the full report within 30 days of becoming aware (60 days where the act was for an improper purpose). Affected individuals are notified of the outline of the event, the categories of personal data involved, the cause, any secondary harm or risk of it, and other relevant matters.

“Promptly” for the initial report is a guideline benchmark; the 30 and 60 days for the full report are deadlines set by the Enforcement Regulations.

Q. Does a meeting transcript raise the reporting threshold?

A. Yes. Meeting transcripts can pick up sensitive personal information such as medical history or a criminal record. A leak of personal data containing sensitive personal information is reportable to the Commission even if it affects a single individual. That is what lowers the reporting threshold compared with other business SaaS. Encrypting data at rest is, among other things, a practical measure for managing that threshold.

Q. Are past incidents published?

#Security control measures

Q. What security control measures do you take?

A. {{COMPANY}} has a basic policy and handling rules for personal data in place, and implements measures following the categories set out in the guidelines under the Act on the Protection of Personal Information (organisational, personnel, physical and technical security measures, and understanding the external environment). The main ones are encryption in transit and at rest, access control limiting permissions to what the work requires, capturing and retaining access records, and continuous checking for vulnerabilities.

The specifics for each category are collected in Our security standards. You can use that page as-is for processor assessments and security questionnaires.

#Processors and sub-processors

Q. How do you supervise processors?

A. Where {{COMPANY}} delegates the handling of personal data externally, we do three things.

  1. set criteria for selecting a processor and confirm the standard of their security measures before selecting them
  2. enter into a contract covering security measures, the conditions for sub-processing, and reporting duties in the event of an incident
  3. review periodically how the processor handles personal data

Equivalent conditions are imposed on sub-processors.

Q. Are sub-processors disclosed?

A. Yes. The main sub-processors used to deliver {{PRODUCT}} are listed below. The current list, with each one's purpose, the personal data involved and where it is processed, is on our website's subprocessor list, where changes are announced at least 30 days in advance as a rule.

  • Vercel (application hosting, temporary storage of recordings; Tokyo region)
  • Supabase (database; Tokyo region)
  • Wasabi (encrypted backups; Tokyo region)
  • Anthropic, OpenAI and Google (writing notes and summaries, extracting information, answering chat questions and similar; United States)
  • ElevenLabs and AssemblyAI (transcription and live captions; United States)
  • PostHog (usage analytics; United States)
  • Stripe (payments) and Resend (sending email)
Q. Is {{COMPANY}} a processor or a third party?

A. For customers' meeting data, {{COMPANY}} acts as a party to whom the customer (the contracting company) has delegated the handling of personal data. Provision accompanying delegation is not provision to a third party, so the customer does not need to obtain third-party provision consent from meeting participants. Instead, the customer supervises us as a processor.

By contrast, where you use {{PRODUCT}}'s integrations to send a note to another service, the destination is not {{COMPANY}}'s processor but a separate provider. That send can constitute provision to a third party. For details see Integrations overview.

Q. Do you have a data processing addendum (DPA)?

A. If your organisation needs data processing terms, contact {{PRIVACY_EMAIL}}. For your meeting data, your organisation is the business handling the personal information, and {{COMPANY}} handles it on your behalf as a processor.

#Certifications and audits

Q. Which certifications do you hold?

A. {{COMPANY}} does not currently hold any certification or third-party assessment. The position on each scheme is collected in one place, in the “Certifications and third-party assessments” table in Our security standards. Please check that table for ISMS certification (ISO/IEC 27001), ISO/IEC 27017, ISO/IEC 27018, the Privacy Mark, a SOC 2 Type II report and ISMAP.

The schemes differ in nature. ISO/IEC 27001 is a third-party certification; ISO/IEC 27017 is an add-on to ISMS certification; ISO/IEC 27018 is a code of practice; the Privacy Mark is a domestic accreditation scheme run by JIPDEC; SOC 2 Type II is an audit firm's report, not a certification. ISMAP is an assessment scheme for government procurement, and anyone can check registration on the public list at the ISMAP portal. {{PRODUCT}} is not currently on the ISMAP cloud service list.

We never describe ourselves as “compliant with”, “equivalent to” or “meeting the criteria of” a scheme we do not hold. Whatever the certification position, the controls we implement are described specifically in Our security standards.

Q. Will you complete an audit or a security questionnaire?

A. Yes. Email {{SUPPORT_EMAIL}} with the form and the deadline. We will tell you what we can answer and whether a non-disclosure agreement is needed first.

Material you can pass to your IT department includes this article, Our security standards and Network troubleshooting.

Q. Our internal security product has blocked {{PRODUCT}}

A. Network troubleshooting lists the destinations that need adding to an allowlist, and the symptoms that appear when traffic is blocked or rewritten. Pass that page to your IT department.

It also helps, when explaining the service in a review, that {{PRODUCT}} sends no recording bot into meetings, runs on the user's own device, and encrypts its traffic.

Q. Is there a contact for reporting vulnerabilities?

A. {{SECURITY_EMAIL}}.

For vulnerabilities found in Japan, we also accept reports through the Information Security Early Warning Partnership run by the Information-technology Promotion Agency (IPA).

#The Telecommunications Business Act

LegislationTelecommunications Business Act, Article 27-12 (notification regarding instructions to transmit information)

Where a party intends to instruct a user's device to transmit information about the user to a third party, it must notify the user in advance, or put in a state where the user can readily ascertain, the content of the information transmitted, the name of the party handling it at the destination, and the purpose for which it is used. The services covered are set out in the Enforcement Regulations as four categories: services mediating others' communications, services transmitting at the request of unspecified users, search services, and services making content available for viewing by unspecified users.

Q. How do you comply with the external transmission rules?

A. {{PRODUCT}}'s website, web app and desktop app may send some information from your device to servers operated by providers other than {{COMPANY}}, for analytics and error detection. The information sent, the names of the providers handling it at the destination, and the purposes of use are listed on our “Disclosures regarding external transmission” page. If you would rather it were not sent, you can opt out by the method given on that page.

Meeting audio, transcribed text, and the body of the notes {{PRODUCT}} generates are not part of that analytics transmission. They are handled only to the extent needed to provide {{PRODUCT}}.

Q. Are you intercepting communications?

A. The {{PRODUCT}} desktop app captures the meeting audio playing on your computer and your microphone audio inside the computer itself. It is not a mechanism by which {{COMPANY}} sits in the meeting service's communication path intercepting the call. The audio captured is sent to {{PRODUCT}}'s servers for transcription and summary generation.

We treat the parts of {{PRODUCT}} that mediate exchanges between users — sharing and notification features — as subject to Article 4 of the Telecommunications Business Act (protection of secrecy). {{COMPANY}}'s officers and employees do not acquire, use or disclose information subject to the secrecy of communications learned in the course of their work, except where required by law or where there is other justifiable cause. That obligation continues after employment ends.

#Recording, consent and audio

Q. Is recording a meeting a criminal offence?

A. The Penal Code contains no provision punishing the recording of a conversation as such. Article 133 (opening sealed letters) covers opening a sealed letter, and Article 134 (disclosure of secrets) covers disclosure by members of a limited list of professions such as doctors and lawyers; neither applies to recording a meeting.

The Act on Wiretapping for Criminal Investigation likewise governs interception carried out by investigative authorities under a warrant issued by a judge, and does not apply to recording by a meeting's participants.

For the full analysis, see How far you can rely on AI meeting notes.

Q. Is consent required from everyone present?

A. Japanese law contains no provision generally requiring consent from everyone present to record a meeting. The legal obligations that do arise are: notifying or publishing the purpose of use of the personal information acquired; obtaining the individual's consent where sensitive personal information is acquired; and obtaining the individual's consent where the case amounts to provision to a third party.

That said, {{COMPANY}} strongly recommends telling participants that recording and transcription are taking place, even where there is no legal obligation. Wording you can use as-is is in How far you can rely on AI meeting notes. For the notice {{PRODUCT}} shows when you start recording, which you can paste into the meeting chat, see About telling people you are recording.

Q. Does a recording bot join the meeting?

A. No. {{PRODUCT}} runs on the user's own device and captures audio directly from the microphone and system audio. No unfamiliar account appears in the participant list for others to see, and the meeting host does not need to allow a bot to join.

Q. Is the audio stored?

A. Recorded audio is sent to {{PRODUCT}}'s servers (Tokyo region) for transcription and deleted as soon as transcription is finished. Audio left over from an upload that failed partway is deleted within 24 hours. What is stored is the transcript text.

For transcription and live captions, the audio is also sent to providers in the United States (ElevenLabs, AssemblyAI and OpenAI). If a recording could not be uploaded, the desktop app keeps its audio on your computer so it can be sent again.

Q. Can conversations be recorded unintentionally?

A. {{PRODUCT}} records when you take the action to start recording. If you have turned on “Start recording automatically” in settings (it is off by default), however, recording starts without a confirmation when the call of a meeting on your calendar starts (desktop apps). Calls with no scheduled meeting still ask first.

Recording can also continue where a meeting overruns or you forget to stop it. Press [Stop] when the meeting finishes. The conditions for starting and stopping are explained in How transcription works.

#Who can see a note

Q. Who can see my notes?

A. A note starts out private. A private note can be opened only by the person who created it, members of the same workspace who are attendees of that meeting, and admins. You can widen who sees it in these ways.

  • Place it in a folder (space): the members of that space can see it
  • Share it with a member: the people you share it with can see it
  • Turn on link sharing: members of the same workspace who have the link can see it (guests excepted)

There are no public links that let people outside the organisation, or people who are not signed in, open a note. The steps are in Sharing controls.

Q. Can an administrator or a colleague see my private notes?

A. Admins can open private notes too, for managing the organisation. When an admin opens a private note, it is recorded in the audit log and the note's owner is notified. A colleague who is not an admin cannot see your private notes unless the note is in a folder they belong to, shared with them, has link sharing turned on, or they attended the meeting.

Q. Does the MCP integration let colleagues see my notes?

A. The MCP integration goes through browser authorisation (OAuth) and reaches only notes you have permission to view. A colleague using the same product cannot reach your notes through it. For details see MCP integration.

#AI models and training

Q. Is data used to train AI models?

A. No. {{PRODUCT}} does not use customer data to train AI models, on any plan. The AI providers we delegate processing to (Anthropic, OpenAI and Google) also state in their API terms (for Google, the paid API) that data sent through the API is not used for training by default.

Unless an organisation's admin has switched it off, {{COMPANY}} may use customer data to evaluate and improve the service. Even then it is not used to train AI models. For details see AI models and training data.

Q. Can we stop our data being used to evaluate and improve the service?

A. Yes. A workspace admin can switch it off in settings, and the change takes effect within 30 days. When {{COMPANY}} staff look at your data, it is recorded in your organisation's audit log, which admins can see under Settings → Workspace → Audit log.

Q. Has our data been used for training in the past?

A. No. {{PRODUCT}} does not use customer data to train AI models, so there is no earlier data that could have been used for training.

#Retention and deletion

Q. How long are notes and transcripts kept?

A. Notes (including their transcripts), imported emails and chat messages are kept for the retention period set for your organisation. The default is 12 months; a workspace admin can change it to 6, 12, 24 or 36 months, or keep forever, under Settings → Workspace → General → Data retention. Notes whose meeting date is older than the period move to the trash automatically and are permanently deleted 30 days later (they can be restored until then). Imported emails and chat older than the period are permanently deleted automatically. For details see Automatic transcript deletion.

The Act on the Protection of Personal Information requires businesses to endeavour to erase personal data without delay once there is no longer a need to use it. We recommend deciding how long the business actually needs a record and setting the retention period accordingly.

Q. Is deleted data gone immediately?

A. It disappears from the screen immediately, but remains for a period in recovery backups and audit logs. Encrypted backups are kept for 30 days, so deleted data disappears from the backups within 30 days. Audit logs are held separately for investigating misuse; they contain only a record of who did what and when, not the body of deleted notes or transcripts (a deleted note's title and date are kept). This is also explained under “What remains after deletion” in Automatic transcript deletion.

#Authentication and account protection

Q. Do you support single sign-on (SSO)?

A. Single sign-on through SAML or similar is not supported. Sign-in goes through {{PRODUCT}} ID, with a Google account or an email address and password.

Q. Is there multi-factor authentication?

A. Yes. {{PRODUCT}} ID supports two-step verification with codes from an authenticator app (TOTP) and single-use backup codes. Each user can turn it on from Settings → Profile, which opens the {{PRODUCT}} ID page (it is optional). Once it is on, signing in with an email address and password asks for a code. If you sign in with Google, use Google's 2-Step Verification as well. Two-step verification is required for signing in to {{COMPANY}}'s own admin tools. How sign-in works is explained in Signing in and connecting your calendar.

Q. Can we set a password policy?

A. There is no per-organisation password policy setting. For sign-in with an email address and password, {{PRODUCT}} ID manages the password. For sign-in with Google, your Google account's policies apply.

Q. What security settings are available to administrators?

A. Workspace admins can do the following.

  • set the data retention period
  • switch use for evaluating and improving the service on or off (AI models and training data)
  • switch web research on external participants, and live captions, on or off
  • invite and remove members
  • review the audit log
  • export the whole organisation's notes and data, and export or delete everything about one person

There is no setting to require single sign-on (SSO) or to put an organisation-wide ceiling on sharing. Where to find the settings screen is covered in Workspaces.

#Questions by sector

Q. Can it be used in healthcare institutions, financial institutions or law firms?

A. How sector-specific regulation and guidelines apply is covered in Use in healthcare, finance and professional services. It explains that clinical information is sensitive personal information, and that healthcare institutions are subject to the three-ministry, two-guideline framework, financial institutions to the FISC security guidelines, and the professions to confidentiality obligations.

Q. Can it be used in schools and education?

A. {{COMPANY}} does not hold any certification or assessment specific to education. Information about enrolment and grades is personal information, so judge it against your school's personal data handling rules and the requirements of its governing body. We suggest starting with records of staff meetings and training, and drawing a line against using it where pupils' information is involved.

#If you cannot find an answer

If this article does not answer your question, contact {{SUPPORT_EMAIL}}. Requests concerning the handling of personal data go to {{PRIVACY_EMAIL}}, and vulnerability reports to {{SECURITY_EMAIL}}. For questions arising in a pre-adoption review, contact your account representative.
